subtopic_detail: Observation rather than treatment for isolated thrombocytopenia with cutaneous bleeding only
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy brought in by his father because of bruises. Over three days he has developed dozens of bruises on both shins and forearms and a rash of tiny red spots across his chest and back that do not fade when pressed.

He had a runny nose and cough a fortnight ago that settled without treatment. He had one nosebleed yesterday that stopped after five minutes of pressure. He has been running around the waiting room and eating a sandwich while you take the history. There is no fever today, no bone or joint pain, no night waking and no weight loss. There is no lymphadenopathy and no palpable liver or spleen edge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae over trunk and limbs, bruises over both shins and forearms, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 121 g/L (110-140), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), neutrophils 3.1 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), blood film shows large platelets with normal red and white cell morphology and no blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin followed by early outpatient review
Oral prednisolone for four days with early outpatient review
Platelet transfusion followed by admission for overnight observation
Bone marrow aspirate before any treatment decision is made
Observation with written safety advice and early outpatient review

subtopic_detail: Acting on an intermediate predictor score in an irritable hip rather than waiting for every criterion
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy who has refused to stand since yesterday morning. His mother says he screams if anyone moves his right leg and that he had a runny nose last week that has settled.

He lies with the right hip flexed and turned outwards and cries with any attempt to move it. He is drinking and interactive between examinations. There is no rash, no other joint involvement and no history of trauma. A hip ultrasound performed in the department shows a moderate right hip effusion with no effusion on the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, right hip held flexed and externally rotated, marked pain on passive internal rotation, no rash and no other joint involvement
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.5 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/hr (less than 15), blood culture collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent ultrasound guided hip aspiration before antibiotics are given
Start intravenous flucloxacillin now and arrange aspiration tomorrow
Admit for observation with analgesia and repeat bloods in 12 hours
Discharge with simple analgesia and general practice review in 48 hours
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before aspiration

subtopic_detail: Deciding oral against intravenous therapy for eyelid cellulitis on the basis of eye examination findings
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 5-year-old girl with two days of a red swollen right upper eyelid that started after her mother noticed an insect bite there.

The swelling has increased so that she now holds the eye half closed, though she opens it fully when asked. Her mother has held her home from school but reports she has eaten normally and been her usual self. Holding the lids apart, the conjunctiva is white, the eye moves fully in all directions without pain, the pupil reacts briskly with no relative afferent defect, and she reads the same line on the chart with each eye. The globe does not protrude and the redness stops at the bony rim of the orbit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right upper lid swelling and erythema confined within the orbital rim, no proptosis, full painless extraocular movements, no relative afferent pupillary defect, equal visual acuity both eyes, no chemosis
data_table.Investigations: Immunisations up to date including Haemophilus influenzae type b

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol drops with review again in 48 hours
Referral to ophthalmology for examination within the next week
Oral antibiotics as an outpatient with review again in 24 hours
Admission for intravenous antibiotics and review again in 24 hours
Computed tomography of the orbits before any antibiotic is started

subtopic_detail: Using a raised gonadotrophin to redirect the investigation of short stature with absent puberty
stem: A 14-year-old girl is the shortest in her year and has not menstruated. Her height is 143 cm, below the 1st centile, with falling height velocity since age eight.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 1 breast with stage 3 pubic hair, low posterior hairline, broad chest, cubitus valgus
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 68 IU/L (1-9), luteinising hormone 24 IU/L (0.1-6), oestradiol less than 40 pmol/L, thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send coeliac serology with thyroid function tests
Send a peripheral blood sample for karyotyping
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
Arrange a growth hormone stimulation test first
Start transdermal oestradiol and review in a year

subtopic_detail: Choosing a scabicide that is age appropriate for a young infant while treating the household
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6-week-old boy whose parents say he has been squirming and crying for the past fortnight and has a rash that is spreading.

He has small red bumps and some blistery spots across his trunk, and his mother shows you the same spots on the soles of both feet, the palms of both hands and across his scalp. Both parents describe intense itching at night that keeps them awake, and you can see thin wavy lines between the fingers of the mother's right hand. The baby is feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile and has no fever. There is no honey coloured crusting and no surrounding spreading redness.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous papules and vesicopustules over trunk, palms, soles and scalp, burrows visible in the mother's finger web spaces, no impetiginised crusting, no cellulitis, weight tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Oral ivermectin for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
Topical corticosteroid for the baby and permethrin for the parents
Oral cefalexin for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
Sulfur ointment for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
Permethrin 5 per cent cream for the baby and all household contacts

subtopic_detail: Reading periorbital bruising with an abdominal mass as metastatic disease rather than injury
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother felt a lump in her tummy while bathing her three days ago.

Over the past month she has been pale and grizzly, has stopped wanting to walk to the park and has been limping on and off without any fall the family can recall. She has purple discolouration around both eyes that her mother assumed came from tripping over a toy a fortnight ago. On examination there is a firm irregular mass in the left upper abdomen that extends across the midline and does not move with respiration. Her blood pressure is normal for age and there is no blood on urine dipstick.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular fixed abdominal mass extending across the midline, bilateral periorbital ecchymoses with no lid swelling or tenderness, pallor, no hepatomegaly, antalgic gait
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), urine dipstick negative for blood and protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a full blood count and arrange orthopaedic review of the limp
Arrange coagulation studies and review the bruising in one week
Send urinary catecholamine metabolites and arrange abdominal imaging
Arrange abdominal ultrasound and send urine for microscopy only
Arrange a skeletal survey for non accidental injury before imaging

subtopic_detail: Treating household threadworm when the index child is below the age threshold for anthelmintics
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-month-old girl whose 4-year-old brother was diagnosed with threadworm a week ago and treated at the pharmacy.

Her mother says the baby has been waking and squirming after midnight for the past four nights, and two nights ago she saw several fine white threads moving around the baby's bottom when she changed her. The baby is feeding well and has gained weight along her centile line. There is no diarrhoea, no blood in the nappy and no fever. The perianal skin is slightly red from scratching with no discharge, no ulceration and no crusting.

data_table.Examination: Mild perianal erythema, no excoriation breach, no discharge, no lymphadenopathy, weight tracking along the 40th centile
data_table.Investigations: Household of five including two adults and three children aged 5 months, 4 years and 7 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Permethrin cream for the baby and mebendazole for the household
Faecal microscopy for the baby before any treatment is started
Hygiene measures for the baby and mebendazole for the household
Mebendazole for the baby and for all household members now
Mebendazole for the baby now and a repeat dose in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Radiographic hip surveillance interval in a non ambulant child with spastic cerebral palsy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a complex care clinic reviewing a 5-year-old girl with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy. She has never taken independent steps, is transported in a moulded seating system and needs support to sit.

Her parents say she seems comfortable, sits happily in her chair through a school day and does not cry with nappy changes or dressing. Passive hip abduction is 45 degrees on each side with no fixed deformity and her legs are the same length. Her last pelvic radiograph was at eighteen months of age and reported no abnormality. She has had no hip imaging since, because she has never complained of pain.

data_table.Examination: Passive hip abduction 45 degrees bilaterally, no leg length discrepancy, no pain on hip range of movement, unable to sit unsupported
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic radiograph at eighteen months of age reported as normal, no imaging since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management of her hips?

options.text: Pelvic radiograph now and every six months with migration percentage measured
Pelvic radiograph only when hip pain or loss of abduction is noticed
Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips now and again at skeletal maturity
Ultrasound of both hips every six months to avoid repeated radiation
Refer for botulinum toxin to the hip adductors and review clinically in a year

subtopic_detail: Interpreting raised transaminases of muscle origin in a boy with motor delay
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver blood tests found while investigating tiredness. He walked at 19 months and his mother says he still cannot keep up in the playground and asks to be carried home from kindergarten.

To stand from sitting on the floor he rolls onto his front, pushes up onto his hands and feet and then walks his hands up his thighs. His calves feel firm and look larger than expected for his build. He speaks in short sentences and his kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about his language. Abdominal examination finds no hepatomegaly, an abdominal ultrasound is normal and his gamma glutamyl transferase is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Rises from the floor by climbing up his own legs, waddling gait, firm enlarged calves, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 310 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 285 U/L (less than 45), gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits, creatine kinase 14200 U/L (less than 200), abdominal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with electromyography of the proximal muscles
Muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunohistochemistry and western blot
Percutaneous liver biopsy to characterise the raised transaminase pattern
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to investigate the language delay
Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene for deletions and duplications

subtopic_detail: Timing the first retinal examination in an extremely preterm infant
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar on the special care nursery round. A girl born at 24 weeks and 2 days gestation weighing 620 g is now 28 days old and stable on continuous positive airway pressure in 25 per cent oxygen.

Her mother asks when her daughter's eyes will be checked, because a friend's baby had eye examinations in hospital. The infant received supplemental oxygen from birth, has had two courses of antibiotics for suspected sepsis and is tolerating expressed breast milk feeds. Growth is tracking along the third centile for corrected age. No ophthalmology review has been arranged so far.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 52/30 mmHg, respiratory rate 54 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in 25 per cent oxygen, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (140-220 at birth), cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: When should her first retinal examination be performed?

options.text: Now, since she has already reached four weeks of postnatal age
Only if supplemental oxygen is still required beyond 28 days of life
At term corrected age, when the retina has completed vascularisation
In the week before discharge home, with outpatient follow up afterwards
At 31 weeks postmenstrual age, which for her falls in about three weeks

subtopic_detail: Escalating beyond phototherapy when neurological signs accompany severe hyperbilirubinaemia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department for a 4-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth. His mother says he has gone a deep yellow colour, has fed poorly since yesterday and has a cry she describes as sharp and different from before.

He was discharged at 36 hours of age when he looked well. Today he is difficult to rouse for a feed, and when you lift him his neck arches backwards and his back stiffens before he settles. Intensive phototherapy was started twenty minutes ago on arrival. His mother is blood group O positive and the baby is A positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 465 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 12 micromol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (140-220), reticulocytes raised, direct antiglobulin test positive, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue intensive phototherapy alone and repeat the bilirubin in four hours
Give intravenous immunoglobulin and continue intensive phototherapy
Stop breastfeeding, give formula feeds and continue intensive phototherapy
Arrange urgent exchange transfusion while intensive phototherapy continues
Commence phenobarbital to induce hepatic conjugation and observe overnight

subtopic_detail: Managing a self limiting viral skin eruption in a child with coexisting dermatitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 5-year-old boy whose mother is upset about spots that keep spreading. They started as three bumps behind his knee eight weeks ago and there are now about thirty across his trunk, arms and both knee creases.

The lesions are 2 to 4 mm, dome shaped, skin coloured and each has a small central dimple. Several sit within patches of dry, scaly, itchy skin that his mother treats intermittently with a moisturiser she buys at the supermarket. He is otherwise well, eats and plays normally, and has not been unwell. His mother has been told by the swimming school that he cannot return until the spots are gone, and she asks you to freeze them off today.

data_table.Examination: Approximately thirty dome shaped umbilicated papules 2 to 4 mm across the trunk, arms and popliteal fossae, surrounding dry scaly erythematous patches, no pustules, no surrounding cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for ten days to cover secondary bacterial infection
Treat each lesion with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy at today's appointment
Prescribe topical imiquimod cream applied three nights a week for sixteen weeks
Explain the natural course and treat the surrounding dermatitis with topical corticosteroid
Refer for curettage of all lesions under general anaesthesia within the month

subtopic_detail: Napkin eruption that involves the skin folds and has not responded to barrier and steroid
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 7-month-old girl whose mother says her bottom has been raw for a fortnight and is getting worse rather than better. She has been changing the nappy more often and applying a zinc barrier cream at every change, and has used 1 per cent hydrocortisone ointment twice daily for the last five days.

The napkin area shows confluent beefy red erythema that extends deep into both inguinal creases and the natal cleft, with a scattering of small red papules and a few pustules on normal looking skin several centimetres beyond the main rash. There are no erosions, no bullae and no perianal fissures. She finished a course of amoxicillin for otitis media three weeks ago. She is afebrile, feeding well and thriving.

data_table.Examination: Confluent erythema involving both inguinal creases and the natal cleft, satellite papules and pustules on adjacent normal skin, oral cavity clear
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Change to a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied twice daily for a week
Continue the barrier preparation alone and change the nappy more frequently
Prescribe oral fluconazole as a single weight based dose with review in a week
Apply topical mupirocin ointment three times daily for seven days to the area
Apply a topical imidazole antifungal cream at each nappy change with the barrier

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of recurrent apnoea in a stable preterm infant
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a boy born at 28 weeks and 3 days gestation, now 11 days old and 1180 g. Nursing staff report six episodes over the last 24 hours in which he stops breathing for around 20 seconds, the heart rate falls into the 80s and the saturation dips, each recovering with gentle tactile stimulation.

The episodes began on day three and have been gradually more frequent. He is in room air with no increased work of breathing between episodes, tolerating full enteral feeds of expressed breast milk, and gaining weight. A septic screen two days ago including blood culture was negative and his C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage, his blood glucose has been consistently normal and his haemoglobin is 132 g/L. He has not yet received any respiratory stimulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute between episodes, blood pressure 54/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), blood culture no growth at 48 hours, haemoglobin 132 g/L, glucose within normal limits, cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin pending cultures
Commence caffeine citrate with a loading dose followed by daily maintenance
Commence nasal continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cm of water pressure
Commence a proton pump inhibitor and thicken feeds to treat gastro oesophageal reflux
Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude seizures presenting as apnoea

subtopic_detail: Imaging an infant with hip risk factors after the neonatal examination signs have disappeared
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 10-week-old girl at her first specialist appointment. She was born at 39 weeks in the frank breech position by caesarean section, and her mother was treated for hip dysplasia as a baby.

Her newborn examination in hospital was documented as normal, and no imaging was arranged because no clunk was felt. Today Ortolani and Barlow tests produce no clunk on either side. There is an extra skin crease on the left thigh compared with the right, hip abduction is 70 degrees on the right and 55 degrees on the left, and with the hips and knees flexed the left knee sits slightly lower than the right. She feeds and grows normally and moves both legs.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow negative bilaterally, left hip abduction 55 degrees and right 70 degrees, asymmetric left thigh crease, left knee lower on Galeazzi testing
data_table.Investigations: No imaging performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents, since the neonatal and current examinations were both normal
Arrange an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph before the orthopaedic appointment
Arrange hip ultrasound and refer to a paediatric orthopaedic service
Fit a Pavlik harness now and review the hip clinically in six weeks
Repeat the clinical examination at six months of age and image only if abnormal

subtopic_detail: Imaging the hip when an adolescent presents with knee pain and a limp
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy brought by his mother with six weeks of aching in the left knee that is worse at the end of a school day. He weighs 74 kg and his body mass index sits well above the 97th centile.

He has not fallen or been tackled and the pain came on without an injury. He walks with the left foot turned outwards and swings the leg through rather than bending it normally. The left knee looks and feels the same as the right, with no effusion, no joint line tenderness, full flexion and extension and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip, the leg rotates outwards on its own and he stops you at about 60 degrees because of groin discomfort. He is afebrile and his C reactive protein is 3 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), knee examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Anteroposterior and frog leg lateral radiographs of both hips
Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the symptomatic left knee
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee to assess for a meniscal tear
Ultrasound of both hips to look for an effusion in the joint
No imaging, with referral to physiotherapy for anterior knee pain rehabilitation

subtopic_detail: Treating a mite infestation across a household rather than the presenting child alone
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy whose mother says he scratches himself raw every night and barely sleeps, though he seems settled during the day. The rash started about five weeks ago.

There are excoriated red papules across his trunk and limbs, and on close inspection short wavy grey lines a few millimetres long between the fingers and along both wrist creases. There are firm red nodules in both axillae. His mother says her own arms have started itching this week and his 6-year-old sister has been scratching for a fortnight. He is otherwise well, afebrile, and there is no honey coloured crusting or surrounding cellulitis. He weighs 15 kg.

data_table.Examination: Burrows in the finger webs and wrist flexures, excoriated papules on the trunk and limbs, nodules in both axillae, no crusting or spreading erythema
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply 5 per cent permethrin cream to the child and every household member on one day
Apply 5 per cent permethrin cream to the child alone and review him in one week
Give a single weight based dose of oral ivermectin repeated after two weeks
Apply undiluted 25 per cent benzyl benzoate emulsion overnight to the whole family
Prescribe a moderately potent topical corticosteroid and an oral antihistamine at night

subtopic_detail: Selecting the test that a chromosomal microarray will not detect in developmental delay
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a developmental clinic reviewing a 4-year-old boy referred with global developmental delay. He said his first words at three, flaps both hands when excited, avoids looking at faces and covers his ears at the kindergarten music session.

His mother mentions that her brother lives in supported accommodation and has never been given a diagnosis, and that her own mother stopped having periods at 38 and now has a hand tremor and an unsteady walk. His face is long with prominent ears and his finger joints hyperextend. A chromosomal microarray requested by the general practitioner has returned with no pathogenic copy number variants. Newborn screening was normal and his hearing test at three was normal.

data_table.Examination: Long face with prominent ears, joint hypermobility, hand flapping, reduced eye contact, no dysmorphic features of a recognised chromosomal syndrome
data_table.Investigations: Chromosomal microarray with no pathogenic copy number variants, newborn screening normal, audiology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum creatine kinase with thyroid function and a full blood count
Standard karyotype with G banding on a peripheral blood sample
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain under general anaesthesia
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids with an acylcarnitine profile
FMR1 CGG repeat analysis performed on a peripheral blood sample

subtopic_detail: Oxygen saturation target in established chronic neonatal lung disease before discharge
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar planning discharge for a boy born at 26 weeks and 5 days gestation who is now 38 weeks postmenstrual age and 2.6 kg. He remains on 0.15 L per minute of nasal prong oxygen and has needed supplemental oxygen every day since birth.

He feeds fully by breast and bottle, has had no apnoeas for three weeks and caffeine was stopped a fortnight ago. In air he settles at saturations of 89 to 91 per cent while asleep, and on his current flow he sits at 95 per cent. His weight has crossed from the 25th to the 5th centile over the last month despite fortified feeds of 160 mL per kilogram per day. A recent echocardiogram shows normal right ventricular pressures. His parents live four hours from the tertiary centre and are keen to go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on 0.15 L per minute nasal prong oxygen, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram with normal right ventricular pressure and no tricuspid regurgitation jet, haemoglobin 118 g/L, chest radiograph with diffuse haziness and coarse interstitial markings

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for his oxygen therapy?

options.text: Wean to room air before discharge and accept saturations of 89 to 91 per cent
Continue oxygen at saturations of at least 93 per cent and arrange home oxygen
Commence a tapering course of systemic dexamethasone to allow oxygen weaning
Start long term oral furosemide with potassium supplementation and wean oxygen
Increase the flow to target saturations above 97 per cent until the growth improves

subtopic_detail: Collapse on day five in a term baby with weak femoral pulses and a pre and post ductal saturation difference
stem: A 5-day-old term boy fed poorly since yesterday and went grey and floppy during a feed. Blood cultures are taken and 10 mL/kg of sodium chloride given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176 /min, respiratory rate 68 /min, SpO2 96% right hand and 88% left foot
data_table.Examination: Mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, barely palpable femoral pulses, liver 3 cm palpable
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18, lactate 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Give repeated fluid boluses and antibiotics for septic shock
Intubate and ventilate with a high inspired oxygen concentration
Start prostaglandin E1 and involve paediatric cardiology
Give intravenous furosemide to offload the circulation
Arrange an echocardiogram in the morning and continue supportive care

subtopic_detail: Eye surveillance planning for a young girl with antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular arthritis
stem: A 4-year-old girl has had a swollen right knee for ten weeks with morning stiffness. She has no eye symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with 15 degree fixed flexion contracture, small left ankle effusion, eyes white and quiet
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her eyes?

options.text: Review only if her eyes become red, painful or photophobic
Arrange annual optometry review of her visual acuity
Refer for slit lamp examination now, then three monthly
Screen her eyes at the same interval as her joint reviews
Start oral prednisolone and rely on it to suppress the eyes

subtopic_detail: Low pre feed glucose at two hours of age in an asymptomatic small for gestational age term baby
stem: A girl born at 38 weeks weighing 2350 g, below the third centile, is 2 hours old. She latched briefly but tired quickly.

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal tone and strong suck, no jitteriness or distress
data_table.Investigations: Pre feed blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L on a laboratory calibrated analyser

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous glucose bolus and maintenance infusion in the nursery
A formula top up alone, repeating glucose before the next feed
Continue skin to skin care and recheck before the next feed
Buccal dextrose gel with a feed, rechecking glucose in thirty minutes
Send a critical sample for insulin, cortisol and ketones first

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of early morning headache with vomiting and a new head tilt in a school aged child
stem: An 8-year-old boy has had six weeks of headaches that wake him before dawn, with vomiting twice a week that eases the headache. For a fortnight he has held his head tilted to the left.

data_table.Examination: Left sixth cranial nerve palsy, unsteady tandem gait, indistinct optic disc margins, normal power and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start migraine prophylaxis and review the diary in four weeks
Refer to an optometrist for vision assessment and glasses
Prescribe an antiemetic and reassure that the pattern will settle
Lumbar puncture for opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
Urgent same day neuroimaging with immediate neurosurgical discussion

subtopic_detail: Joint pains and fever after a sore throat in a child from a high incidence community with echocardiographic valve changes
stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a high incidence remote community had an untreated sore throat two weeks ago. For five days he has had migratory aching in both knees, both ankles and one wrist. No joint is swollen, red or hot.

data_table.Investigations: ESR 62 mm/h, antistreptolysin O markedly elevated, PR interval 220 ms
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiogram: mild mitral regurgitation meeting pathological criteria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Acute rheumatic fever; four weekly benzathine benzylpenicillin
Streptococcal pharyngitis; ten days of oral penicillin
Reactive arthritis; non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Defer diagnosis; repeat echocardiography in four weeks
Viral illness; review at the community clinic in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Bedwetting five nights a week in a seven year old who has never been reliably dry overnight
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old boy and his mother about bedwetting. He wets on about five nights a week and has never had more than three consecutive dry nights.

He has no daytime wetting, no urgency and no straining, and he opens his bowels daily with soft stools. He drinks most of his fluid after school because he does not like the school toilets. He is otherwise well, growing along the fiftieth centile and doing well at school, and he has recently started refusing sleepovers with his cousins. Examination of his abdomen, spine, lower limb neurology and external genitalia is normal, and his urine dipstick shows no glucose, protein, blood, nitrites or leucocytes. His mother is willing to be woken at night and the family is committed to a treatment plan.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable faecal loading, normal lumbosacral spine with no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose, protein, blood, nitrites and leucocytes; bladder diary shows normal daytime voiding frequency and volumes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe desmopressin each night and continue it until he has been dry for three consecutive months
Start oxybutynin at night to increase his functional bladder capacity while he is asleep
Arrange an enuresis alarm program with structured family support and review after several weeks
Advise that he drinks nothing after four in the afternoon and reassess the pattern in three months
Refer him to a paediatric urologist for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic assessment first

subtopic_detail: Immunisation planning for a well four year old newly arrived in Australia with no written vaccination records
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4-year-old girl who arrived in Australia six weeks ago with her family after two years in a refugee camp. She is being enrolled in kindergarten next month.

Her mother believes she received some injections as a baby but has no documentation and no way of contacting the clinic that gave them. The child is thriving, has had no serious illness and takes no medication, and she has never had an allergic reaction to a vaccine or to egg. Her examination is normal and her growth is on the twenty fifth centile for height and weight. Her mother is anxious that the child should not receive injections she has already had.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and thriving, no chronic illness, no immunosuppression, no scars suggestive of previous vaccination, no allergies
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination normal, no immunisation record available on the Australian Immunisation Register

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her immunisation?

options.text: Wait until documentary evidence of her previous vaccinations can be obtained from her country of origin
Perform serology for every vaccine preventable disease and immunise only against those she lacks
Give one vaccine at each visit at monthly intervals to minimise the chance of an adverse reaction
Treat her as unvaccinated and begin an age-appropriate catch up schedule at today's visit
Give only the vaccines required for kindergarten entry now and complete the remainder after she settles

subtopic_detail: Short stature with absent pubertal signs in a fourteen year old boy whose bone age is markedly delayed
stem: A 14-year-old boy is the smallest in his year. He has grown 4.5 cm in each of the past two years, parallel to but below the third centile. His father did not shave until 19.

data_table.Examination: Height 149 cm on the third centile, testicular volume 3 mL, full visual fields
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology and thyroid function normal; bone age 11 years 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence growth hormone, monitor growth velocity
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
Request a karyotype and gonadotropin levels
Give three months of low dose testosterone
Explain the pattern and review six monthly

subtopic_detail: Imaging decisions after a first febrile urinary tract infection that responded promptly in an eight month old
stem: An 8-month-old girl is reviewed ten days after her first urinary tract infection: three days of fever to 39.2 degrees C, a catheter specimen growing Escherichia coli, and afebrile within 30 hours of oral antibiotics. Antenatal ultrasound scans were normal.

data_table.Examination: Well, thriving on the 50th centile, normal abdomen and blood pressure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: No routine imaging; advise prompt urine testing with any future fever
Renal tract ultrasound now to exclude a structural abnormality
Dimercaptosuccinic acid scan in four to six months for renal scarring
Micturating cystourethrogram to look for vesicoureteric reflux
Nightly trimethoprim prophylaxis until her second birthday

subtopic_detail: Sudden severe scrotal pain overnight in an adolescent with an absent cremasteric reflex
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 14-year-old boy who woke at two in the morning with severe left scrotal pain and has vomited twice. It is now five hours since the pain began and he is pale and reluctant to walk.

He has had no dysuria, no urethral discharge, no fever and no recent trauma, and he is not sexually active. He describes a similar but briefer episode three months ago that settled after twenty minutes. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and exquisitely tender with the testis sitting higher than the right and lying transversely. There is no cremasteric reflex on the left and elevating the testis does not relieve his pain. His urine dipstick is negative for nitrites and leucocytes. The on call surgical team is in the hospital and theatre is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left testis high riding and transverse, exquisitely tender, absent left cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation, right testis normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and act on the findings when they are available
Refer him for immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum with bilateral fixation as indicated
Start oral antibiotics for epididymo orchitis and review him in the clinic within 48 hours
Give strong analgesia and reassess him in the morning when the surgical clinic list is running
Send a first pass urine sample for nucleic acid testing and treat according to the result obtained

subtopic_detail: Loose soiling most days of the week in a well grown six year old who opens his bowels fully only every eight to ten days
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general outpatient clinic seeing a 6-year-old boy whose parents have brought him because he has been soiling his underwear four or five days a week for three months. They describe the soiling as loose and runny and think he has ongoing diarrhoea, and his teacher has twice sent him home from school.

He opens his bowels fully into the toilet about once every eight to ten days, and his mother says those motions are so large they block the toilet. He passed meconium on the first day of life and his weight and height have tracked along the 50th centile throughout. His lower back and neurological examination are normal, and his abdomen is soft with a firm mass palpable in the left iliac fossa. His general practitioner prescribed a fixed low dose stool softener which the family gave for four weeks without any change.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with a firm non-tender mass in the left iliac fossa, normal perianal appearance and anal position, normal lower back with no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes
data_table.Growth: Weight and height both on the 50th centile with no change in centile over two years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange an abdominal radiograph to confirm the extent of faecal loading
Refer for a rectal suction biopsy to exclude an aganglionic segment
Start an escalating oral macrogol regimen with a scheduled toileting plan
Give a phosphate enema now before starting any maintenance treatment
Prescribe a daily stimulant laxative alone and review him in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of knee pain and a limp in a heavy twelve year old whose knee examination is entirely normal
stem: A 12-year-old boy has six weeks of worsening left knee pain and a limp, with no injury. His weight is above the 97th centile. A knee radiograph two weeks ago was normal.

data_table.Examination: Normal left knee; the hip flexes into obligate external rotation and internal rotation is painful
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee and review with the result
Ultrasound of the left hip to look for a joint effusion
Simple analgesia and activity modification with review in four weeks
Urgent pelvis radiographs and strict non weight bearing
Blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics for a joint infection

subtopic_detail: A lumbosacral dimple with a hair tuft found at the newborn check in a baby with a normal neurological examination
stem: A 2-day-old term boy has a mark on his lower back noted at the newborn check. He feeds well and has passed urine and meconium.

data_table.Examination: Single midline lumbosacral dimple 6 mm across, base not visible, 35 mm above the anal verge, adjacent tuft of dark hair; normal tone and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents that no imaging or follow-up is needed
Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine under general anaesthetic
Review at the six-week check and image only if symptoms appear
Plain radiograph of the lumbosacral spine before discharge
Spinal ultrasound within the first three months of life

subtopic_detail: Deciding whether a six year old using reliever three to four times a week has crossed the threshold for regular preventer treatment
stem: A 6-year-old boy with asthma uses salbutamol via spacer as needed, with no preventer. Over three months he has used it three or four times most weeks, wakes coughing twice a month, has missed two school days and stops partway through soccer. Spacer technique is correct.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear with no wheeze at rest, SpO2 98 per cent in air

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue as-needed salbutamol and recheck technique
Start an inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta2 agonist
Start montelukast 5 mg each evening as preventer
Start a two week course of oral prednisolone and review
Start a regular low dose inhaled corticosteroid

subtopic_detail: Jaundice persisting at four weeks in a thriving breastfed baby whose parents describe pale nappies and dark wee
stem: A four-week-old exclusively breastfed girl is still jaundiced and has gained 780 g since birth. Her parents report pale creamy stools for two weeks and urine that stains the nappy dark yellow.

data_table.Examination: Alert, jaundiced sclerae, liver edge 2 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 62 micromol/L; newborn screening normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer today to a paediatric liver service for urgent investigation
Reassure this is breast milk jaundice and review in two weeks
Start phototherapy and repeat the serum bilirubin in twelve hours
Check thyroid function and repeat the bilirubin in one week
Request an outpatient abdominal ultrasound at the next appointment

subtopic_detail: A groin lump that comes and goes with crying in a six week old born at 32 weeks, alongside an incidental umbilical swelling
stem: A 6-week-old boy born at 32 weeks has a right groin lump, first seen four days ago, that appears when he cries and disappears when he settles. He is thriving.

data_table.Examination: Soft easily reducible swelling above and lateral to the right pubic tubercle, non-tender; testes descended; 15 mm reducible umbilical swelling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the groin swelling?

options.text: Reassure and review both swellings at twelve months
Arrange an ultrasound of the groin before deciding on referral
Refer to a paediatric surgeon for repair within days
Refer for elective repair after his first birthday
Apply a supportive binder and review him in six weeks

subtopic_detail: A toddler refusing to use an arm after being swung by the hands, but with elbow swelling and bony point tenderness
stem: A 2-year-old girl was swung by her hands between two adults and has not used her left arm since. Her grandmother adds she also came off a slide onto grass.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held adducted, forearm pronated; swelling and marked point tenderness over the lateral bony prominence of the elbow; no wrist tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hyperpronation manoeuvre, then reassess the arm after fifteen minutes
Elbow radiographs before attempting any reduction manoeuvre
Broad arm sling with review in the fracture clinic next week
Supination and flexion manoeuvre, then a collar and cuff
Ultrasound of the elbow to look for a joint effusion first

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of nappy area rash unresponsive to barrier cream that now involves the skin creases with satellite lesions
stem: A 9-month-old boy has had a nappy rash for three weeks despite a thick zinc barrier cream at every change. It improved briefly and has since spread.

data_table.Examination: Confluent bright erythema over buttocks and perineum extending into the inguinal and gluteal creases; satellite papules and pustules on the lower abdomen; adherent white plaques on the tongue

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: A topical imidazole antifungal cream at every nappy change
A potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily
Oral cefalexin for five days with the barrier cream
Continue the barrier cream and review in two weeks
A single dose of oral fluconazole with the barrier cream

subtopic_detail: A long narrow head with a palpable ridge in a five month old whose ears are symmetrical and whose head circumference is tracking normally
stem: A 5-month-old boy is referred because his head has looked long and narrow since six weeks of age and has not changed with repositioning. He was born at term and his development is normal.

data_table.Examination: Elongated narrow skull with frontal prominence and occipital pointing, ears symmetrically placed, firm midline sagittal ridge
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 75th centile, tracking since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise repositioning and tummy time, review in three months
Refer urgently to a paediatric craniofacial service
Refer for a moulding helmet fitted over one month
Reassure the parents that this is a normal variant
Arrange cranial ultrasound to assess the sutures

subtopic_detail: Pallor and irritability in a toddler drinking over a litre of cow's milk daily with a ferritin of 6
stem: A 22-month-old boy has been pale, irritable and tired for three months and no longer wants to walk far. He drinks about 1.2 litres of cow's milk a day and refuses meat and vegetables. His stools are normal.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L, mean cell volume 62 fL, ferritin 6 microg/L, coeliac serology negative with normal total immunoglobulin A

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the full blood count
Arrange a single dose intravenous iron infusion as a day procedure
Request haemoglobin electrophoresis before any specific treatment
Start oral iron and limit cow's milk to 500 mL daily
Refer for upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy

subtopic_detail: Persistent toe walking at five with bulky calves and a boy who climbs up his own legs to stand
stem: A 5-year-old boy has always walked on his toes. He walked at 18 months, cannot keep up on the oval and needs a rail on stairs. Rising from the floor, he walks his hands up his own thighs.

data_table.Examination: Bulky firm calves, ankle dorsiflexion 5 degrees with knee extended, normal tone and reflexes, downgoing plantar responses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for serial casting to improve ankle range
Refer to orthopaedics for Achilles tendon lengthening
Measure his serum creatine kinase before any treatment
Refer to physiotherapy and review in six months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of his brain

subtopic_detail: A rapidly growing red lesion on the upper eyelid of a three month old that partly closes the eye when she is tired
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3-month-old girl whose parents are worried about a mark on her left upper eyelid. It was a faint pink patch at two weeks of age that they were told would fade, and it has been growing steadily since.

It is now a bright red raised lesion measuring 22 mm across the upper lid. Her mother has photographs on her phone showing it has roughly doubled in size in the past six weeks. By the end of the day, when the child is tired, the lesion droops enough that the upper lid covers the top half of the pupil, and her parents have noticed she prefers to look to the right. The lesion is soft, compressible, not ulcerated and not tender. She was born at 34 weeks and is otherwise thriving and developing normally, and there are no other similar lesions on her skin.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible non ulcerated lesion 22 mm across the left upper eyelid causing mechanical ptosis over the superior half of the pupil when tired, no other cutaneous lesions, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Growth: Weight and length on the 25th centile corrected for gestation, development appropriate for corrected age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her when she is twelve months old
Apply topical timolol gel twice daily and review her in six weeks
Refer her for surgical excision of the lesion in the next few weeks
Refer her for pulsed dye laser treatment over the coming months
Refer her urgently for assessment and oral propranolol treatment

subtopic_detail: A head circumference crossing from the 50th to above the 97th centile over three months with a tense fontanelle and vomiting
stem: A five-month-old boy has vomited most mornings for a fortnight. His head circumference was on the 50th centile at three months and is above the 97th today. He has stopped holding his head up.

data_table.Examination: Fontanelle full and tense when upright, prominent scalp veins, downward eye deviation; no retinal haemorrhages
data_table.Growth: Father's head circumference 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that this is benign familial macrocephaly and review monthly
Arrange urgent neuroimaging and discuss with a neurosurgical service
Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection before imaging
Request an outpatient MRI brain at the next appointment
Measure the head circumference again in four weeks and plot it

subtopic_detail: rapidly enlarging vascular birthmark over the upper eyelid obscuring part of the visual axis at ten weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10-week-old girl whose parents point out a red raised lesion on her left upper eyelid. It was a faint pink patch at two weeks and has grown noticeably each week since.

The lesion is now 15 mm across, bright red, raised and compressible, and it partly covers the upper half of the pupil when she is upright and relaxed. It is not ulcerated and not bleeding. She was born at term, is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile. There is no other lesion on the skin, no bruit over the liver, no stridor and no other abnormality on examination, and the rest of the eye looks normal with a symmetrical red reflex. Her parents say a relative was told to leave a similar mark alone because it would disappear on its own.

data_table.Examination: 15 mm raised compressible bright red lesion of the left upper eyelid partly covering the upper pupil, no ulceration, symmetrical red reflex
data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Other findings: No additional cutaneous lesions, no hepatic bruit, no stridor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her at the 12 month immunisation visit for regression
Apply topical timolol gel twice daily and photograph the lesion weekly at home
Refer urgently for oral propranolol with cardiovascular screening and ophthalmology review
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and neck before starting any treatment
Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment as the definitive management of the lesion

subtopic_detail: loss of consciousness after a sudden fright with pallor preceding the event and a brief stiffening
stem:
You are the doctor in an emergency department. A 16-month-old boy is brought in after an episode at home. He bumped his head lightly on a table, looked startled, went pale and limp within seconds without crying out, and lost consciousness for about 20 seconds with some stiffening of his arms.

He came round on his own and was back to normal within a few minutes, with no drowsiness and no confusion afterwards. His mother says this is the fourth similar episode in three months, always triggered by a sudden fright or minor knock, and always with pallor first. He is thriving and has normal development. His diet is mainly cow milk, about a litre a day, with limited meat. He is afebrile and examination is normal with a soft abdomen, no murmur, no organomegaly and a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Episode description: Sudden fright or minor knock, pallor within seconds, limpness, 20 seconds of unconsciousness with brief stiffening, rapid full recovery
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 68 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (15-150), electrocardiogram with normal intervals
data_table.Development: Normal milestones, thriving, diet mainly cow milk with limited meat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the mechanism, treat the iron deficiency, and give first aid advice for episodes
Start sodium valproate and arrange an outpatient electroencephalogram within four weeks
Refer for cardiac electrophysiology study to exclude an inherited arrhythmia syndrome
Admit for continuous video electroencephalographic monitoring to capture a typical event
Advise the parents to prevent all episodes by avoiding any situation that startles him

subtopic_detail: thin midline membrane joining the labia minora in an asymptomatic preschool girl with a normal urinary stream
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed that her vulva looks different while helping her in the bath. The mother is worried that something is missing or has been damaged.

The girl is toilet trained, passes urine in a single forward stream without spraying, and has never had dysuria, discharge or a urinary tract infection. On examination, with the mother present and after explaining what you are doing, the labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent membrane, with a small opening anteriorly through which urine passes. The vulval skin elsewhere is normal in colour and texture, with no thickened white plaques, no fissures, no bruising and no bleeding. Growth and development are normal.

data_table.Examination: Thin translucent midline membrane between the labia minora with a patent anterior opening, surrounding vulval skin normal
data_table.History: Continent, single forward urinary stream, no dysuria, discharge or previous urinary tract infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric gynaecologist for separation under general anaesthesia
Prescribe topical clobetasol ointment once daily to the vulva for four weeks
Apply topical oestrogen cream twice daily for six weeks and review the response
Report the finding to child protection services as a possible sign of sexual abuse
Explain the finding, advise simple vulval care, and review only if symptoms develop

subtopic_detail: repetitive vomiting and pallor two hours after a first feed of rice cereal with no urticaria or wheeze
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 6-month-old boy is brought in pale and floppy. He has vomited more than ten times over the past hour. His mother says he was completely well this morning and had his first ever bowl of rice cereal two hours before the vomiting started, mixed with his usual formula which he has taken since birth.

He has no rash, no lip or tongue swelling, and his breathing is quiet with no noisy breathing or cough. He is lethargic but rousable and his hands feel cool. There was a similar but milder episode three weeks ago, two hours after his only previous taste of rice cereal, which settled at home over an afternoon and was attributed to a stomach bug. He is afebrile, and there is no diarrhoea, and no one else at home is unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176 beats per minute, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and lethargic, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, chest clear with no wheeze or stridor, skin free of urticaria or angioedema
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glucose 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly into the lateral thigh, repeated if needed
Normal saline 20 mL/kg as a rapid bolus with intravenous ondansetron, then reassess
Intravenous ceftriaxone after blood cultures, with a fluid bolus for suspected sepsis
Oral rehydration solution given in small frequent volumes with review in four hours
Intravenous hydrocortisone with a non-sedating oral antihistamine and observation

subtopic_detail: developmental regression with microcytic anaemia and abdominal pain in a child living beside a smelter
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital. A 2-year-old girl is referred with four months of intermittent abdominal pain, constipation and irritability. Her parents say she has stopped using the ten words she had at 18 months and now mostly points. The family moved 18 months ago to a house built in the 1920s, three streets from a lead and zinc smelter, and renovations stripping old paint were done while they lived there.

She eats little meat and drinks about a litre of cow milk each day. There has been no vomiting, no fever, no diarrhoea, and no blood in the stool. On examination she is alert and interactive but quiet, with pale conjunctivae and no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising and a normal neurological examination with no focal deficit and a normal gait. Her weight and length have tracked along the 25th centile throughout.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, abdomen soft with palpable faecal loading, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, normal tone gait and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 66 fL (73-85), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-450), basophilic stippling noted on the film

lead_in: Which investigation should you request to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Venous blood lead level, taken with attention to avoiding external contamination
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to look for marrow infiltration or failure
Urinary catecholamines with an abdominal ultrasound looking for a solid tumour
Haemoglobin electrophoresis with iron studies to separate thalassaemia from deficiency
Coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A on a normal gluten containing diet

subtopic_detail: scaly scalp patch with broken hairs and occipital lymph nodes unresponsive to topical antifungal cream
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy whose mother has been treating a patch on his scalp for six weeks. She has used a topical clotrimazole cream from the pharmacy twice daily throughout, and the patch has slowly enlarged.

On examination there is a 4 cm round scaly patch over the left occiput with hairs broken off a few millimetres above the skin, and a few small mobile lymph nodes at the occiput on the same side. The scalp is not boggy, there is no pus, no crusted honey coloured exudate and no fluctuance. He is systemically well and afebrile, and the rest of his skin and his nails are normal. A skin scraping and plucked hairs have been sent for fungal microscopy and culture, with results expected in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Round scaly occipital patch with hairs broken close to the scalp, ipsilateral occipital lymphadenopathy, no boggy swelling or pustules
data_table.Treatment to date: Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for six weeks with progressive enlargement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start oral griseofulvin daily with fatty food and continue it for six to eight weeks
Switch to ketoconazole shampoo twice weekly and review the patch in one month
Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to treat bacterial infection of the hair follicles
Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment daily to settle the inflamed scaly patch
Wait for the fungal culture before starting any systemic treatment, and keep him home

subtopic_detail: thick fissured hyperkeratotic crusts on palms and soles in a child from a remote community with little itch
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote community clinic in the Northern Territory. A 7-year-old girl is brought in with thick grey crusted plaques on both palms and soles that have built up over several months, with deep painful fissures. Her scalp and back have thick scale as well.

Her grandmother says the girl barely scratches, which is why nobody thought it was the same thing her cousins had. Two other children in the household have an itchy papular rash between the fingers and on the wrists. This girl was treated for nephrotic syndrome last year and is taking prednisolone. She is systemically well, afebrile, with no cellulitis, no discharging sores and no joint swelling. Skin scrapings taken today are reported within the hour as showing numerous mites and eggs.

data_table.Examination: Thick grey hyperkeratotic fissured crusts on palms, soles and scalp, minimal excoriation, no cellulitis or purulent sores
data_table.Household: Two other children with an itchy papular eruption of the finger webs and wrists
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone, ongoing since treatment for nephrotic syndrome last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: A single dose of oral ivermectin today, repeated once in seven days, for this child only
Topical permethrin 5% cream applied once tonight and repeated after one week
Multi-dose oral ivermectin with topical permethrin and keratolytic, plus household treatment
Oral cefalexin for ten days with daily bleach baths and dressings to the fissures
Cease prednisolone immediately and review the skin in one week before treating the mites

subtopic_detail: clockwork monthly fevers with aphthous ulcers and pharyngitis and complete wellness between episodes
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar in a fever clinic. A 4-year-old boy has had fevers to 39.5 degrees Celsius every four weeks for the past eight months. Each episode lasts four days and his mother can predict the next one on the calendar.

During episodes he has mouth ulcers, a sore throat and tender neck glands, and he looks miserable but is never admitted. Between episodes he is entirely well, attends kindergarten, and his weight and height have tracked steadily along the 50th centile. Two throat swabs taken during previous episodes grew normal flora, and a full blood count during a well period was normal. He has received all scheduled immunisations, has had no rash, no joint swelling, no abdominal pain and no diarrhoea, and there has been no overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile and well today, all vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination during episodes: Temperature to 39.5 degrees Celsius, aphthous oral ulcers, exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymph nodes
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count during a well interval normal, two throat swabs during episodes grew normal flora, growth along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the next episode?

options.text: Prescribe oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for ten days at the start of the next episode
Arrange genetic testing for familial Mediterranean fever before any treatment is started
Admit during the next episode for bone marrow examination and a whole body scan
Give a single dose of oral prednisolone at the onset of fever and record the response
Refer for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy as the definitive treatment for the syndrome

subtopic_detail: choosing seasonal immunisation for a preterm infant approaching their first winter with a well sibling at school
stem:
You are the doctor running a general practice baby clinic in early autumn. A 3-month-old boy born at 32 weeks gestation attends for his scheduled immunisations. He was in the special care nursery for three weeks with no chronic lung disease and has been well since discharge, feeding and growing along the 25th centile.

His mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy but says she was not offered any vaccines during it and received none. His 4-year-old sister is well and fully immunised. There is no family history of immunodeficiency, and the baby has had no wheeze, no admissions and no oxygen requirement since going home. His mother is worried because a neighbour's baby was admitted to intensive care last winter with a chest infection, and she asks what can be done to protect him through the coming season.

data_table.History: Born at 32 weeks, three weeks in special care, no chronic lung disease, no oxygen at home
data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 25th centile since discharge

lead_in: In addition to his scheduled vaccines, what should you recommend today?

options.text: Palivizumab given monthly through the winter season to this infant only
A single dose of nirsevimab before the season, since his mother was not vaccinated
Influenza vaccine for the infant now, with a second dose given four weeks later
Defer all additional protection until 6 months of corrected age and review then
Vaccinate the mother against respiratory syncytial virus now so her milk protects him

subtopic_detail: asymptomatic hip migration on surveillance imaging in a non-ambulant child with bilateral spasticity
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric rehabilitation clinic. A 5-year-old girl with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy attends for review. She has never walked and uses a supportive seating system, which corresponds to level four on the standard functional classification.

Her parents report no pain at all, and she tolerates sitting, standing frame sessions and nappy changes without distress. On examination hip abduction in flexion is 35 degrees on the right and 30 degrees on the left, with no fixed flexion contracture and no leg length discrepancy. A surveillance anteroposterior pelvic radiograph performed this month is reported with a migration percentage of 38 per cent on the right and 34 per cent on the left. The films from 12 months ago showed 24 per cent and 22 per cent. She has no scoliosis and her seating has not changed.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral spasticity, hip abduction in flexion 35 degrees right and 30 degrees left, no pain on hip movement, no fixed contracture
data_table.Imaging: Migration percentage right 38 per cent and left 34 per cent, compared with 24 per cent and 22 per cent 12 months ago
data_table.Function: Non-ambulant, supportive seating, level four on the gross motor functional classification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pelvic radiograph in 12 months as part of routine surveillance imaging
Prescribe regular oral baclofen and review the hip clinically in three months
Reassure the family that intervention is unnecessary while the hips remain pain free
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics now given the migration percentage and its rate of change
Arrange botulinum toxin injections to the hip adductors as the definitive management

subtopic_detail: painless ear discharge through a persistent drum perforation for more than six weeks in a remote community child
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote community clinic. A 5-year-old boy is brought in because his right ear has been running for three months. His grandmother says it never hurts him and he never has fever with it, but she has to wipe it most days.

On otoscopy, after you dry the canal with rolled tissue spears, there is a large central perforation of the right tympanic membrane with mucoid discharge coming through it. The canal skin is not swollen and the pinna is not tender to move. The left drum is dull and retracted but intact. He has no facial weakness, no swelling behind the ear, no headache and no neck stiffness, and he is systemically well. His school teacher has reported that he does not respond when called from across the room and has fallen behind with reading.

data_table.Examination: Large central right tympanic membrane perforation with mucoid discharge, non-tender pinna and mastoid, left drum dull and retracted
data_table.Duration: Discharge continuous for three months, painless, no fever
data_table.Function: Teacher reports poor response to speech across the classroom and falling behind with reading

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin for seven days with review at the clinic once the course is finished
Framycetin with gramicidin and dexamethasone ear drops applied three times daily
Urgent transfer for intravenous antibiotics and a computed tomography scan of the mastoid
Refer for grommet insertion into both ears at the next visiting surgical outreach clinic
Dry mopping with topical ciprofloxacin drops and referral for formal audiology assessment

subtopic_detail: breast development in a tall adolescent boy whose testes remain small despite advanced pubic hair
stem: A 14-year-old boy has had breast development for 18 months. He is above the 97th centile for height, his parents are average, and his arm span exceeds his height by 7 cm. He needed extra help with reading at school.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical breast tissue, testes 4 mL and firm, advanced pubic hair
data_table.Investigations: Morning testosterone low for age, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Testicular ultrasound for a hormone secreting tumour
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging for a prolactinoma
Clinical review in six months without further testing
Urine drug screen for anabolic androgenic steroids
Karyotype analysis on a peripheral blood sample

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease with delayed presentation past day 10
stem: A 3-year-old boy has had fever for eleven days, a truncal rash from day three, cracked lips, red eyes without discharge and a swollen left neck lump. His fingertips are now peeling. Blood cultures are negative at 24 hours.

data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 158 mg/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L; echocardiogram normal coronary arteries and function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold immunoglobulin because he is past day ten, and observe
Discharge on ibuprofen with paediatric outpatient review in two weeks
Change to intravenous ceftriaxone and repeat the blood cultures
Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse, holding immunoglobulin
Immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high dose aspirin, repeat echocardiography

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at-risk newborn
stem: A 2-hour-old boy born at 39+4 weeks to a mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes has fed once with a shallow latch. He is quiet, pink and well perfused. Heel-prick glucose is 1.9 mmol/L (threshold 2.6).

data_table.Examination: Birth weight 4420 g (97th centile); alert, normal tone, no jitteriness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose intravenously and special care admission
Critical hypoglycaemia screen before any further intervention
30 mL/kg of formula by bottle, rechecking in six hours
Repeat the glucose at four hours as a physiological nadir
200 mg/kg of 40% buccal dextrose gel and a feed, recheck at 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia from excess cow's milk intake
stem: An 18-month-old girl looks pale. She drinks about 900 mL of cow's milk daily and refuses meat, egg and vegetables. There is no bleeding or family history of haemoglobinopathy. Iron studies are pending.

data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 82 g/L, mean cell volume 62 fL, platelets 468 x10^9/L
data_table.Blood film: Microcytic hypochromic cells, no basophilic stippling or target cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral iron 3 mg/kg daily, milk under 500 mL daily, plus coeliac serology
Bone marrow biopsy before any oral iron therapy is started
Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion as first line treatment
Haemoglobin electrophoresis first, deferring iron until thalassaemia excluded
An over the counter paediatric multivitamin containing 4 mg iron daily

subtopic_detail: Bruising in a non-mobile infant and mandatory reporting
stem: A 4-month-old boy has a bruise on his left cheek, which his mother attributes to the family cat jumping over him. He is not rolling and cannot sit unsupported.

data_table.Skin survey: Left cheek bruise 2 cm x 1 cm; 1 cm linear bruise on the left pinna
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, coagulation profile and blood film normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the mechanism, arrange general practice review and discharge
Admit for skeletal survey, MRI brain and child protection referral
Request von Willebrand studies before any further investigation
Photograph the bruises, discharge, and request a child health nurse visit
Radiograph the skull and left ribs; if normal, manage as accidental

subtopic_detail: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and biliary atresia workup
stem: A 5-week-old breastfed girl has prolonged jaundice, pale stools for ten days and dark urine for a week. She is alert, on the 25th centile, with a 2 cm liver edge.

data_table.Bilirubin: Total 152 micromol/L, conjugated 68 micromol/L (reference less than 20)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure about breast milk jaundice and repeat bilirubin in two weeks
Admit for phototherapy and reassess the total bilirubin at 24 hours
Admit for urgent hepatology review, hepatobiliary ultrasound and liver biopsy
Trial two weeks of formula feeding, then repeat both bilirubin fractions
Send urine culture and thyroid function, referring only if abnormal

subtopic_detail: Hemiplegic migraine masquerading as acute ischaemic stroke
stem: A 10-year-old girl woke with headache, left lip and hand tingling, then left arm weakness peaking over 45 minutes and present for two hours. A similar left-sided episode six months ago resolved fully over four hours.

data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain normal, glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within the thrombolysis window
Arrange urgent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and MRA before treatment
Give intranasal sumatriptan and defer imaging until the deficit settles
Load intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg and repeat CT brain in six hours
Start aspirin and clopidogrel and arrange echocardiography before imaging

subtopic_detail: Recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula versus anastomotic stricture after primary repair
stem: A 6-week-old girl had repair of type C oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula on day one and a normal contrast study before discharge at four weeks. She now coughs and becomes cyanosed with most feeds, with a witnessed apnoea yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Right lower lobe consolidation; oesophagogram shows an anterior air column above the anastomosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue in the upper oesophageal pouch
A 24-hour multichannel intraluminal impedance and pH study
Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scintigraphy for biliary reflux
An outpatient videofluoroscopic swallow study by speech pathology
Fluoroscopic balloon dilatation of a presumed anastomotic stricture

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in adolescent girl
stem:
