You are the GP registrar seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother for tiredness that has worsened over three months. She is falling asleep in afternoon classes and has stopped athletics training. Her periods began at 12 and for the last year have lasted seven days with heavy flow requiring a pad every two hours on the first two days. She eats a self-described vegetarian diet with no red meat and drinks two mugs of tea with lunch.

She reports no bruising, no black stools, no weight loss, no recurrent infections. She is not sexually active. There is no family history of thalassaemia or coeliac disease.

On examination she has pale conjunctivae and mild angular cheilitis; the remainder of the examination including abdominal palpation is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (120-160), MCV 71 fL (80-100), MCH 22 pg (27-32), platelets 384 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), ferritin 6 microg/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 8% (20-45), CRP <5 mg/L (<5), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days with vitamin C and arrange menstrual review
Commence oral ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron daily and repeat full blood count in six weeks
Arrange an intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion in the day-oncology unit within the week
Refer for upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy before starting iron replacement
Trial ferrous sulfate 100 mg twice daily with meals and add proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis escalation of respiratory support
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 6-month-old boy brought in by ambulance with three days of coryza, cough and worsening breathing since this morning. He is bottle-fed and today has taken only half his usual volumes with brief episodes where he pulls off and pants. He has had no fever, no apnoeas witnessed, and no wheeze audible to the parents. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean and has no comorbidities.

On examination he is alert but working hard: subcostal and intercostal recession, tracheal tug, bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. Capillary refill is under two seconds and he is well perfused.

He has been on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min for two hours since triage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 89% on 1 L/min nasal prong oxygen, temperature 37.4°C
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for respiratory syncytial virus; venous blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg (35-45) HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-26) lactate 1.6 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase nasal prong oxygen to 2 L/min and reassess in one hour with a repeat blood gas
Start high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to keep SpO2 at 90% or above
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess response before escalating support
Administer nebulised 3% hypertonic saline and continue low-flow oxygen for six hours
Proceed directly to CPAP at 6 cmH2O in the emergency department resuscitation bay

subtopic_detail: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia phototherapy decision
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a term baby girl on the postnatal ward at 54 hours of age. She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery weighing 3.6 kg, is exclusively breastfeeding with good latch, and has passed meconium and urine. Her mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the baby's cord blood group is B positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. There are no dysmorphic features and no cephalhaematoma.

The midwife has escalated because the baby looks visibly yellow to the face and chest today. A transcutaneous bilirubin reading was 305 micromol/L, prompting a serum sample.

Serum total bilirubin is 320 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 8 micromol/L. Weight loss from birth is 7.4%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert baby, moderate jaundice to chest and abdomen, tone and reflexes normal, no cephalhaematoma, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin total 320 micromol/L (conjugated 8), haemoglobin 168 g/L (140-220 neonate), reticulocytes 4.5%, ABO incompatibility with positive direct antiglobulin test

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother and repeat serum bilirubin in 24 hours because ABO incompatibility is usually mild
Arrange urgent exchange transfusion via the umbilical vein without further phototherapy
Commence intensive phototherapy now and repeat serum bilirubin in four to six hours
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give formula while continuing observation without phototherapy
Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and monitor without phototherapy

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease presenting as antibiotic-unresponsive cervical lymphadenitis
stem: A 4-year-old boy has had fever for six days and a swollen left neck, unimproved after 48 hours of oral cefalexin.

data_table.Examination: 3 cm firm left anterior cervical node, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, truncal rash, normal hands and feet
data_table.Investigations: CRP 132 mg/L, platelets 468 x10^9/L, ALT 62 U/L, albumin 30 g/L, sterile pyuria; blood cultures negative, neck ultrasound shows no abscess

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Continue cefalexin and add clindamycin for atypical adenitis
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and repeat ultrasound
Single dose of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg
Echocardiography and intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin
Excisional biopsy of the node for mycobacterial culture

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in an infant - malrotation with midgut volvulus
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 5-week-old boy with three episodes of green vomiting in the last four hours. He was born at term and has been formula-fed since day 4 after breastfeeding did not establish. His mother reports that until today he has been feeding well with progressive weight gain. There has been no diarrhoea, no fever, no unwell contacts.

He cried inconsolably when the ambulance service placed the intravenous cannula, then became quiet, mottled and drowsy en route.

On examination he is pale, floppy and cool peripherally, with a tender-looking distended abdomen; capillary refill is four seconds and he is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178 /min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 58 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4°C
data_table.Examination: Mottled infant, drowsy but rousable, distended and tender abdomen, no visible peristaltic wave, no palpable olive, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L (22-26), lactate 5.8 mmol/L (<2), base excess -12, glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and arrange urgent upper GI contrast study before surgical referral
Perform bedside abdominal ultrasound to look for a pyloric olive before considering surgical referral
Trial oral rehydration solution 10 mL every ten minutes for two hours before any further investigations
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone empirically and arrange urgent lumbar puncture in the resuscitation bay
Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, insert nasogastric tube on free drainage, and phone paediatric surgery

subtopic_detail: Bruising in a non-mobile infant
stem: A 4-month-old girl is brought in by her mother's partner, who says she rolled off the couch onto a rug. She was not yet rolling at her 4-month check last week.

data_table.Examination: Alert and well perfused; 1 cm yellow-brown left cheek bruise and 2 cm medial right upper arm bruise

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for a full non-accidental injury workup and notify child protection
Reassure and document the bruises, with general practitioner review
Full blood count and coagulation studies, discharging if normal
Refuse to release the child until police attend the department
Discharge to the mother when she arrives and confirms the story

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA with subclinical cerebral oedema
stem: A 7-year-old girl is six hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis. Over 45 minutes she has become withdrawn, with headache, one vomit and incontinence.

data_table.Investigations: Glasgow coma scale 13, pH 7.24, glucose 12 mmol/L (32 earlier), potassium 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Add 5% glucose to the fluids and continue insulin unchanged
3% saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes, cutting fluids by a third
Stop insulin for 30 minutes and correct the potassium first
A 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus for cerebral perfusion
Increase insulin to 0.1 units/kg/hour to clear the ketones

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease presenting after nursery discharge
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 6-day-old boy brought in by his parents because he has become mottled and off feeds over the last four hours. He was born at 39 weeks by uneventful vaginal delivery, passed the routine 24-hour saturation screen with pre-ductal SpO2 96% and post-ductal SpO2 95%, and was discharged at 48 hours. Feeding has been described as 'okay' until yesterday when volumes dropped.

Today he is grey, cool and lethargic. Femoral pulses are difficult to palpate; brachial pulses are volume-adequate. Precordium is quiet with no murmur audible. His liver is 3 cm below the costal margin.

A pre-ductal (right hand) SpO2 reads 84% and post-ductal (right foot) SpO2 reads 68% on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172 /min, blood pressure 62/34 mmHg (right arm), respiratory rate 68 /min, temperature 36.2°C
data_table.Cardiovascular examination: Weak femoral pulses, strong brachial pulses, quiet precordium, no murmur, hepatomegaly 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.14, HCO3 10 mmol/L, lactate 8.4 mmol/L (<2), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, chest X-ray: mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, normal pulmonary vascularity

lead_in: What is the single best immediate intervention?

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 20 minutes and repeat if perfusion does not improve
Intubate and ventilate with FiO2 1.0 to correct the hypoxia and hyperventilate for pulmonary vasodilatation
Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 5 to 10 nanogram/kg/min and prepare for intubation if apnoea develops
Give intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg and lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg for suspected neonatal septic collapse
Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 microgram/kg and prepare for tension pneumothorax needle decompression

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis - oxygen escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old boy admitted overnight with his first episode of coryza followed by wheeze and feeding difficulty. He is exclusively breast fed and is now taking about half his usual volume per feed. His mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy at 39+2 weeks and he has had no previous admissions.

On arrival he is quietly alert with mild subcostal recession, wet cough, wheeze and crackles bilaterally. He has had no apnoeas. He is on room air with continuous SpO2 monitoring.

Over the last hour his oxygen saturations have drifted from 94% to 88% with feeds and 91% at rest. Nasal suction has cleared moderate secretions. Chest signs are unchanged and he is not in extremis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152 /min, respiratory rate 58 /min, SpO2 89% on room air at rest, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Subcostal recession, no head bobbing, no nasal flare, capillary refill 2 s, alert and consolable
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR pending, no chest x-ray performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen therapy?

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe on room air with hourly checks
Escalate directly to heated humidified high flow nasal cannula 2 L/kg/min from room air now
Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg on oxygen and reassess in twenty minutes
Start low flow oxygen 1 to 2 L/min via nasal prongs titrated to SpO2 at or above 90%
Continue room air observation with two hourly nasal suction and repeat saturation in one hour

subtopic_detail: Croup - dexamethasone dose selection
stem:
You are the paediatric intern seeing a 22-month-old boy in the emergency short stay unit at 2 am with two nights of coryza and a barking cough. His mother reports he woke tonight with a hoarse cry and noisy breathing on inspiration.

He is sitting on his mother's lap alert and interactive. He has audible stridor at rest which improves when he settles. There is mild suprasternal recession. Chest is otherwise clear on auscultation with no wheeze or crackles. He drinks water when offered and there is no drooling.

He was fully immunised on schedule and has had no previous croup admissions. There is no history of foreign body inhalation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest that settles when calm, mild suprasternal recession, no cyanosis, colour normal, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose to give now?

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg single dose now with four hours observation
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose now with four hours observation
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now with four hours observation
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for three days with GP review tomorrow
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution alone with three hours observation

subtopic_detail: Gastroenteritis rehydration escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the short stay unit reviewing an 18-month-old girl brought in by her father with 24 hours of watery diarrhoea and three episodes of non bilious vomiting. Her older brother had similar symptoms last week that settled. She has been offered clear fluids at home but vomits within ten minutes of each offer and has passed no urine in the six hours prior to arrival.

She is quiet on her father's lap and cries with a few tears. Mucous membranes are dry. Capillary refill is 2 seconds centrally. Her weight three weeks ago at a nurse review was 11.2 kg; today she weighs 10.6 kg.

A single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg was given on arrival forty minutes ago with brief effect; she has since had one further small vomit after 30 mL of oral rehydration solution.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes with tears, capillary refill 2 s, alert, no abdominal tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Repeat oral ondansetron 4 mg and continue small oral sips of rehydration solution every five minutes
Insert an IV cannula, give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and continue at full maintenance rate
Insert a nasogastric tube and rehydrate with oral solution at 25 mL/kg in the first hour then reassess
Admit for observation on continued small oral offers of dilute apple juice every hour by cup
Give loperamide 0.2 mg/kg orally to slow bowel transit and continue oral rehydration solution

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media - antibiotic decision
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 22-month-old girl brought by her father with two days of low grade fever and pulling at her right ear. She had one episode of vomiting overnight and has been more irritable than usual but is taking her usual fluids and about two thirds of her normal food. She is fully immunised.

On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is red and bulging with loss of normal landmarks. There is no perforation or discharge. The left ear is normal. She has a clear runny nose and a normal oropharynx with no exudate. Chest is clear. There is no neck stiffness and she is not photophobic.

She has no known drug allergies and has not been given any antibiotics in the previous six months. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and lives at home with parents in Adelaide.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane red and bulging with no perforation, left ear normal, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily for seven days as first line antibiotic monotherapy
Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for five days with a return in 48 hours if not improving
Analgesia and safety net advice with a delayed antibiotic script to fill only if not improved in 48 hours
Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops for seven days without any oral antibiotic and review in one week
Refer to the emergency department for intravenous ceftriaxone and admission for observation

subtopic_detail: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia workup
stem: A 3-week-old breastfed boy has been jaundiced since day 4. His stools have become paler over the past week and his urine is dark. He feeds well and is gaining weight.

data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus, firm liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 168 micromol/L (<26), conjugated bilirubin 42 micromol/L (<15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add ursodeoxycholic acid and review liver enzymes in one month
Reassure about breast milk jaundice and review at six weeks
Start phototherapy and repeat the bilirubin in six hours
Urgent paediatric hepatology referral for cholangiography this week
Abdominal ultrasound with repeat conjugated bilirubin in one month

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-month-old boy admitted with six days of persistent fever above 39 degC that has not responded to paracetamol. His mother reports he has been miserable and off his feeds. He had a red rash on his trunk on day three that has faded. His hands looked puffy yesterday.

On examination today he is irritable with bilateral non exudative conjunctivitis and dry cracked red lips. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Hands and feet show mild oedema without desquamation. A chest x-ray on admission was normal. Blood and urine cultures at 48 hours are negative. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone was started three days ago with no improvement.

He has no known allergies and no significant past history. He was fully immunised at 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172 /min, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctivitis without exudate, cracked lips, no lymphadenopathy, hand and foot oedema, systolic flow murmur
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 18.4 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 145 mg/L (<5), ALT 68 U/L (<45), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis 30 white cells per HPF with no growth on culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram and give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high dose aspirin now
Continue ceftriaxone for a further 48 hours pending viral PCR results and clinical reassessment
Start intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg/day for three days as first line monotherapy
Arrange lumbar puncture and start empirical intravenous aciclovir for suspected HSV encephalitis
Discharge home on paracetamol with outpatient paediatric review in one week after clinic booking

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis observation duration
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 5-year-old girl brought in by ambulance 90 minutes ago after her first known peanut exposure at a friend's house. Within ten minutes of eating a peanut butter biscuit she developed urticaria, facial swelling and audible wheeze.

Paramedics gave a single intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram at the scene with rapid resolution of wheeze and improvement in tachycardia within five minutes. On arrival she was well perfused with clear chest and no stridor. She received a second intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram in the department 30 minutes ago after a brief return of wheeze, again with prompt response.

She has been observed for 90 minutes since arrival with no further symptoms. She is now bright and alert, drinking water, and has passed urine. Her parents have arrived with her ASCIA action plan blank and her EpiPen Jr script filled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 102/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, chest clear, no urticaria, no facial swelling, no stridor, no wheeze

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan from this presentation?

options.text: Admit overnight for a supervised peanut challenge in the paediatric ward the following morning
Discharge now with an EpiPen Jr and GP follow up next week to complete the anaphylaxis action plan
Admit for 24 hours of hourly observations and oral prednisolone daily for three days as inpatient
Observe to four hours after the last adrenaline dose then discharge with ASCIA plan and immunology referral
Start an oral antihistamine for three days and dispense an EpiPen 300 microgram for future emergency use

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA cerebral oedema
stem: A 9-year-old girl is four hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis with insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour and 48-hour rehydration fluids. She has vomited once and has a headache.

data_table.Neurology: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, from 14 on admission
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.22, glucose 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase insulin to 0.15 units/kg/hour and give 10 mL/kg saline
Give 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg, elevate the head, halve fluids, call PICU
Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the acidosis faster
Arrange urgent CT head before starting any osmotic therapy
Stop dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour now

subtopic_detail: First UTI imaging in a child under 24 months per RCH CPG
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18-month-old girl in the short stay ward. She was admitted 48 hours ago with a first febrile urinary tract infection, culture positive for Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim, and switched from IV to oral trimethoprim after 24 hours with rapid resolution of fever. Antenatal ultrasounds through the pregnancy were reported as normal with normal kidneys and bladder documented on the 20 week morphology scan. There is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux, no history of poor urinary stream, no palpable abdominal mass and she is now feeding, playing and afebrile for 36 hours.

Her mother works in a rural community two hours from the tertiary centre and asks what imaging her daughter needs before discharge to prevent kidney damage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, playing, abdomen soft, no flank fullness, no back or spinal abnormalities, external genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture Escherichia coli >10^8 CFU/mL sensitive to trimethoprim, creatinine 28 micromol/L, C reactive protein 42 mg/L falling from 96, blood culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No routine renal tract imaging, provide safety net advice about recurrent fever with prompt urine collection
Renal tract ultrasound during this admission before discharge, with paediatric outpatient follow up
Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal cortical scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring
Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux prior to discharge home to a rural community
Renal tract ultrasound plus prophylactic trimethoprim for 6 months to prevent culture proven recurrence

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation per RCH CPG
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a district general emergency department. A 7-month-old previously well infant presents with 3 days of coryza, cough and rising work of breathing. His mother reports poor feeding for the last 12 hours and no wet nappy for 4 hours. He has no cyanosis at rest and is not sleepy. On examination he has bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, moderate subcostal recession and tracheal tug. There is no focal consolidation on auscultation.

His nasopharyngeal aspirate later confirms respiratory syncytial virus. He is nursed sitting up in a cot. A junior colleague has already commenced high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.4 within the first 10 minutes of arrival citing severity and pulls you aside asking whether that is correct first line oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 87% on room air, temperature 37.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, subcostal recession, tracheal tug, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate later positive for respiratory syncytial virus; capillary blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 46 mmHg lactate 1.4 mmol/L; chest X ray not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: Continue high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with fraction of inspired oxygen 0.4 as commenced
Low flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 target 90%, review at 60 minutes
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back with review of oxygen needs after the third dose
Nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent every 4 hours to reduce airway oedema
Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation because of respiratory rate above 60

subtopic_detail: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis fluid regimen and cerebral oedema risk
stem: A 9-year-old boy weighing 28 kg has new type 1 diabetes with ketoacidosis. He is drowsy but rousable, 7% dehydrated, and has had one 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus.

data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.05, glucose 34 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: Which fluid and insulin plan is most appropriate?

options.text: 0.9% saline, potassium 20 mmol/L, 7% deficit over 48 hours, insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour
Two further 20 mL/kg saline boluses now, then immediate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour
0.9% saline, potassium 40 mmol/L, 5 to 7% deficit over 48 hours, insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour
0.45% saline with 5% dextrose, deficit over 24 hours, immediate insulin infusion
0.9% saline at twice maintenance for 4 hours, immediate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months investigation choice
stem: A 6-week-old term boy has six hours of fever and is taking half his usual feeds. He is quiet but consolable, with no rash and no focus of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, respiratory rate 46/min, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 18 mg/L, urine dipstick negative, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and review if fever persists
Oral amoxicillin and admission, deferring lumbar puncture
Intravenous cefotaxime alone, deferring lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture, intravenous cefotaxime, amoxicillin and aciclovir
High flow oxygen, 20 mL/kg saline bolus and intensive care review

subtopic_detail: Croup severity based dexamethasone dose per RCH
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on evening shift. A 2-year-old boy presents with a barking cough for 8 hours and stridor. He has no drooling, is tolerating small sips and is not toxic. His mother reports similar symptoms 6 months ago that settled with a single oral dexamethasone dose from a regional emergency department. He has no allergies and is fully vaccinated. There is no foreign body history. On examination he has occasional inspiratory stridor when upset but no stridor at rest, mild suprasternal recession only when crying, and normal air entry bilaterally.

He becomes calmer sitting on his father's lap. The bedside nurse asks what dexamethasone dose to draw up before you review him again in 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession when crying, no stridor at rest, tolerating oral fluids
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; no chest X ray required in typical croup

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose now, review at 30 minutes and discharge if he remains clinically stable
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose today with no additional oral steroid required at this visit
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 now, observe for 3 hours, no oral steroid required at this visit
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose now, arrange urgent retrieval to a tertiary paediatric intensive care unit
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now, observe for 30 minutes then discharge home with croup advice

subtopic_detail: ASCIA banded adrenaline dose for paediatric anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar on a Sunday afternoon at a suburban emergency department. A 4-year-old boy who weighs 16 kg presents 20 minutes after eating a peanut biscuit at a birthday party. He has widespread urticaria, facial swelling, harsh stridor at rest and vomiting. His mother reports mild wheeze at home which is now worse. He has a documented previous mild peanut reaction and carries no adrenaline autoinjector. He is placed supine with legs elevated because he is pale and tachycardic.

An ASCIA action plan is on the ward wall. The intern preparing the drug asks whether to use 10 microg/kg by weight, or the ASCIA banded intramuscular dose. Your consultant emphasises the AU standard. He has no known intercurrent medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Urticaria over the trunk, facial and periorbital swelling, stridor at rest, wheeze, pale, capillary refill 3 s
data_table.Investigations: Not required at this point; peak flow deferred

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of intramuscular adrenaline?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microg into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microg into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes
Intramuscular adrenaline 10 microg/kg = 160 microg via 1:10,000 preparation into the deltoid
Intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microg/kg/min immediately without an intramuscular dose
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as first line

subtopic_detail: Refractory paediatric septic shock with severe hypokalaemia after fluid resuscitation
stem: A 3-year-old boy (15 kg) has fever, vomiting and a spreading purpuric rash. After ceftriaxone and 60 mL/kg of 0.9% saline he remains shocked on peripheral adrenaline 0.1 microg/kg/min.

data_table.Investigations: pH 7.22, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, potassium 2.4 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.05 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before retrieval?

options.text: A fourth 20 mL/kg saline bolus with adrenaline increased to 0.3 microg/kg/min now
Potassium infusion 0.5 mmol/kg/hour through a large bore line with cardiac monitoring
Potassium chloride 20 mmol intravenously over 15 minutes, then reassess perfusion
Intravenous hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg, deferring potassium replacement
Intubation and renal replacement therapy for the lactic acidosis

subtopic_detail: Neonate with duct dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease refractory to prostaglandin E1
stem: A 3-day-old term neonate in a regional nursery is cyanosed, SpO2 62 per cent despite 100 per cent oxygen. Prostaglandin E1 has run 20 minutes at 0.1 microg/kg/min without improvement. Retrieval is 90 minutes away.

data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: d-transposition of the great arteries, intact ventricular septum, restrictive foramen ovale, ductus small

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase prostaglandin E1 to 0.4 microg/kg/min and add nitric oxide
Cease prostaglandin E1 and commence dobutamine 10 microg/kg/min
Bedside balloon atrial septostomy under echocardiographic guidance
Intubate and hyperventilate to a pCO2 of 25 mmHg in 100 per cent oxygen
Peripheral extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in this nursery

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis after conservative measures
stem: A 7-year-old boy has never been dry at night. Days are dry, with no urgency or constipation. A reward chart over three months has not helped. He leaves for his first school camp in six weeks.

data_table.Examination: Growth on the 50th centile, no palpable bladder or faecal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative

lead_in: Which treatment is most appropriate now?

options.text: Continue the reward chart with evening fluids stopped from 6 pm
Nightly enuresis alarm for at least eight weeks, with a parent wake protocol
Oral oxybutynin 5 mg at bedtime with evening fluid restriction
Oral desmopressin 120 microg wafer at bedtime for the camp, alarm afterwards
Refer for urodynamic studies before any specific treatment

subtopic_detail: Neonatal testicular torsion presenting on day 2 of life with a firm hemiscrotal mass
stem: A term boy is reviewed on day 2 of life. The left hemiscrotum has been firm, bluish and non-tender since birth, and the testis cannot be distinguished from the surrounding oedema. The right testis is normal.

data_table.Investigations: Scrotal ultrasound shows an enlarged heterogeneous left testis with absent intratesticular Doppler flow and a normal right testis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative plan?

options.text: Manual detorsion at the cotside now under nitrous oxide analgesia
Warm compresses with repeat scrotal ultrasound in 24 hours
Urgent exploration with left orchidectomy and contralateral orchidopexy
Semi-urgent exploration in a few days for left orchidectomy alone
Repeat Doppler at 6 and 12 hours before any operative decision

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa in a swimmer with intact tympanic membrane
stem: A 12-year-old competitive swimmer has 4 days of increasing left ear pain and itching, worse on chewing and on pulling the pinna. She is afebrile, with no vertigo and no facial weakness.

data_table.Examination: Tender tragus, oedematous erythematous left ear canal with debris, tympanic membrane intact after clearance

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line therapy?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
Aural toilet and topical ciprofloxacin with dexamethasone drops
Aluminium acetate ear drops alone for 5 days, then review
Warm saline bulb syringe irrigation twice daily at home
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days

subtopic_detail: Metformin candidacy in adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation
stem: A 14-year-old girl has a body mass index of 34 kg/m^2 (above the 99.5th centile) and acanthosis nigricans. Six months of a structured dietitian and exercise program produced no metabolic improvement.

data_table.Investigations: Blood pressure 132/82 mmHg (above the 95th centile), fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.1%, 2-hour glucose 9.4 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy should be added to intensified lifestyle intervention?

options.text: Referral for bariatric surgery with sleeve gastrectomy
Orlistat 120 mg with each meal as first line therapy
Liraglutide 3 mg subcutaneously daily as first line
Insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously at bedtime
Metformin 500 mg daily, titrated to 2 g over four weeks

subtopic_detail: Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome first relapse definition and next line therapy after multiple relapses
stem: A 5-year-old boy with steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome diagnosed 8 months ago presents with his fourth relapse. Each previous relapse responded to prednisolone within 10 days. He now has a weight z score 3 SD above baseline, striae and cushingoid facies.

data_table.Examination: Periorbital oedema, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol, albumin 22 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 intravenously as a single dose
Prednisolone 60 mg/m^2 daily with a 12 week wean
Urgent percutaneous renal biopsy before any agent
Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg daily with prednisolone induction
Lisinopril 5 mg daily alone in place of steroids

subtopic_detail: Differentiating multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children from Kawasaki disease at initial workup
stem: An 8-year-old girl has five days of fever, non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a maculopapular rash, extremity oedema and cervical lymphadenopathy. She has abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Household SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed five weeks ago.

data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 45 ng/L (less than 15), lymphocytes 0.7 x10^9/L, platelets 128 x10^9/L, ejection fraction 48% with no coronary aneurysm

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children over Kawasaki disease?

options.text: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis with cracked, fissured lips
Older age, abdominal symptoms, lymphopenia and raised troponin
Five days of unremitting fever with a truncal maculopapular rash
Unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy measuring more than 1.5 cm
Extremity oedema with a polymorphous rash over the trunk

subtopic_detail: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia recognition with severe thrombocytopenia at birth
stem: A term boy has widespread petechiae and a small subgaleal haematoma at 6 hours of age. His mother is well, with a booking platelet count of 285 x10^9/L and no antiplatelet medication.

data_table.Investigations: Platelets 15 x10^9/L (150-450), haemoglobin 168 g/L, coagulation profile normal, cranial ultrasound no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate transfusion strategy?

options.text: Antigen matched platelets, HPA-1a negative if unknown, with immunoglobulin 1 g/kg
Random donor platelets 10 mL/kg immediately, without any immunoglobulin cover
Maternal washed apheresis platelets with oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily
Serial platelet counts six-hourly, transfusing only below 5 x10^9/L or if bleeding
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg over 30 minutes as the sole intervention

subtopic_detail: Severe combined immunodeficiency unmasked by live rotavirus vaccine complication after routine immunisation
stem: A 5-month-old boy has 6 weeks of watery diarrhoea, weight fallen from the 25th to below the 3rd centile, and oral candidiasis. A sibling died at 8 months of infection.

data_table.Investigations: Lymphocytes 0.6 x10^9/L, CD3 0.02 x10^9/L, T cell receptor excision circles absent
data_table.Microbiology: Lavage: Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus; stool vaccine strain rotavirus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ganciclovir, deferring immunology
Discharge on home oxygen with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and monthly review
Protective isolation, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative products, urgent transplant referral
Continue the schedule with rotavirus and measles-mumps-rubella at 12 months
Trial oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for presumed eosinophilic enteropathy

subtopic_detail: Escalation of respiratory support in an infant with bronchiolitis on general paediatric ward
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the general ward at 2 am. A 4-month-old term infant was admitted 6 hours ago with a 3 day history of coryza, cough and increasing work of breathing. His mother says he took only 30 percent of his usual feeds today and has had 2 wet nappies in 24 hours. His weight is 6.4 kg and he is fully immunised.

On examination he is alert but tachypnoeic with moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze and fine crackles. His nappy is dry. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Feeding: 30% of baseline oral intake in past 12 hours, 2 wet nappies in 24 hours
data_table.Chest: Bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, no tracheal tug

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate respiratory intervention?

options.text: Start low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min via a humidified circuit, titrate to keep SpO2 at or above 90 percent, and reassess work of breathing in one hour
Start high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min via humidified circuit and admit to the high dependency unit for close monitoring now
Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000, and repeat if the work of breathing persists
Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, review in one hour, and start oxygen only if the SpO2 drops further overnight
Intubate and ventilate now with pressure support because his respiratory rate and recession predict imminent respiratory failure requiring definitive airway

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid selection and disposition in moderate viral croup in an emergency department
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 22-month-old girl is brought in at midnight with a 12 hour history of barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing that started after a 2 day coryzal illness. She is settled on her mother's lap and pink. She has stridor audible only when she becomes upset and moderate intercostal recession at rest. Her chest is otherwise clear.

She has no drooling, no toxic appearance and no history of intubation, asthma or immunodeficiency. She is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Airway: Barking cough, hoarse voice, stridor only on agitation, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Work of breathing: Moderate intercostal recession at rest, no tracheal tug, no fatigue

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 now, and admit to a monitored bed for at least 4 hours
Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and observe in the emergency short stay area for 4 hours before deciding disposition
Give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days at home, arrange general practice review the following morning and discharge the child now
Give humidified air by face mask alone and reassess in one hour, avoiding any corticosteroid because of the risk of secondary bacterial tracheitis
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg immediately and arrange urgent ear nose and throat review for consideration of nasoendoscopy to exclude epiglottitis

subtopic_detail: Investigation of a febrile well appearing infant under three months in emergency
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 5-week-old boy is brought in by his parents because of a rectal temperature of 38.4 degC at home an hour ago. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery, is exclusively breast fed and has been feeding normally. He looks pink, alert and content in his father's arms in the cubicle. He has no rash, no bulging fontanelle and no focal signs of infection.

His mother had negative group B streptococcus screening in pregnancy. He has had no contact with anyone with known infection and has not travelled overseas. He is not on any medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 76/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.General: Alert, well perfused, no rash, anterior fontanelle soft and flat
data_table.Focus of infection: Ears, throat and skin unremarkable; no cough, no vomiting, no diarrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, give paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally and discharge home with advice to return if the fever exceeds 39 degC or the infant becomes unwell
Take a bag urine specimen only, discharge home once the sample is sent and arrange telephone follow up with the general practitioner in 24 hours
Full septic screen including blood culture, urine catheter specimen, lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin now
Take blood cultures and inflammatory markers only and start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily, deferring lumbar puncture until results are back
Admit for 48 hours of observation without any investigations or antibiotics, and perform investigations only if the fever recurs above 38 degC on the ward

subtopic_detail: First hour management of severe acute asthma in a school aged child in emergency
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 6-year-old girl is brought in by ambulance with a 12 hour history of worsening wheeze and cough after a viral upper respiratory illness. She is on inhaled salbutamol as needed and fluticasone 100 mcg twice daily. She has needed her reliever every hour at home overnight.

On arrival she is anxious, sits forwards and can only speak in single words. She has widespread wheeze with markedly reduced air entry at the bases, subcostal and tracheal tug and moderate use of accessory muscles. She is not obviously exhausted and there is no cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 /min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Respiratory: Widespread wheeze, reduced air entry at bases, subcostal and tracheal tug, single word sentences
data_table.Peak flow: Unable to perform because of dyspnoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first hour management?

options.text: Give intravenous salbutamol infusion 5 mcg/kg/min immediately as a bolus and continuous infusion in preference to inhaled bronchodilator via spacer therapy
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg immediately as first line therapy and start non-invasive ventilation while awaiting paediatric intensive care review
Give a single dose of nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000, oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and start empirical amoxicillin for likely bacterial pneumonia today
Give salbutamol 12 puffs via metered dose inhaler and spacer every 20 minutes for one hour, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and titrated oxygen to SpO2 above 94 percent
Give inhaled fluticasone 500 mcg via spacer every hour and defer systemic corticosteroid until the child has failed 4 hours of inhaled controller escalation

subtopic_detail: Choice of reduction versus surgical exploration in confirmed ileocolic intussusception with equivocal peritonism
stem: A 9-month-old boy has 8 hours of episodes of drawing his knees up and crying, settling between episodes but becoming progressively lethargic. He has vomited twice, once bile stained, and passed blood stained mucus per rectum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, central capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Abdomen: Soft, right upper quadrant fullness, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Target sign with preserved Doppler perfusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Barium enema now, without resuscitation or antibiotics
Immediate laparotomy and manual reduction, bypassing enema
Nasogastric polyethylene glycol and repeat ultrasound in 4 hours
Intravenous ondansetron and discharge once vomiting settles
Resuscitate, cross match, give antibiotics, then air enema reduction

subtopic_detail: Choosing intensive phototherapy versus exchange transfusion in a term neonate with rising bilirubin
stem: A term 3.4 kg boy is 60 hours old. His mother is blood group A rhesus positive and he is O rhesus positive. He is alert and feeding well.

data_table.Bilirubin trend: 380 micromol/L at 52 hours, 405 micromol/L at 60 hours on single surface phototherapy
data_table.Laboratory: Haemoglobin 145 g/L (145-225), direct antiglobulin test positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to exchange transfusion now without escalating phototherapy
Escalate to intensive phototherapy, recheck bilirubin in 4 hours, cross match
Stop phototherapy for 6 hours and repeat the bilirubin off treatment
Give intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and defer further phototherapy
Continue single surface phototherapy and recheck in 12 hours

subtopic_detail: Secondary prophylaxis regimen in a first episode of acute rheumatic fever without carditis in a high risk community
stem: An 11-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote Northern Territory community had a first episode of acute rheumatic fever 6 weeks ago with polyarthritis and a positive antistreptolysin O titre.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography at the index episode and today shows no valvular abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate secondary prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg once weekly for 3 years, then repeat echocardiography
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily for 5 years, then stop
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units intramuscularly every 28 days until age 21
No prophylaxis, with aspirin only if arthritis recurs in the next year
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units intramuscularly every 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Emergency management of suspected cerebral oedema during treatment for paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis with borderline neurology
stem: A 9-year-old boy is 4 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis with a 10 mL/kg saline bolus, deficit fluids and insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour. He now has a new headache.

data_table.Neurology: Glasgow Coma Score 15 to 13, pupils reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and CT brain before osmotherapy
Bolus 20 mL/kg saline and run 1.5 times maintenance fluid
Increase insulin to 0.1 units/kg/hour and give bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg
Give 3% saline 3 mL/kg, cut fluids a third, call retrieval
Continue fluids, give paracetamol and reassess in 15 minutes

subtopic_detail: Admission threshold for bronchiolitis in a well-perfused infant with borderline saturations and adequate feeding
stem: A 4-month-old term infant has 3 days of coryza and 1 day of cough. He is taking 60% of his usual feeds and has had no apnoeas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 /min, RR 55 /min, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild subcostal recession, bilateral crackles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with low flow oxygen targeting saturation above 92%
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and admit if there is no response
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days and reassess
Discharge home on room air with general practice review tomorrow
Start high flow humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg per minute now

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic versus observation decision in uncomplicated acute otitis media in a well 18 month old with bilateral disease
stem: An 18-month-old girl has 2 days of ear tugging, fever and disturbed sleep, and had acute otitis media 6 months ago. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.ENT: Both tympanic membranes bulging, opaque and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days with analgesia
Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days with analgesia
Analgesia with a delayed amoxicillin script if no better at 48 hours
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 22.5 mg/kg twice daily, 7 days
Refer for tympanocentesis and culture directed antibiotic choice

subtopic_detail: Combined oral contraceptive request in a Gillick competent 15 year old without parental involvement
stem: A 15-year-old girl requests the combined oral contraceptive pill. She attends alone with one sexual partner aged 15 and declines to involve her parents. She explains correctly how to take the pill and manage a missed pill, and there are no safeguarding concerns.

data_table.Medical: BP 112/68 mmHg, BMI 22 kg/m2, no migraine, non-smoker

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline until a parent attends to give consent, as she is 15
Prescribe and telephone her parents once the script is dispensed
Prescribe and discuss long-acting reversible contraception options
Offer condoms only until she turns 16, avoiding any prescription
Report the sexual activity to child protection before prescribing

subtopic_detail: Follow up plan for a 40 hour old term breastfed newborn with a serum bilirubin just below the phototherapy line on the AU nomogram
stem: A 40-hour-old term girl is breastfeeding 2 to 3 hourly with five wet nappies in 24 hours and 5% weight loss. Her direct antiglobulin test is negative.

data_table.Investigations: Serum total bilirubin 240 micromol/L; Australian phototherapy line at this age 280 micromol/L
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, normal tone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start intensive phototherapy now and prepare for exchange transfusion
Give a 60 mL formula top up now and plan no repeat measurement
Discharge today with general practitioner review at two weeks of age
Continue breastfeeding with support and repeat serum bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours
Perform a full septic screen and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin

reference_ranges.value: phototherapy line ~280 micromol/L at 40 hours (AU consensus nomogram)

subtopic_detail: Approach to a 3 year old with 6 days of fever and only 2 clinical criteria but supportive laboratory features suggestive of incomplete Kawasaki disease
stem: A 3-year-old boy has 6 days of fever to 39.6 degrees C unresponsive to antipyretics. He is irritable, with bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection and a peeling perineal rash, but no adenopathy or lip changes.

data_table.Bloods: CRP 128 mg/L, ESR 82 mm/hr, platelets 512 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 68 U/L
data_table.Other: Sterile pyuria; blood and respiratory virus cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care and observe for further clinical criteria
Start intravenous flucloxacillin and benzylpenicillin for occult infection
Give intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg alone and reassess on day 8
Arrange outpatient rheumatology review in one week before treatment
Give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin and echocardiography

subtopic_detail: Nephrology referral criteria in a child with new IgA vasculitis and unexpected proteinuria on urinalysis
stem: A 6-year-old boy has a palpable purpuric rash over his buttocks and lower legs for 5 days with migratory ankle pain, 10 days after an upper respiratory illness.

data_table.Urine: 3+ protein, 2+ blood, red cell casts; protein:creatinine 320 mg/mmol (normal below 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric nephrologist today for biopsy consideration
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks and review
Reassure and repeat urinalysis at general practice in 4 weeks
Start oral ramipril 2.5 mg daily and defer specialist input
Give intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg and discharge home

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic pathway in a stable 22 month old with witnessed aspiration event and normal early chest radiograph
stem: A 22-month-old boy choked on peanuts 4 hours ago. He coughed forcefully, went red in the face, then settled, and has coughed intermittently since.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108 /min, RR 26 /min, SpO2 97% on room air
data_table.Clinical: Alert; mild expiratory wheeze right lower zone, bilateral air entry
data_table.Imaging: Inspiratory chest radiograph normal, no foreign body or hyperinflation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with advice to return if breathing or cough worsens
Refer today for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
Obtain expiratory and lateral decubitus films before considering bronchoscopy
Give nebulised salbutamol and oral prednisolone for viral wheeze
Request a contrast computed tomography scan of the chest today

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial stabilisation of critical coarctation of the aorta presenting as circulatory collapse in a 3 week old missed at the neonatal check
stem: A 3-week-old term boy has 24 hours of poor feeding, greyness with feeds and mottling. The newborn check was normal. The nearest cardiac centre is 3 hours away by retrieval team.

data_table.Perfusion: Right arm BP 96/58, right leg BP 58/34 mmHg, femoral pulses weak

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus and reassess
Intubate and start adrenaline 0.1 microgram/kg/min
Prostaglandin E1 10 nanogram/kg/min, watching for apnoea
Oral propranolol 0.5 mg/kg for outflow obstruction
Face mask oxygen 10 L/min to a pre-ductal saturation of 100%

subtopic_detail: Assessment and initial management of a paediatric iron overdose from prenatal multivitamins
stem: A 22-month-old boy weighing 12 kg presents 90 minutes after being found with his mother's ferrous sulfate tablets, 65 mg elemental iron each; about 20 are missing. He has vomited twice with dark material in the emesis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, BP 92/54 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert but pale, mild epigastric tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Abdominal radiograph and serum iron 4 to 6 hours after ingestion
Gastric lavage now with activated charcoal 1 g/kg by orogastric tube
Empirical intravenous deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour before any iron level
Discharge after an hour of observation with review tomorrow
Oral acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg over an hour, repeated 4-hourly twice

subtopic_detail: Recognition and first line management of paediatric anaphylaxis to peanut in a school aged child
stem: A 7-year-old girl weighing 24 kg arrives 20 minutes after one bite of a peanut butter sandwich. Within 5 minutes she developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling and cough.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 34 /min, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Examination: Short phrases, periorbital angioedema, bilateral wheeze, no stridor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and nebulised salbutamol, deferring adrenaline
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram into the mid anterolateral thigh
Intravenous adrenaline 10 microgram/kg as a slow bolus over 5 minutes
Oral cetirizine 10 mg with intravenous fluid and 4 hours of observation
Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram into the deltoid, repeated at 10 minutes

subtopic_detail: Nasal secretions and feeding in bronchiolitis
stem: A 5-month-old girl admitted with bronchiolitis is snuffly with visible nasal secretions. She repeatedly comes off the bottle after a few sucks and has taken half her usual volume overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 146, RR 50, SpO2 94 percent in room air, temperature 37.5
data_table.Examination: Mild recession, blocked nose, widespread crackles, alert and settled

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Superficial nasal suction with saline drops before feeds
Deep nasopharyngeal suction on a set schedule every 4 hours
Nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent given before each feed
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 milligrams before each feed
Topical phenylephrine nose drops before each feed overnight

subtopic_detail: Peanut anaphylaxis banded IM adrenaline in a 4 year old
stem:
You are the emergency department paediatric registrar. A 4-year-old boy weighing 17 kg is brought in by ambulance 25 minutes after biting a chocolate bar containing peanut. He has known egg allergy but no prior peanut exposure.

His parents describe rapid onset facial swelling, a widespread bumpy red rash, and a barking noise on breathing in with progressive difficulty getting his words out. On arrival he is sitting upright, drooling, and pale. Vital signs are pulse 172, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 90 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. His parents report he uses a preventer inhaler daily for asthma but is well between attacks.

He has audible inspiratory stridor and marked intercostal recession; auscultation reveals bilateral expiratory wheeze. He has never had an EpiPen prescribed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Facial angioedema, widespread urticaria, inspiratory stridor with drooling, bilateral expiratory wheeze

lead_in: What is the single best initial dose and route of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 micrograms IV bolus over 1 minute through peripheral access
Adrenaline 300 micrograms IM into the mid outer thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
Adrenaline 170 micrograms IM calculated as 10 micrograms per kilogram of body weight
Adrenaline 150 micrograms IM into the mid outer thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with high-flow oxygen at 6 L/min

subtopic_detail: Moderate croup steroid dose selection in a 2 year old
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 2-year-old boy weighing 13 kg is brought in at 2 am with a barking cough and a hoarse voice. He was well the day before with only coryza; his mother says the noisy breathing woke him. He is fully immunised and has no other medical history.

On assessment he has a barking cough on triage, and stridor is audible only when he becomes upset. His chest wall shows mild suprasternal indrawing at rest with no substernal recession. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. He is alert, playing intermittently with a toy, and drinks small sips of water on request.

His parents report no drooling, no cyanosis and no previous croup admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Barking cough; stridor when agitated only; mild suprasternal indrawing at rest; alert and interacting

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days with no scheduled observation
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose with observation for 4 hours
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with 3 hour observation after last neb
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg with 3 hour observation and discharge if stable
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose with observation for 3 hours

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months without a source in a 5 week old
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 5-week-old boy weighing 4.2 kg is brought in by his parents because he has felt hot and has been feeding poorly for 6 hours. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth. His mother had a group B streptococcus swab that was not returned before delivery and she received no intrapartum antibiotics.

On examination he is drowsy but rouseable. His fontanelle is flat and there is no rash. Vital signs are pulse 178, blood pressure 68/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius rectally. His capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and his peripheries feel cool. A rapid capillary blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0). His father, a paediatric intensive care nurse, asks whether the workup can be limited to blood and urine given his uncomplicated antenatal history.

A bedside ultrasound of the bladder shows adequate volume for catheter sampling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 68/44 mmHg, RR 62, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rouseable, flat fontanelle, CRT 3 seconds centrally, cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 3.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his investigation and management?

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin with next day paediatric outpatient review by the GP
Blood cultures and urine culture only with IV ceftriaxone and a 4 hour observation
Full septic workup including lumbar puncture with empirical IV cefotaxime and IV benzylpenicillin
Blood cultures alone with IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy and paediatric review
CRP and procalcitonin, defer LP until markers return, then decide on antibiotics

subtopic_detail: New onset paediatric DKA fluid rate in a 9 year old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 9-year-old girl weighing 30 kg presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 4 kg weight loss and 8 hours of vomiting. She is drowsy but rouseable. There is no history of diabetes.

On examination her respirations are deep and rapid and her breath smells of nail polish remover. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Her capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and her tongue is dry. Point-of-care testing shows glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), venous pH 7.10 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-32), ketones 5.6 mmol/L (<0.6). Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (30-70).

A nurse asks whether to start a 20 mL/kg saline bolus given the delayed capillary refill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 108/70 mmHg, RR 34, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), venous pH 7.10 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-32), ketones 5.6 mmol/L (<0.6), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (30-70)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial fluid management?

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 20 minutes then reassess before further fluid
0.9 percent sodium chloride 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes then reassess before further fluid
Immediate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h with no crystalloid until glucose is under 15 mmol/L
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV bolus over 30 minutes to reverse the acidosis
Hartmann's solution 20 mL/kg over 20 minutes then insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h

subtopic_detail: Therapeutic hypothermia eligibility in HIE in a term neonate
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar. A term male neonate is delivered by category 1 caesarean at 39+2 weeks for prolonged fetal bradycardia following a cord prolapse. Time from decision to delivery was 22 minutes. His Apgar scores are 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes and 4 at 10 minutes. He required positive pressure ventilation with intubation at 3 minutes and one dose of adrenaline.

Cord arterial pH is 6.92 with base deficit 17 mmol/L. At 40 minutes of age he is intubated on synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation. He has spontaneous breathing between mechanical breaths, no seizures, but marked hypotonia and absent gag. His pupils are equal and reactive. Blood glucose is 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-6.0). His weight is 3450 grams.

At 55 minutes of age he opens his eyes to painful stimuli only, has no spontaneous movements, and demonstrates absent primitive reflexes. The retrieval team is 90 minutes away. The consultant neonatologist by phone asks you to decide the next intervention.

data_table.Apgar scores: 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes, 4 at 10 minutes
data_table.Neurological examination at 55 minutes: Marked hypotonia, absent gag, opens eyes to pain only, no spontaneous movement, absent primitive reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-6.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Warm to 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius with radiant warmer until the retrieval team arrives
Initiate passive cooling to target rectal temperature 33.5 degrees Celsius while awaiting retrieval
Give phenobarbital 20 mg/kg intravenous loading dose for seizure prophylaxis
Bolus 10 mL/kg of 10 percent glucose intravenously to correct hypoglycaemia
Give a further dose of intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg to support blood pressure

subtopic_detail: Suspected urea cycle disorder in a 4 day old neonate
stem: A 4-day-old boy weighing 3.6 kg is transferred with 12 hours of vomiting after feeding well from birth. He is deeply drowsy, hypotonic and hypothermic, with deep sighing respirations.

data_table.Investigations: Glucose 4.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.48, pCO2 24 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L, ammonia 480 micromol/L (under 100), urine ketones negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Start high protein nasogastric feeds to prevent catabolism
Intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin for sepsis
Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg intravenously as a loading dose
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg intravenously over 30 minutes
Stop protein, give 10 per cent dextrose at 8 mg/kg/min, dialyse

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen therapy escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the ward. A 5-month-old previously well infant was admitted 6 hours ago with a 3 day coryzal illness, cough, and increasing work of breathing. He is feeding at half his usual volumes and has had no apnoeas.

On assessment now he is alert and consolable in his father's arms. Chest auscultation reveals widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. He has moderate subcostal recession, tracheal tug, and nasal flaring. He is not grunting.

Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 58, SpO2 88% in room air, temperature 37.8. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. Nasopharyngeal swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 92/58, RR 58, SpO2 88% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and consolable; widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze; moderate subcostal recession, tracheal tug, nasal flaring; no grunting
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg (35-45), HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-32); NPA positive RSV
data_table.Feeding: 50% of usual volumes over past 12 hours; no apnoeas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to keep SpO2 at or above 90%
Commence high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and reassess in 1 to 2 hours
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back three times and reassess bronchodilator response
Escalate to bilevel non-invasive ventilation because SpO2 remains below 90% in room air
Continue room air observation with hourly work of breathing scoring and no supplemental oxygen

subtopic_detail: Croup severity based dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 2-year-old is brought in at 2200 by his mother with a barking cough and hoarse voice that woke him. He is normally well and fully immunised.

In the cubicle he is settled on his mother's knee, drinking a small amount of water, with an audible barking cough between sentences. There is mild inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when he is quiet. Chest wall recession is limited to mild suprasternal indrawing. He is alert with normal colour.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.9. His mother declines nasal prong oxygen because it distresses him and reports no drooling or difficulty swallowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 34, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Barking cough with hoarse voice; mild inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when quiet; mild suprasternal indrawing only; alert with normal colour
data_table.Feeding and swallow: Drinking water in cubicle; no drooling; no dysphagia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen?

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally once with disposition review at 30 minutes
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally once with disposition review at 30 minutes
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once with disposition review at 30 minutes
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily for 3 days with review before further doses
Withhold corticosteroids and observe for 4 hours before making a treatment decision

subtopic_detail: UTI imaging after first typical episode
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 14-month-old girl in outpatients 2 weeks after her first admission with pyelonephritis. She was fully immunised, was born at term after uncomplicated antenatal ultrasounds, and has had no prior infections.

During admission urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. She defervesced within 24 hours of intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and completed oral cefalexin at home. Renal function and electrolytes on discharge were within normal limits.

Today she is thriving on the paediatric growth centiles. Her parents ask what imaging she needs. Antenatal renal ultrasounds at 20 and 32 weeks were reported as normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 50th centile
data_table.Illness course: Defervesced within 24 hours of IV antibiotics; oral course completed
data_table.Renal function: Discharge creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What imaging is most appropriate now?

options.text: Arrange a DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to look for renal cortical scarring in this child
Arrange an outpatient renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks to exclude an anatomical abnormality
Reassure the family that no routine renal tract imaging is required after this first typical UTI
Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram to grade reflux before considering long term prophylaxis
Commence long term oral trimethoprim prophylaxis until an outpatient specialist review takes place

subtopic_detail: Rehydration route after failed oral rehydration
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. An 18-month-old boy has had 2 days of loose watery bowel motions and vomiting. His mother has been offering oral rehydration solution at home but he continues to vomit small amounts within 10 minutes of every offer.

In the department he is alert but tired, with sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and skin turgor is reduced. Peripheries are warm. He weighs 11 kg, previously 12 kg.

Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.6. He has just received a single oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg and again vomited a 30 mL sip of oral rehydration solution 15 minutes later.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 92/54, RR 28, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Weight: 11 kg today; 12 kg at well child check 3 weeks ago (approximately 8% loss)
data_table.Examination: Alert but tired; sunken eyes; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally; reduced skin turgor; warm peripheries
data_table.Interventions so far: Ondansetron 2 mg oral 15 minutes ago; 30 mL oral rehydration solution vomited again

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Admit for observation and offer clear fluids ad libitum without a structured rehydration plan
Cannulate and give a 20 mL/kg intravenous saline bolus followed by intravenous maintenance fluids
Give a further oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg and continue small volume oral rehydration solution sips
Insert a nasogastric tube and rehydrate at 25 mL/kg/hour of oral rehydration solution for 4 hours with electrolyte review
Give an intramuscular metoclopramide 0.15 mg/kg dose to control vomiting before further oral trials

subtopic_detail: Fever workup under 3 months
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 5-week-old term boy is brought in by his parents for feeding poorly for the past 6 hours and one episode of vomiting.

He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery. His mother was group B streptococcus positive on antenatal screening but received two doses of intrapartum benzylpenicillin. Antenatal serology, including hepatitis and syphilis, was within normal limits.

On examination he is pale, mottled to the knees, and only briefly responsive to handling. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no rash. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally. Peripheries are cool.

Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 68/38, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 38.4. Point-of-care glucose is 3.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 68/38, RR 62, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled to knees, only briefly responsive; anterior fontanelle soft; no rash; capillary refill 3 seconds; cool peripheries
data_table.Antenatal: Term normal vaginal delivery; mother GBS positive with 2 doses intrapartum benzylpenicillin; hepatitis and syphilis serology within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial workup and empirical antibiotic plan?

options.text: Observation on the paediatric ward for 24 hours without immediate empirical antibiotics or lumbar puncture
Blood culture, urine, and oral amoxicillin as an outpatient with 24 hour paediatric review
Blood culture and urine only, deferring lumbar puncture until CRP and procalcitonin results
Blood culture, urine, chest x ray, and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone with lumbar puncture only if unwell
Full septic workup including blood culture, urine, and lumbar puncture, then intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin

subtopic_detail: Adrenaline dosing in paediatric anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the paediatric consultant on for the emergency department. A 4-year-old girl weighing 16 kg develops generalised urticaria, lip swelling, and a hoarse cough 5 minutes after her first taste of a cashew.

She has a personal history of eczema and known egg allergy managed by an accredited paediatric allergist. There is an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan in her school bag. No adrenaline autoinjector has yet been used tonight.
