On assessment she is anxious and pale with audible inspiratory stridor and mild subcostal recession. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral wheeze. Peripheries are warm.

Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 84/48, respiratory rate 38, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.8. Intravenous access has not yet been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 84/48, RR 38, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Anxious, pale; audible inspiratory stridor; mild subcostal recession; bilateral wheeze; warm peripheries
data_table.Background: Eczema; known egg allergy; ASCIA action plan in bag; no autoinjector given yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adrenaline dose and route to give immediately?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram from an EpiPen Junior into the mid anterolateral thigh
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram from an EpiPen into the mid anterolateral thigh
Intravenous adrenaline 160 microgram (10 microgram/kg) undiluted through a peripheral cannula
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow oxygen for the airway compromise
Subcutaneous adrenaline 160 microgram (10 microgram/kg) into the upper arm

subtopic_detail: DKA initial fluid choice
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the resuscitation cubicle. A 9-year-old girl weighing 30 kg presents with a 3 week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and 3 kg weight loss, and 24 hours of vomiting.

She is alert but exhausted. She has deep sighing respirations. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Mucous membranes are dry.

Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.4. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.08, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L. Sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine within normal limits. She has an intravenous cannula sited.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/58, RR 34, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Alert but exhausted; deep sighing respirations; capillary refill 3 seconds; dry mucous membranes; cool peripheries
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.08, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid regimen?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 600 mL (20 mL/kg) over 15 minutes as an urgent resuscitation bolus for shock
0.9% sodium chloride 300 mL (10 mL/kg) over 30 to 60 minutes then reassess before deficit fluid
5% dextrose in 0.45% saline 300 mL over 30 minutes as the initial fluid to prevent hypoglycaemia
Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann) 300 mL over 30 minutes to correct the metabolic acidosis directly
Commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour before any fluid is given to shut down ketogenesis

subtopic_detail: Order of hour one interventions
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 4-year-old with a 2 day febrile illness is triaged looking mottled, drowsy, and cool to the elbows. There is a petechial rash over the ankles that does not blanch.

Vital signs on arrival: pulse 172, blood pressure 74/38, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 39.8. Capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally.

You have called for senior support and a resuscitation trolley is at the bedside. Intraosseous access is available if peripheral cannulation fails. Blood culture bottles and intravenous cefotaxime are drawn up and ready. A 20 mL/kg saline bolus is prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172, BP 74/38, RR 40, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 39.8
data_table.Examination: Mottled, drowsy, cool to elbows; non blanching petechial rash over ankles; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Available: IO kit ready, cefotaxime drawn up, 20 mL/kg saline bolus prepared, blood culture bottles at bedside

lead_in: What is the most appropriate order of interventions in the first hour?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus then defer antibiotics until formal blood cultures return in the laboratory in 6 hours
Commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min immediately, then attempt IV access for antibiotics
Obtain IV or IO access, draw blood cultures, give IV cefotaxime within the hour, then a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
Arrange urgent CT brain first to exclude raised intracranial pressure before any antibiotic, fluid, or vasoactive drug
Give oral paracetamol only and rescreen vital signs at 30 minutes before deciding on further intervention

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizures with disconfirming metabolic profile
stem: A term girl born 60 hours ago, with normal Apgars and cord pH 7.28, has recurrent 30-second episodes of rhythmic jerking of the right arm and leg. She is alert between events.

data_table.Cranial ultrasound: Left middle cerebral artery territory hyperechoic lesion
data_table.Pending: Septic screen, ammonia and lactate pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start therapeutic whole body cooling to 33.5 degrees C for 72 hours
Load intravenous levetiracetam 40 mg/kg, with fewer adverse effects
Give intravenous 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg and calcium gluconate 1 mL/kg
Load intravenous phenobarbital 20 mg/kg and transfer for aEEG
Await the lactate and ammonia before starting any antiepileptic

subtopic_detail: Sudden refusal to use an arm after a longitudinal pull in a toddler
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 2-year-old girl brought in by her father an hour after he lifted her by one hand to stop her stepping off a kerb. She cried briefly and has not used the arm since.

She is settled on her father's lap with the right arm held loosely at her side, forearm turned inwards. She reaches confidently for a sticker with her left hand and ignores it when you offer it on the right. There is no swelling, no bruising and no deformity, and she does not cry when you palpate the clavicle, humerus, forearm or wrist. She cries only when you attempt to turn the palm upwards. She is fully immunised, has no previous presentations and was born at term.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling or bruising, no bony tenderness along clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna or wrist, distal pulses present, capillary refill under 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a hyperpronation manoeuvre at the elbow and observe for return of arm use
Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm before attempting any reduction manoeuvre
Apply a broad arm sling and arrange fracture clinic review within the following week
Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection given the injury mechanism described
Give oral ibuprofen and review in four hours to see whether arm use returns spontaneously

subtopic_detail: Persistent moist umbilical lesion after cord separation in a well infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-week-old boy whose mother reports the belly button has stayed wet since the cord came away at day twelve. She has been dabbing it with cooled boiled water and finds a small yellow stain on his singlet each day.

He is breastfeeding well, has regained above birth weight and is tracking along the 50th centile. At the umbilicus there is a pink moist stalk about 4 mm across sitting within the umbilical ring, with no surrounding redness or induration of the abdominal wall and no discharge that smells of urine or faeces. Pressing gently around the umbilicus does not cause him to cry.

data_table.Examination: Pink moist stalk 4 mm at the umbilicus within the ring, scant serous discharge, no periumbilical erythema, no induration, abdomen soft, no palpable mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise salt application by the parents twice daily and reassess the umbilicus after four weeks
Apply silver nitrate to the lesion with protection of the surrounding skin and review in one week
Take a swab and start oral flucloxacillin for presumed umbilical infection of the cord stump
Arrange an abdominal ultrasound scan to define the anatomy before any local treatment is given
Refer to paediatric surgery for elective excision of the lesion under general anaesthetic

subtopic_detail: Persistent head turn preference with a neck lump in a young infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-week-old girl referred by her maternal child health nurse because she always turns her head one way. She was born at term by vacuum extraction after a prolonged second stage.

Her mother says she feels a firm oval lump about the size of an olive low in the right side of the neck. The head rests tilted towards the right shoulder with the chin pointing left, and you can passively rotate the chin to the right only about halfway before firm resistance. The right sternocleidomastoid is thickened and firm without warmth or overlying redness. She fixes and follows across the midline with both eyes, and her hips abduct fully and symmetrically with no clunk.

data_table.Examination: Head tilt to the right with chin rotation to the left, firm 2 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid, passive chin rotation to the right restricted to approximately 45 degrees, no lymphadenopathy, red reflex present bilaterally, hips stable with full symmetrical abduction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a magnetic resonance scan of the brain and cervical cord to exclude a posterior fossa lesion
Reassure the mother that the posture resolves spontaneously and review at the twelve month check
Refer for physiotherapy with a home stretching and positioning program and arrange clinical review
Arrange urgent ultrasound of the neck mass and cervical spine radiographs before any treatment
Refer to ophthalmology for assessment of an ocular cause of the persistent head posture

subtopic_detail: Progressive asymmetry of the infant skull noticed by parents at four months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4-month-old boy whose parents are worried that the back of his head looks lopsided. They noticed it at about eight weeks and think it has become more obvious.

He sleeps on his back and spends much of the day in a car capsule that they carry between the house and the car. Viewed from above, the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits forward of the left, and the right side of the forehead is slightly fuller than the left. The sutures feel open with no palpable ridge, and the anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. He smiles socially, follows across the midline and lifts his head well when placed on his tummy. Head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with ipsilateral anterior ear displacement and ipsilateral frontal bossing, sutures palpably open with no ridging, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, full passive neck rotation both directions, head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for consideration of early suture release and cranial vault surgery
Arrange fitting of a cranial orthotic helmet now to correct the asymmetry before growth slows further
Recommend side lying and prone sleep positions overnight to take pressure off the flattened occiput
Advise repositioning with increased supervised tummy time and arrange review in six to eight weeks
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction of the sutures

subtopic_detail: Painless fluctuating scrotal swelling present since birth in an infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 11-month-old boy whose parents report that one side of his scrotum has been puffy since he was born. They say it looks bigger in the evening and smaller when he wakes.

He is thriving and has had no vomiting, no irritability and no change in his bowel habit. The right hemiscrotum is enlarged and non-tender, the swelling transilluminates, and you can get above it with your fingers so that the cord above is normal. Both testes are palpable within the scrotum and are of equal size. The swelling does not reduce with gentle pressure and there is no palpable thickening at the external ring.

data_table.Examination: Right hemiscrotal swelling that transilluminates, non-tender, upper border palpable with normal cord above, both testes descended and equal, no palpable inguinal component, abdomen soft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for surgical repair within the next few weeks given the risk of bowel becoming trapped
Arrange scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to characterise the swelling and assess testicular blood flow
Aspirate the fluid in clinic to relieve the swelling and to confirm the nature of the contents
Refer urgently to the emergency department for exploration given the possibility of testicular torsion
Reassure the parents and review at two years of age, referring if the swelling persists then

subtopic_detail: Red swollen foreskin with dysuria in an uncircumcised boy
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 4-year-old uncircumcised boy brought in by his father with a sore penis for two days. He has been crying when he passes urine and holding on, and his father noticed the end of the penis looks red and puffy.

His father has been retracting the foreskin daily at bath time because he read it should be pulled back to keep it clean. On examination the distal foreskin and glans are erythematous and oedematous with a small amount of thick discharge at the preputial opening. The foreskin is not retracted and returns easily to its resting position when you release it. He is passing urine in a normal stream and the abdomen is soft with no loin tenderness. He is afebrile and drinking normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Erythema and oedema of the distal prepuce and glans, thick discharge at the preputial opening, foreskin lies in normal position and is not trapped behind the glans, no cellulitis of the shaft, no inguinal lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise saline bathing with topical treatment and stop the daily forcible retraction of the foreskin
Attempt manual reduction of the foreskin now with ice and sustained compression of the glans
Collect a clean catch urine sample and commence oral trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection
Refer for circumcision to prevent recurrent episodes and to allow easier hygiene in the future
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin because of the risk of ascending infection of the urinary tract

subtopic_detail: Crops of umbilicated papules with surrounding dermatitis in a school aged child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6-year-old girl whose mother has noticed small bumps spreading across her daughter's trunk and armpit over three months. Two of them have become red and itchy in the past week and the mother is worried the school will exclude her.

There are around twenty firm dome shaped papules 2 to 4 mm across, several with a central dimple, clustered in the right axilla and scattered on the adjacent trunk. Two lesions are surrounded by a patch of dry itchy dermatitis. There is no honey coloured crust, no pustule, no surrounding warmth and no lymphadenopathy. She has mild atopic dermatitis controlled with an emollient and swims twice weekly at the local pool. She is otherwise well and fully immunised.

data_table.Examination: Approximately twenty firm umbilicated papules 2 to 4 mm on right axilla and trunk, two with surrounding eczematous change, no crusting or pustulation, no regional lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange immunological assessment including lymphocyte subsets given the number of lesions present
Explain that the lesions resolve without treatment and treat the surrounding dermatitis topically
Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to treat secondary bacterial infection of the lesions
Refer for cryotherapy to all lesions and exclude her from swimming until the skin has cleared
Prescribe topical permethrin to the whole body and treat all household contacts on the same day

subtopic_detail: Parental concern about inward pointing feet in a walking toddler
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 2-year-old boy whose grandmother insists his feet point inwards and that he needs special boots. His parents say he trips a little more than his older sister did but plays happily at the park all afternoon.

He walks with both feet turned inwards to a similar degree and runs without difficulty. With him lying prone and the knees flexed, the foot points inwards relative to the thigh on both sides. Passive hip rotation is symmetrical with internal rotation of about 50 degrees and external rotation of about 45 degrees on each side. The lateral border of each foot is straight and there is no crease at the midfoot. There is no pain, no limp and no asymmetry, and he has met all developmental milestones.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bilateral in-toeing gait, thigh foot angle inwardly directed and equal bilaterally, hip internal rotation 50 degrees and external rotation 45 degrees bilaterally, straight lateral foot borders, no pain or limp, normal neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for serial casting of both feet to correct the inward deviation of the forefoot
Arrange physiotherapy for a supervised program of hip external rotation strengthening exercises
Reassure the family that the gait corrects with growth and review if pain or asymmetry develops
Prescribe corrective boots with a torsion bar to be worn overnight until the gait has normalised
Arrange radiographs of both hips and lower limbs to measure the degree of femoral anteversion

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear after a low energy twist with normal initial radiographs
stem: A 20-month-old boy has refused to walk since yesterday, after catching his foot and twisting as he came off a slide. He cried briefly, then played on until bath time. He is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Crawls readily, full painless hip, knee and ankle range, pain on gentle torsion of the mid tibia
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L, tibia and fibula radiographs show no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound and joint aspiration
Refer to child protection for a skeletal survey
Arrange a same-day technetium bone scan of the leg
Immobilise in an above-knee backslab, review in one week
Discharge with analgesia since radiographs are normal

subtopic_detail: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent athlete with night pain and a thigh mass
stem: A 13-year-old basketballer has had anterior right knee pain for ten weeks, worse despite six weeks of rest and now waking him at night. He has lost 3 kg over four months.

data_table.Examination: Firm deep swelling over the distal femur, tibial tuberosity not tender, small knee effusion
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-170), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (100-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Graded quadriceps loading with activity modification
Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee as initial imaging
Empirical oral antibiotics for subacute osteomyelitis
Open biopsy of the thigh mass at the local hospital
Plain radiographs with prompt paediatric orthopaedic referral

subtopic_detail: Abrupt pallor and lethargy after a facial rash illness in a child with a known red cell disorder
stem: A 7-year-old girl with hereditary spherocytosis is pale and lethargic. A week ago she had a red rash on both cheeks and a lacy rash on her arms.

data_table.Examination: Marked pallor, spleen 3 cm below the costal margin, unchanged
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 54 g/L (baseline 108), reticulocytes 6 x10^9/L (baseline 210), bilirubin 14 micromol/L, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the single most important investigation?

options.text: Parvovirus B19 serology with polymerase chain reaction testing
Repeat direct antiglobulin testing with a red cell eluate
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for infiltration
Abdominal ultrasound measuring the spleen for sequestration
Iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation

subtopic_detail: Worsening bow legs in a heavy toddler beyond the age of expected remodelling
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy referred because his legs bow outwards. His mother says other people have started commenting and that it looks worse now than when he began walking at eleven months.

He weighs above the 97th centile for age and his height is on the 50th centile. Standing with the medial malleoli together, the gap between the knees measures 7 cm, and the bowing is more pronounced on the left than the right. As he walks you notice the left knee thrusts outwards during stance. He has no bone pain, no fractures and no dental problems, and he drinks around 600 mL of full cream cow milk daily alongside a varied diet with fish and eggs.

data_table.Examination: Intercondylar distance 7 cm with asymmetry left greater than right, lateral thrust of the left knee during stance phase, no wrist or costochondral widening, no frontal bossing, weight above 97th centile, height 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.55 mmol/L (1.10-1.95), alkaline phosphatase 260 U/L (children 100-400), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe night splints for both legs and arrange physiotherapy to correct the walking pattern
Arrange standing long leg alignment radiographs and refer to paediatric orthopaedics for review
Reassure the family that the alignment corrects spontaneously and arrange review in twelve months
Commence high dose oral colecalciferol with elemental calcium supplementation and repeat bloods
Refer for a skeletal survey and genetic assessment to investigate a possible underlying bone dysplasia

subtopic_detail: Nipple pain and poor weight gain attributed to a restrictive lingual frenulum
stem: A 12-day-old girl feeds every two hours for fifty minutes with audible clicking. Her mother has cracked nipples and shooting pain each feed, unchanged after two days of lactation support.

data_table.Examination: Frenulum inserts near the tongue tip; tongue cannot lift above mid mouth or past the lower gum
data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3420 g, 3140 g day four, 3180 g today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical antifungal for mother and infant for thrush
Division of the upper lip frenulum with oral motor therapy
Frenotomy with continued lactation support and weight review
Continue lactation support alone and reassess in two weeks
Transfer to expressed milk by bottle to heal the nipples

subtopic_detail: Widespread itchy eruption with palmar involvement in an infant under two months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 7-week-old boy whose parents report he has been scratching and unsettled for two weeks and that a rash has spread over him. His mother has an intensely itchy rash on her wrists and between her fingers that is worse at night.

He has erythematous papules and pustules on the palms and soles, scattered papules over the trunk, and several nodules in the axillae and groin. There are burrows visible on the instep of the left foot. He has a low grade eczema history but this eruption looks different to his parents and has not responded to emollient and one percent hydrocortisone. He is feeding well and weight is tracking on the 25th centile. There is no fever and no honey coloured crusting.

data_table.Examination: Papules and pustules on palms and soles, burrows on the left instep, nodules in axillae and groin, scattered truncal papules, scalp spared of nodules, no crusting or cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Weight on the 25th centile, no laboratory tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for the infant?

options.text: Topical benzyl benzoate 25 percent applied to the body below the neck on three consecutive nights
Escalation to a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily for the whole eruption
Oral cefalexin suspension for seven days to treat presumed bacterial infection of the pustular lesions
Topical permethrin 5 percent applied to the whole body including scalp, with all contacts treated
Oral ivermectin given as a single weight based dose with a repeat dose after seven days elapse

subtopic_detail: Sharply marginated perioral and perineal erosions with diarrhoea in a breastfed preterm infant
stem: A 4-month-old girl born at 30 weeks, exclusively breastfed, has a nappy rash unresponsive to two weeks of topical antifungal. She has had loose stools for a month and has lost the ability to roll.

data_table.Examination: Sharply marginated erosive plaques periorally, perineally, on fingertips and heels; no satellite lesions; sparse lightened hair
data_table.Growth: Weight has fallen from the 25th to the 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 28 g/L (35-50), alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L (100-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to nystatin with hydrocortisone cream
Refer for skin biopsy with immunofluorescence
Trial an extensively hydrolysed formula
Arrange sweat chloride and faecal elastase testing
Measure serum zinc and start zinc supplementation

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis versus transient synovitis in the acutely limping preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy in the emergency department. For two days he has refused to put any weight on his right leg, and his mother says he was off his food and hot to touch overnight. He had a runny nose that settled a fortnight ago.

He lies with the right hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and cries with any attempt at internal rotation. There is no rash and no other joint is involved. Ultrasound of the right hip shows a moderate effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.9 C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.9 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 56 mm/h (<15), blood culture collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for hip joint aspiration before antibiotics are started
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any invasive intervention
Start intravenous flucloxacillin now and repeat the inflammatory markers in 24 hours
Admit for observation on regular paracetamol and repeat the hip ultrasound tomorrow
Oral ibuprofen with orthopaedic review in 48 hours if he is still not weight bearing

subtopic_detail: Choosing hip ultrasound or radiograph by age in late-presenting developmental dysplasia
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 6-month-old girl brought in by her father, who has noticed that her nappy is harder to fasten on one side and that one leg looks shorter when she lies on her back. She was born at term in the breech position and her newborn hip examination was recorded as normal.

On examination there is asymmetry of the thigh skin creases and limited abduction of the left hip to 50 degrees. The Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative.

data_table.Examination: Left hip abduction limited to 50 degrees, asymmetric thigh creases, apparent left femoral shortening, Ortolani and Barlow negative, spine and lower limb neurology normal

lead_in: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Static and dynamic ultrasound of both hips performed by a paediatric sonographer
Computed tomography of the pelvis with three-dimensional acetabular reconstruction
Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under general anaesthesia within two weeks
Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis with the hips in the neutral position
Repeat clinical hip examination by the child health nurse at the 12-month check

subtopic_detail: Topical versus oral antibiotic threshold in childhood impetigo
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-year-old girl whose mother reports three crusty yellow patches around her right nostril and upper lip that appeared four days ago and are slowly spreading outwards. Her older brother had something similar last month.

She is systemically well, eating normally and has been at school throughout. Examination shows three discrete lesions, the largest 15 mm across, with honey-coloured crust and no surrounding spreading erythema, warmth or induration. There is no lymphadenopathy and no other body site is affected.

data_table.Examination: Three crusted lesions on the right perinasal skin and upper lip, largest 15 mm, no cellulitic margin, no regional lymphadenopathy, remainder of skin clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Topical fusidic acid twice daily with school exclusion until all crusts have gone
Topical mupirocin 2% applied three times daily for five days after crust removal
Oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole twice daily for a three-day short course
Oral cefalexin given four times daily for a seven-day course starting today
Topical hydrogen peroxide 1% cream applied twice daily until the crusting settles

subtopic_detail: Timing of diagnostic audiology after a refer result on newborn hearing screening
stem:
You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 3-week-old boy in the newborn follow-up clinic. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and went home on day two. The state newborn hearing screening program recorded a refer result in the left ear on both the initial automated screen and the repeat screen before discharge, with a pass in the right ear.

He is feeding and growing well, and his mother says he startles to the dog barking. Examination including the external ears and a search for craniofacial or neck anomalies is unremarkable, and there is no family history of childhood deafness.

data_table.Examination: Normal pinnae and patent canals bilaterally, no preauricular pits or tags, no neck sinuses, no dysmorphic features, weight on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat surgery for tympanometry and microsuction of the left ear
Reassure the parents and rescreen with automated testing at the 6-week immunisations
Refer for diagnostic auditory brainstem response testing to be completed by 3 months
Arrange congenital cytomegalovirus urine testing and defer audiology until that returns
Arrange developmental surveillance with formal speech assessment at 12 months of age

subtopic_detail: Separating true infantile esotropia from pseudostrabismus on cover testing
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-month-old girl whose grandmother is convinced that her left eye turns inwards, particularly in photographs. Her mother has not noticed it and says the baby looks at her normally during feeds.

The baby has a broad flat nasal bridge and prominent skin folds at the inner corners of both eyes. The corneal light reflex is displaced laterally in the left eye. On cover testing, covering the right eye produces an outward movement of the left eye to take up fixation. She was born at term and her development is age appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Prominent bilateral epicanthic folds, corneal light reflex displaced temporally in the left eye, cover test shows outward refixation movement of the left eye, red reflex present and symmetric bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist for assessment within the next few weeks
Commence part-time occlusion of the right eye with patching for two hours each day
Arrange urgent ocular ultrasound to exclude an intraocular mass before any referral
Refer to an optometrist for cycloplegic refraction and spectacle correction if needed
Reassure that this is pseudostrabismus from the epicanthic folds and review in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Slit lamp surveillance interval for silent uveitis in antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular arthritis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the rheumatology clinic reviewing a 3-year-old girl diagnosed six weeks ago with arthritis of the right knee and left ankle, persisting for four months with no other joints involved. She has no fever, no rash and no systemic features.

Her parents report that her eyes have never been red, sore or watery and that she does not avoid bright light. Antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1:320 and rheumatoid factor is negative. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections are planned and her arthritis is otherwise well controlled on naproxen.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis of the right knee and left ankle with 10 degree fixed flexion at the knee, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, white eyes with normal pupils and visual behaviour
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive 1:320, rheumatoid factor negative, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (<5), haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140)

lead_in: What ophthalmological follow-up should be arranged?

options.text: Slit lamp examination every 3 months, continuing for several years from diagnosis
Ophthalmology review only if her eyes become red, painful or sensitive to bright light
Fundoscopy every 3 months performed in the rheumatology clinic by the treating team
Visual acuity testing every 3 months by the orthoptist with slit lamp only if reduced
Slit lamp examination every 12 months, continuing for several years from diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Imaging acute haematogenous bone infection when the plain radiograph is still normal
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 9-year-old boy with five days of increasing pain in the left lower thigh and two days of fever. His mother says he has been limping and will not run, and that he grazed the same knee playing football a fortnight ago. The graze has healed.

He is tender to firm pressure over the distal femoral metaphysis with no overlying warmth or fluctuance. The knee itself has a full painless range of movement and no effusion on ultrasound. A radiograph of the femur shows only subtle soft tissue swelling with no periosteal reaction or lytic change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 64 mm/h (<15), blood cultures collected, femoral radiograph shows soft tissue swelling only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat plain radiograph of the femur in 10 days to look for new periosteal reaction
Computed tomography of the femur with reconstruction to assess the cortex and marrow
Technetium-99m bone scan of the whole skeleton, arranged as an inpatient this week
Ultrasound of the distal femur to look for a subperiosteal collection and guide aspiration
Magnetic resonance imaging of the femur with contrast, arranged as an inpatient today

subtopic_detail: Gonadotrophin stimulation to separate central from peripheral early puberty in a girl under eight
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6-year-old girl referred because her mother noticed breast development four months ago that has continued to progress. She has also grown out of two shoe sizes this year and has developed body odour, but there is no pubic or axillary hair.

She has no headaches, no visual symptoms and no history of central nervous system insult. There are no cafe-au-lait patches and the abdominal examination is normal. Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 90th centile over 18 months, and a bone age radiograph reads 9 years against a chronological age of 6 years.

data_table.Examination: Breast Tanner stage 3, pubic hair Tanner stage 1, no axillary hair, no cafe-au-lait macules, no abdominal mass, fundi normal, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 9 years at chronological age 6 years, oestradiol detectable, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, early morning basal luteinising hormone equivocal

lead_in: Which investigation will best clarify the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test with serial luteinising hormone sampling
Pelvic ultrasound measuring uterine length and assessing both ovaries for a mass lesion
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary with dedicated hypothalamic views
Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin with alpha fetoprotein and a repeat oestradiol
Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone with androstenedione and an early morning cortisol level

subtopic_detail: Interpreting coeliac serology taken after gluten has already been withdrawn from the diet
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 8-year-old girl whose parents removed wheat from her diet three months ago because of bloating and loose stools, with good symptomatic improvement. They now want the diagnosis confirmed.

Her weight has tracked along the 10th centile and her height along the 25th, both unchanged over two years. Her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease. Blood taken last week shows a tissue transglutaminase IgA of 3 U/mL with a total IgA within the normal range, and a normal full blood count with ferritin 34 micrograms/L (15-200).

data_table.Examination: Weight on the 10th centile, height on the 25th centile, abdomen soft and non-tender, no clubbing, no mouth ulcers, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase IgA 3 U/mL (<15), total IgA within normal limits, haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), ferritin 34 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that coeliac disease is excluded and continue the gluten free diet
Request HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing and stop further investigation if both come back positive
Request deamidated gliadin peptide IgG antibodies to improve the sensitivity of testing
Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsies on her current diet
Reintroduce gluten for at least six weeks and then repeat the tissue transglutaminase IgA

subtopic_detail: Adding oral ivermectin to topical therapy for hyperkeratotic crusted scabies in a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital admitting a 7-year-old Aboriginal boy flown in from a remote community with thick, scaly, fissured plaques over his hands, feet, elbows and scalp that have built up over several months. His grandmother says the whole family has had itchy skin, and that his skin has been getting crustier despite two courses of a cream from the clinic.

He has widespread hyperkeratotic crusting with underlying erythema and several fissures that are weeping. He is afebrile with no cellulitic margin. Skin scrapings show numerous mites and eggs. He has no history of immunosuppression and his weight is 22 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Thick hyperkeratotic plaques on hands, feet, elbows and scalp with fissuring, no spreading erythema or warmth, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Skin scrapings show numerous mites and eggs, white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin for secondary infection followed by topical permethrin on discharge
Topical permethrin 5% applied on two occasions one week apart with household treatment
Oral ivermectin in repeated doses combined with topical permethrin and a keratolytic agent
Topical benzyl benzoate applied daily for one week with oral antihistamines for itching
Oral ivermectin as a single weight-based dose with review in the outpatient clinic weekly

subtopic_detail: Murmur characteristics that mandate echocardiography in an otherwise well school-aged child
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a pre-participation check on a 10-year-old boy before he joins a representative football squad. He has no symptoms, exercises without breathlessness and has never fainted. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death or inherited heart disease.

He is well grown with normal femoral pulses and no cyanosis or clubbing. Auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal edge in the third intercostal space, unchanged when he sits forward, with a normal first and second heart sound and no thrill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, no thrill, normal first and second heart sounds, femoral pulses present and synchronous with radial, no hepatomegaly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange serial blood pressure measurement in all four limbs and review the findings in a month
Reassure and review in 12 months, as this has the features of a Still's vibratory murmur
Reassure and review in 12 months, as the murmur has all the features of a venous hum
Arrange an electrocardiogram and chest radiograph and refer only if either is abnormal
Refer for echocardiography and paediatric cardiology assessment before clearing him to play

subtopic_detail: Referred knee pain with a normal anteroposterior hip film in an adolescent with a high body mass index
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy with six weeks of aching in the left knee, worse after sport and better with rest, which his father attributes to a growth spurt. There was no injury. For the past week he has been walking with his left foot turned outwards.

He is afebrile and systemically well. The left knee has a full range of movement, no effusion, no joint line tenderness and no ligamentous laxity. When the left hip is flexed it rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation is limited to 10 degrees. His body mass index is on the 97th centile. An anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis is reported by the emergency consultant as showing no fracture and no joint space loss.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Left knee examination normal, obligatory external rotation on left hip flexion, left hip internal rotation limited to 10 degrees, left leg externally rotated on standing, no thigh or calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), anteroposterior pelvic radiograph reported as showing no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Make him non-weight bearing and obtain frog-leg lateral views of both hips urgently
Arrange outpatient magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee within the next two weeks
Request an ultrasound of the left hip to look for an effusion suggesting joint infection
Discharge with simple analgesia, activity modification and general practitioner review in a month
Request thyroid function tests and a bone profile before arranging any further hip imaging

subtopic_detail: Marrow examination before corticosteroids when arthritis is accompanied by disproportionate night pain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old girl referred with eight weeks of joint pain and swelling affecting both knees and the left wrist. She has had intermittent fevers to 38.2 C and has become reluctant to walk in the mornings.

Her parents describe her waking crying at night with pain in her shins that settles with cuddling, and say she has stopped wanting to be picked up under the arms. Examination confirms synovitis of both knees. She has no rash and no lymphadenopathy, and her liver and spleen are not enlarged. The rheumatology consultant is considering starting oral prednisolone while awaiting the antinuclear antibody result.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Synovitis of both knees and the left wrist, tenderness over both tibial shafts away from any joint, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-135), white cell count 4.1 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), neutrophils 1.6 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-400), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (<5), lactate dehydrogenase raised, blood film not yet examined

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for presumed systemic arthritis and review the response in one week
Start naproxen and repeat the full blood count with inflammatory markers in two weeks
Discuss urgently with haematology and arrange bone marrow examination before any corticosteroid
Arrange ferritin, triglycerides and fibrinogen to assess for macrophage activation syndrome
Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging to map the extent of the bone involvement

subtopic_detail: School exclusion period and notification for mumps in a vaccinated child
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 7-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with 3 days of fever and a tender swelling in front of and below both ears. He is finding it hard to open his mouth wide enough to eat.

His mother confirms from the immunisation record that he received two doses of measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, the second at 18 months. The family returned 16 days ago from a holiday in Fiji, where an older cousin had a similar illness with facial swelling.

On examination the swelling obscures the angle of the jaw on both sides. The testes are normal in size and non-tender and there is no neck stiffness. A buccal swab has been collected for viral polymerase chain reaction and the result is pending. His mother asks when he can return to school.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral swelling obscuring the angle of the jaw, oral mucosa moist, no neck stiffness, testes normal
data_table.Investigations: Buccal swab for viral polymerase chain reaction pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about school exclusion and public health action?

options.text: Exclude until the facial swelling has completely resolved, and notify the public health unit
Exclude for 5 days from the onset of the facial swelling, and notify the public health unit
Exclude for 9 days from the onset of the facial swelling, and notify the public health unit
Allow immediate return to school because he is vaccinated, and notify the public health unit
Exclude for 4 days from the onset of the fever, and notify the public health unit

subtopic_detail: Management of extensive molluscum contagiosum on a background of atopic dermatitis
stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to your general practice by her mother, who has counted about 30 small firm bumps with a dimple in the centre across the girl's trunk and both armpits. They appeared over 4 months and a few have become red and crusted in the last fortnight.

She has had eczema since infancy, currently managed with a moisturiser alone. Her mother is scratching at the bumps herself when bathing her, and wants them scraped off before the girl starts kindergarten in 6 weeks.

The girl has had no serious or recurrent infections, her growth has followed the 50th centile, and her immunisations are up to date. On examination there are dome-shaped pearly papules with dry, itchy, excoriated pink patches surrounding many of them. There is no cellulitis and she is systemically well.

data_table.Examination: About 30 dome-shaped umbilicated papules on trunk and axillae, surrounding dry excoriated pink patches, no spreading erythema or fluctuance
data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking the 50th centile since birth

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for curettage of all lesions under general anaesthesia before she starts kindergarten
Apply liquid nitrogen cryotherapy to each lesion at fortnightly intervals until they clear
Prescribe oral cefalexin for 7 days and exclude her from kindergarten until the lesions clear
Request lymphocyte subsets and immunoglobulins to investigate the extensive lesion count
Treat the surrounding dermatitis with a topical corticosteroid and allow the lesions to resolve

subtopic_detail: Timing of factor replacement relative to imaging in a suspected joint bleed in severe haemophilia A
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on for the emergency department. A 6-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A, established on twice-weekly prophylaxis, is brought in 40 minutes after falling from a scooter onto his right arm.

He tells you his elbow feels tingly and full rather than painful, and he is holding it slightly bent and refusing to straighten it. His last prophylaxis dose was 3 days ago. He has no inhibitor on his most recent annual screen.

On examination the right elbow looks the same size as the left with no visible swelling or bruising, and the skin is not warm. He resists the last 20 degrees of extension. Distal pulses and sensation are normal. The emergency consultant asks whether you want a radiograph and an orthopaedic opinion first.

data_table.Examination: Right elbow held in slight flexion, no visible swelling or bruising, resists terminal extension, normal distal pulses and sensation
data_table.Treatment history: Twice-weekly factor VIII prophylaxis, last dose 3 days ago, no inhibitor on most recent annual screen

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give a factor VIII concentrate dose now, before any imaging or orthopaedic assessment
Give a desmopressin dose now, before any imaging or orthopaedic assessment
Apply ice and a sling now, with review in 24 hours if the symptoms have not settled
Give an oral tranexamic acid dose now, before any imaging or orthopaedic assessment
Arrange a radiograph now, before deciding whether factor replacement is required

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing constitutional delay from pathological delayed puberty in a 14-year-old boy
stem:
A 14-year-old boy attends your general practice with his father, who is worried that his son is the shortest boy in his year and still looks like a child next to his friends. The boy is embarrassed and says he is teased in the change rooms.

He is otherwise well, with a normal appetite, no headaches, no visual symptoms and no anosmia. His bowels are regular and he has had no weight loss. He plays soccer twice a week. His father recalls being the shortest in his own class until he was 16 and then growing 25 cm.

On examination his height is on the 3rd centile, tracking along that line on the growth chart, with a growth velocity of 5 cm over the last year. Testicular volume is 5 mL bilaterally by orchidometer with early pubic hair. A bone age film reports a skeletal age of 12 years 6 months.

data_table.Growth: Height on the 3rd centile tracking along the same line, growth velocity 5 cm in the past 12 months, weight on the 10th centile
data_table.Examination: Testicular volume 5 mL bilaterally, early pubic hair, no anosmia, normal visual fields to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 12 years 6 months at a chronological age of 14 years 2 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request luteinising hormone, follicle stimulating hormone, testosterone and a karyotype
Request coeliac serology, thyroid function and inflammatory markers looking for chronic disease
Reassure the family and review with repeat growth measurements in 6 months
Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamic region
Start a short course of monthly intramuscular testosterone to induce the growth spurt

subtopic_detail: Preventive therapy for a young household contact of smear positive pulmonary tuberculosis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing children referred by the tuberculosis control unit. A 3-year-old girl is brought in because her father was diagnosed 3 weeks ago with sputum smear positive pulmonary tuberculosis and is now on directly observed therapy. She shares a bedroom with her parents.

She has no cough, no fever and no night sweats. Her weight is on the 50th centile and has tracked there since her 12-month check. She was born overseas and received bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination at birth, and the scar is visible on her left shoulder.

Examination is unremarkable with clear chest auscultation and no lymphadenopathy. A tuberculin skin test read at 72 hours shows 12 mm of induration. Her chest radiograph is reported as normal with clear lung fields and no hilar lymphadenopathy. Her father asks what happens next for his daughter.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, bacille Calmette-Guerin scar on left shoulder
data_table.Investigations: Tuberculin skin test 12 mm induration at 72 hours; chest radiograph normal with no hilar lymphadenopathy
data_table.Growth: Weight on the 50th centile, tracking since 12 months of age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start daily isoniazid for 9 months with monthly clinical review
Start daily isoniazid and rifampicin for 6 months with monthly clinical review
Repeat the tuberculin skin test in 8 weeks before deciding on any therapy
Request an interferon gamma release assay before deciding on any therapy
Observe without therapy and repeat the chest radiograph in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Recognising raised intracranial pressure in a child previously labelled as having migraine
stem:
A 9-year-old girl is brought to your general practice by her mother. Six weeks ago another doctor diagnosed migraine and advised paracetamol and a symptom diary, but her mother is not satisfied.

The diary shows that on most mornings she wakes around 5 am with a headache, vomits once, and then feels well enough to go to school. There is no aura, no photophobia and no family history of migraine. She has not missed school and her marks are unchanged.

Her mother has noticed over the past fortnight that the girl holds her head tilted towards the left shoulder while watching television, which is new. On examination she is alert and orientated, with normal power and reflexes in all four limbs and no sensory loss. Fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins in both eyes. Her gait is slightly wide based when asked to walk heel to toe.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Blurred optic disc margins bilaterally, persistent left head tilt, wide based tandem gait, normal power reflexes and sensation in all limbs
data_table.History: Headache on waking with a single vomit then improvement, no aura, no photophobia, no family history of migraine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start propranolol as migraine prophylaxis and review her symptom diary in 6 weeks
Refer to ophthalmology for formal assessment of the optic discs within 2 weeks
Arrange a lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure and relieve her symptoms
Arrange same day magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and discuss with neurosurgery
Arrange a non-contrast computed tomography head scan within the next week

subtopic_detail: Acting on a migration percentage threshold during cerebral palsy hip surveillance
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community child development clinic. A 6-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System level V, attends for his annual review with his mother.

He is fully dependent for transfers and uses a supportive seating system. He takes baclofen and had botulinum toxin injections to both adductors 18 months ago. His mother reports no change in his comfort, and he shows no distress on handling or during nappy changes.

On examination hip abduction is 30 degrees on the right and 45 degrees on the left, with no fixed flexion contracture. The annual anteroposterior pelvis radiograph performed last week is reported with a migration percentage of 42 per cent on the right and 18 per cent on the left, compared with 26 per cent and 16 per cent a year ago.

data_table.Examination: Hip abduction 30 degrees right and 45 degrees left, no fixed flexion contracture, no pain on handling
data_table.Imaging: Anteroposterior pelvis radiograph migration percentage 42 per cent right and 18 per cent left; previous year 26 per cent right and 16 per cent left
data_table.Medications: Baclofen; botulinum toxin to adductors 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pelvis radiograph in 6 months and continue the current surveillance schedule
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for assessment for hip reconstructive surgery
Repeat botulinum toxin injections to both adductors and reassess him in 6 months
Fit a night-time hip abduction brace and reassess him clinically in 6 months
Increase the baclofen dose and arrange physiotherapy review of his standing program

subtopic_detail: Referred knee pain with obligate external rotation in an adolescent
stem: A 13-year-old boy has five weeks of dull left knee ache after sport, with no injury. He has limped for a fortnight. His body mass index is on the 97th centile.

data_table.Examination: Left knee full painless range with no effusion; the left leg rolls into obligate external rotation on hip flexion
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Outpatient magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee
Ultrasound of the left hip looking for an effusion
Physiotherapy for a graded quadriceps loading program
Blood cultures and urgent hip aspiration under imaging
Non-weight-bearing, pelvic radiographs, orthopaedic referral

subtopic_detail: Immediate airway and pouch management in a newborn who cannot pass a nasogastric tube
stem: A term girl born 2 hours ago has needed repeated suctioning for frothy oral secretions and went dusky at her first feed. A size 8 French nasogastric tube meets resistance at 11 cm from the gums. Surgical transfer is 2 hours away.

data_table.Antenatal: 20-week scan: polyhydramnios with a non-visualised stomach bubble
data_table.Examination: Pink in air, no respiratory distress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wide bore replogle tube on continuous low suction, nil by mouth
Contrast swallow to define the obstruction before transfer
Elective intubation and ventilation for the road transfer
Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin for presumed sepsis
Slow continuous nasogastric feeds until retrieval arrives

subtopic_detail: First line genetic testing for global developmental delay with a suggestive maternal pedigree
stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred to your developmental paediatrics clinic because he has no single words and does not point to share interest. He flaps both hands when excited and becomes distressed by the hand dryer in public toilets.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a normal newborn bloodspot screen and a normal newborn hearing screen. Formal audiology at age 3 confirmed normal hearing thresholds bilaterally.

His mother mentions that her brother lives in supported accommodation and has never worked because of an intellectual disability that was never explained. Her own mother stopped having periods at 38 and developed a tremor and unsteadiness in her early sixties that has been attributed to ageing.

On examination his head circumference is on the 90th centile, he has a long face with prominent ears, and his joints are hypermobile. He makes poor eye contact throughout the consultation.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 90th centile, long face with prominent ears, generalised joint hypermobility, hand flapping, poor eye contact
data_table.Investigations: Normal newborn bloodspot screen; audiology at age 3 with normal thresholds bilaterally
data_table.Family history: Maternal uncle with unexplained intellectual disability; maternal grandmother with cessation of periods at 38 and a late-onset tremor with unsteadiness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial genetic investigation?

options.text: Standard karyotype with fluorescence in situ hybridisation for common microdeletions
Methylation studies of chromosome 15 for Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes
Chromosomal microarray in parallel with FMR1 CGG trinucleotide repeat analysis
MECP2 sequencing and deletion or duplication analysis for a Rett spectrum disorder
Whole exome sequencing of the child with both parents sequenced as a trio

subtopic_detail: Sequencing imaging before tissue sampling of an abdominal mass in a preschool child
stem: A 3-year-old girl has a smooth firm left upper abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. She is well, with no bruising or weight loss. Her general practitioner has booked computed tomography and core biopsy for next week.

data_table.Investigations: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg (above the 95th centile), haemoglobin 118 g/L, urine dipstick blood one plus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with the planned computed tomography and core biopsy
Request a bone marrow aspirate and urinary catecholamine measurement
Start an antihypertensive and review the abdomen in two weeks
Urgent abdominal ultrasound with renal vein and caval Doppler
Contrast computed tomography of chest and abdomen as first imaging

subtopic_detail: Escalating airway management when prone positioning fails in a newborn with a cleft soft palate
stem: A term boy of 36 hours has a cleft of the soft palate and a receding chin. He is nursed prone for noisy breathing when supine. Overnight he had three sleep desaturations to 78% and one during a feed.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO2 96% in air awake and prone, comfortable at rest
data_table.Investigations: Capillary gas pH 7.30, carbon dioxide 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 27 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue prone nursing and review after a further 24 hours
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and arrange craniofacial review
Intubate electively and transfer him ventilated to intensive care
Start nasogastric feeds and continue nursing him prone
Refer for mandibular distraction osteogenesis as definitive management

subtopic_detail: Frenotomy decision for ankyloglossia when the feeding problem is positional
stem: A 9-day-old girl's mother has severe nipple pain at every feed; the baby slips off the breast and clicks.

data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3400 g, nadir 3100 g, today 3250 g; six heavy nappies
data_table.Examination: Tongue elevates to mid-mouth and lateralises fully; thin membrane behind the lower gum ridge
data_table.Feeding assessment: Shallow latch, head held away from the breast; pain settles on repositioning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Structured lactation support for attachment and positioning
Frenotomy of the lingual frenulum within a week
Formula top-up after each breastfeed, review in a week
Topical nystatin to the nipples and the baby's mouth
Division of the upper labial frenulum under anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Radial head subluxation where the mechanism reported does not fit the classic pull
stem:
You are the resident in a suburban emergency department. A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her father because she will not use her left arm. He says she was swinging between him and her older sister by the hands when she suddenly cried out, and she has held the arm still against her body since.

She settled quickly and is now playing with a sticker using her right hand. She has no bruising anywhere and no previous fractures. Her father reports no fall and no direct blow.

On examination she holds the left arm slightly flexed at the elbow with the forearm turned palm-down. She resists turning the palm upward. There is no swelling, no deformity and no point tenderness over the clavicle, the humerus, the olecranon or the distal radius. She moves the fingers, wrist and shoulder normally and the radial pulse is present.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held flexed with forearm pronated, resists supination, no swelling or deformity, no point tenderness over clavicle, humerus, olecranon or distal radius, normal finger, wrist and shoulder movement, radial pulse present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the elbow before attempting any manipulation
Perform a supination and flexion reduction manoeuvre at the bedside without prior imaging
Apply an above-elbow backslab and arrange fracture clinic review within the following week
Perform a skeletal survey and notify the child protection team before any elbow manipulation
Arrange an ultrasound of the elbow joint to exclude an effusion before attempting manipulation

subtopic_detail: Referral threshold for persistent middle ear effusion with documented language delay
stem: A 4-year-old boy does not respond when called across the room and turns the television up loud. He uses short phrases rather than sentences, with no ear discharge or pain.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes retracted and dull with fluid levels
data_table.Investigations: Flat tympanograms bilaterally; audiogram conductive loss averaging 35 dB; same findings 4 months ago; expressive language below the third centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Watchful waiting with repeat audiogram in 3 months
Four-week course of oral amoxicillin, review at completion
Ear, nose and throat referral for ventilation tubes
Intranasal corticosteroid for 8 weeks, then tympanometry
Nasal balloon autoinflation three times daily for 3 months

subtopic_detail: Formula selection after a non-IgE cow milk reaction that recurred on an extensively hydrolysed feed
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric outpatient clinic. A 10-week-old boy is brought in by his mother with 4 weeks of loose, mucousy stools streaked with blood and increasing irritability after feeds.

He has been formula fed since birth. Four weeks ago his general practitioner changed him from a standard cow milk formula to an extensively hydrolysed formula, which he has taken exclusively since. His mother reports the stools improved for about a week and then returned to being loose and blood-streaked.

He has never had hives, facial swelling, wheeze or vomiting within minutes of a feed. His weight has dropped from the 50th centile at birth to the 15th centile today. On examination he is alert and well perfused, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no perianal fissure, no skin rash and no organomegaly.

data_table.Growth: Birth weight 50th centile, today 15th centile
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, abdomen soft and non-tender, no perianal fissure, no rash, no organomegaly
data_table.Feeding: Extensively hydrolysed formula exclusively for 4 weeks after standard cow milk formula; initial improvement then relapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a soy based formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
Request skin prick testing to cow milk protein and withhold any formula change pending results
Change to a lactose free cow milk formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
Change to an amino acid based formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
Request faecal calprotectin and colonoscopy and withhold any formula change pending results

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing positional head flattening from suture fusion in an infant with a ridged head shape
stem:
You are the resident in a community child health clinic. A 5-month-old boy is brought in by his father because the back of his head looks flat and one ear looks pushed forward.

He was born at term and sleeps on his back. His father says he has always preferred to turn his head to the right and that he spends most of his waking time in a bouncer. Head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile since birth.

On examination the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits anterior to the left and the right forehead is more prominent than the left, so that the head viewed from above is a parallelogram. The anterior fontanelle is open and soft. There is no palpable ridge over any suture. Passive neck rotation is restricted to the left with a firm thickening palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid.

data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with right ear anterior and right frontal bossing, parallelogram head shape from above, anterior fontanelle open and soft, no palpable sutural ridge
data_table.Neck: Passive rotation restricted to the left, firm thickening palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a craniofacial surgeon for assessment of premature fusion of the lambdoid suture
Request a computed tomography scan of the skull with three-dimensional reconstruction of the sutures
Arrange fitting of a moulding helmet orthosis now and review the head shape in 3 months
Advise front sleeping overnight to offload the flattened occiput and review the head shape in 3 months
Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretching and advise repositioning and supervised tummy time

subtopic_detail: Timing of propranolol for a segmental facial haemangioma still in proliferative phase
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric dermatology clinic. A 7-week-old girl is brought in by her mother, who says a faint pink patch on the left cheek noticed in the first fortnight has become a raised red lesion that is enlarging weekly.

She was born at 34 weeks and weighed 1900 g. Her mother says the lesion bleeds slightly when rubbed against a bunny rug but is not painful and the baby feeds and sleeps normally.

On examination there is a bright red plaque measuring 45 mm across the left cheek, extending to the lateral upper lip and the left lower eyelid margin. The lid lesion does not currently obstruct the visual axis. There is no ulceration. There is a second 6 mm red papule on the left shoulder. Cardiovascular examination is normal and there is no lumbosacral lesion. A recent ophthalmology review documented normal fundi and no astigmatism.

data_table.Examination: Bright red plaque 45 mm across the left cheek extending to the lateral upper lip and left lower eyelid margin, visual axis clear, no ulceration, second 6 mm papule on the left shoulder
data_table.Investigations: Ophthalmology review: normal fundi, no astigmatism; cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral propranolol with dose escalation and monitoring under specialist supervision
Observe with serial photographs and review in 3 months, expecting spontaneous involution
Start topical timolol maleate gel applied twice daily and review the lesion in 3 months
Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment of the cheek lesion and review the lesion in 3 months
Start oral prednisolone with a weaning schedule and monitoring under specialist supervision

subtopic_detail: Management of a limping toddler with a normal radiograph and a low-energy twisting mechanism
stem: An 18-month-old boy has refused to bear weight on his right leg since yesterday, after catching his foot in trampoline netting and twisting as he fell. He is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Crawls readily, full painless hip and knee movement, swelling over the distal shin, pain on gentle tibial torsion
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L, tibia and fibula radiographs show no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with analgesia and general practitioner review
Apply an above-knee backslab with orthopaedic review
Urgent hip ultrasound to look for a joint effusion
Technetium bone scan of both lower limbs, then review
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and tibial MRI

subtopic_detail: First-line antiseizure choice for childhood absence epilepsy in a girl of childbearing potential
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric neurology clinic. A 7-year-old girl is brought in by her father after her teacher reported that she blanks out in class up to 20 times a day, each time for a few seconds, and then carries on mid-sentence.

Her father has noticed the same at home and says she does not fall or shake, and there is no confusion afterwards. Development and school performance were previously normal, though her reading has slipped this term.

In clinic she is asked to blow on a paper windmill for 3 minutes. Twice she stops blowing, stares, and her eyelids flutter, then she resumes without any awareness of the pause. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. An electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background, with no photoparoxysmal response and no polyspike bursts. She has never had a myoclonic jerk or a generalised convulsion.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal; hyperventilation for 3 minutes provoked two episodes of behavioural arrest with eyelid flutter and no postictal confusion
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram: generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background, no photoparoxysmal response, no polyspike bursts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Sodium valproate, titrated to response with monitoring for weight gain and tremor
Lamotrigine, titrated slowly to response with monitoring for rash and hypersensitivity
Ethosuximide, titrated to response with monitoring for gastrointestinal upset
Carbamazepine, titrated to response with monitoring for rash and hyponatraemia
Levetiracetam, titrated to response with monitoring for irritability and behavioural change

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic and wound decision for a facial dog bite presenting outside the primary closure window
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 5-year-old girl is brought in 14 hours after the family dog bit her cheek when she leaned over its food bowl.

Her mother washed the wound with soap and water at home and did not seek care overnight because the child settled and slept. The dog is fully vaccinated, lives at home and has never left Australia.

Her immunisations are documented as up to date including four doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine. On examination there are two puncture wounds and a 20 mm curved laceration over the right cheek, 15 mm below the lower eyelid. The wound edges are moderately swollen with surrounding erythema extending 10 mm, and there is a small amount of serous discharge. She is afebrile, eating normally, and there is no facial nerve weakness and no bony step.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Two puncture wounds and a 20 mm curved cheek laceration 15 mm below the right lower eyelid, moderate oedema with 10 mm surrounding erythema and serous discharge, no facial nerve weakness, no bony step
data_table.Immunisation: Four doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral amoxicillin with clavulanate, with immediate primary suture closure in the department
Copious irrigation and oral cefalexin monotherapy, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
Copious irrigation and a tetanus immunoglobulin injection, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
Copious irrigation and oral amoxicillin with clavulanate, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
Copious irrigation and rabies immunoglobulin with vaccine, and plastic surgery review for delayed closure

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a markedly raised creatine kinase found during investigation of speech delay in a boy
stem:
You are the resident in a general paediatric clinic. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his mother because he is difficult to understand and is not keeping up with his kindergarten group.

His mother says he walked at 19 months, struggles with stairs and asks to be carried after short walks. He has never lost a skill he had acquired. There is no family history of neuromuscular disease.

On examination he rises from the floor by turning prone and pushing his hands up his thighs. His calves are firm and bulky. Power is 4/5 at the hip girdle and 5/5 distally, reflexes are present and symmetrical and plantar responses are flexor. There is no ptosis, no facial weakness and no fasciculation. Blood taken to investigate the developmental concern shows alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (<40), bilirubin 8 micromol/L (<20) and creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60-300).

data_table.Examination: Gowers manoeuvre positive, calf hypertrophy, proximal power 4/5 with distal power 5/5, reflexes present and symmetrical, plantar responses flexor, no ptosis or facial weakness
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (<40), bilirubin 8 micromol/L (<20), creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request liver ultrasound and a viral hepatitis screen and refer to a paediatric hepatology service
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer to a paediatric neurodisability service
Request an open muscle biopsy for dystrophin immunostaining and refer to a neuromuscular service
Request nerve conduction studies with electromyography and refer to a neuromuscular service
Request dystrophin gene deletion and duplication analysis and refer to a neuromuscular service

subtopic_detail: Choosing between alkalinisation and dialysis in adolescent salicylate poisoning with a falling pH
stem: A 15-year-old girl took an unknown quantity of aspirin 6 hours ago. Her ears are ringing; she is agitated but oriented and passing urine freely.

data_table.Investigations: Salicylate 640 mg/L at 4 hours and 810 mg/L at 6 hours; arrival gas pH 7.47, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L; repeat pH 7.29, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L
data_table.Treatment so far: 2 L intravenous sodium bicarbonate over 2 hours; urine pH 7.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?
