options.text: Urgent haemodialysis with continued bicarbonate infusion
Continue bicarbonate alone and repeat the concentration
Repeated activated charcoal every 4 hours by nasogastric tube
Rapid sequence intubation with controlled ventilation
Intravenous acetylcysteine by the standard regimen

subtopic_detail: Chelation threshold and source control for an asymptomatic child with an elevated blood lead level
stem: A 3-year-old boy is referred after community screening found an elevated blood lead level. He is asymptomatic and frequently mouths dirt and paint flakes. The family lives in a 1950 weatherboard house with peeling paint; his father works at the smelter and changes clothes at home.

data_table.Investigations: Venous blood lead 28 micrograms/dL, haemoglobin 104 g/L, mean cell volume 68 fL, ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150), abdominal radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous sodium calcium edetate chelation
Notify public health for environmental assessment
Commence oral succimer chelation as an outpatient
Give calcium and vitamin D supplementation daily
Arrange whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol

subtopic_detail: Whether to continue antibiotic prophylaxis after a second febrile urinary infection with high grade reflux
stem: A 14-month-old girl is reviewed after her second febrile Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, treated 4 months and 5 weeks ago. She is thriving, has no constipation and is taking no medication.

data_table.Investigations: Renal ultrasound: bilateral hydronephrosis with dilated ureters, normal cortical thickness. Micturating cystourethrogram: grade IV reflux on the left, grade III on the right, no posterior urethral valve. Creatinine 26 micromol/L (15-35). Post-treatment urine culture sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: No prophylaxis, with prompt treatment of future infections
Referral for ureteric reimplantation surgery now
Nightly low dose oral trimethoprim prophylaxis
Nightly low dose oral amoxicillin prophylaxis
Dimercaptosuccinic acid scan before any decision

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing structural clubfoot from positional foot deformity in the newborn and the timing of Ponseti casting
stem:
You are the resident reviewing a 3-day-old boy on the postnatal ward before discharge. His mother says both of his feet 'turn in and point down' and that they have looked this way since birth.

He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy with normal liquor volume. Birth weight was 3300 g and he is feeding well.

On examination both forefeet are adducted and both heels are held in varus and equinus. Neither foot can be brought up past 20 degrees of plantarflexion despite firm pressure, and there is a deep transverse crease across each medial arch. Both calves are visibly thinner than expected for his size. Hip abduction is full and symmetrical with no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral forefoot adduction with hindfoot varus and equinus; neither foot correctable past 20 degrees of plantarflexion
data_table.Skin and soft tissue: Deep transverse medial arch crease bilaterally; bilateral calf wasting
data_table.Hips: Full symmetrical abduction, Ortolani and Barlow negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for Ponseti serial casting to start this week
Teach the parents passive stretching exercises and review the feet at six weeks
Arrange a foot and ankle ultrasound before deciding on orthopaedic referral
Apply overnight below-knee splints and refer to orthopaedics at three months
Arrange a hip ultrasound at six weeks and refer if the feet remain deformed

subtopic_detail: Minimum interval between two parenteral live vaccines when catching up an incompletely vaccinated child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15-month-old girl who arrived in Australia six weeks ago. Her mother brings a handwritten card from their previous country listing three doses of a diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis containing vaccine and two doses of polio vaccine, with no record of any measles containing vaccine.

Ten days ago the family attended a different practice, where she was given a measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. The mother now wants 'everything else she has missed' done today so the child can start childcare.

The girl is well, afebrile and thriving, with no immunosuppressive conditions and no medications. She has had no blood products or immunoglobulin. You determine that she still requires varicella vaccine and a Haemophilus influenzae type b containing vaccine.

data_table.Vaccines documented: Three doses diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine, two doses polio vaccine
data_table.Recent vaccine: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine given 10 days ago at another practice
data_table.Still required today: Varicella vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b containing vaccine
data_table.Examination: Well and afebrile, growth on the 50th centile, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the varicella vaccine?

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine today at a separate injection site
Administer the varicella vaccine at least four weeks after the measles vaccine
Check varicella and measles serology first and vaccinate only if she is not immune
Administer the varicella vaccine one week from now with paracetamol cover
Repeat the measles vaccine today and give the varicella vaccine in three months

subtopic_detail: Choice of scabicide in an infant below the minimum age for topical permethrin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 6-week-old boy whose mother says he has become 'covered in angry spots' over the past fortnight and cries and squirms most of the night.

He was born at term and is breastfed and thriving. His mother has had an intensely itchy rash on her wrists and between her fingers for about six weeks, and his 4-year-old sister has a similar itchy rash.

On examination there are erythematous papules and pustules scattered over the trunk, and vesicles and burrows involving both palms and both soles as well as the scalp. Skin scrapings taken in clinic show a mite and several ova on light microscopy.

data_table.Examination: Papules and pustules on trunk; vesicles and burrows on palms, soles and scalp
data_table.Investigations: Skin scraping microscopy shows a mite and ova
data_table.Household: Mother and 4-year-old sister both have an itchy rash of about six weeks duration
data_table.Growth and feeding: Exclusively breastfed, weight tracking on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Apply permethrin 5 per cent cream to the infant and treat all household contacts
Apply benzyl benzoate 25 per cent lotion to the infant and all household contacts
Apply sulfur 5 per cent ointment to the infant and treat all household contacts
Give a single dose of oral ivermectin to the infant and all household contacts
Apply hydrocortisone 1 per cent to the infant and treat the contacts with permethrin

subtopic_detail: Management of cyanotic breath-holding spells when iron studies are abnormal
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric assessment unit reviewing an 18-month-old boy brought in after an episode at home. His mother says he was told he could not have a biscuit, cried hard for about fifteen seconds, then 'went silent, turned blue around the lips and flopped'. He was limp for roughly ten seconds, then took a breath and was crying and reaching for her within half a minute.

There have been six such episodes in four months, every one of them beginning with a period of prolonged crying after frustration or a minor injury. He has never had an episode during sleep, at rest or during exercise, and there has been no jerking of the limbs and no incontinence.

He is developmentally normal and drinks about a litre of cow milk daily. Cardiovascular examination is normal with equal volume femoral pulses. Blood tests are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 120/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 68 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 microgram/L (15-150), electrolytes and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal tone and development, normal heart sounds, equal volume femoral pulses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram before starting any specific treatment
Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for an echocardiogram and exercise testing
Commence oral sodium valproate and review the frequency of episodes in eight weeks
Commence oral iron supplementation and review the frequency of episodes in eight weeks
Arrange a 12 lead electrocardiogram and withhold treatment until the result is available

subtopic_detail: Threshold for specialist assessment of an asymptomatic murmur first heard in early infancy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar performing a 6-week health check on a 5-week-old girl. Her mother has no concerns and says she feeds for about twenty minutes on each side without stopping to rest, and has never gone sweaty or dusky during a feed.

She was born at 38 weeks by elective caesarean section for breech presentation. Birth weight was 3200 g and she now weighs 4100 g. Her newborn examination at 12 hours of age was documented as normal with no murmur heard.

On examination she is pink and alert. There is a grade 2/6 systolic murmur heard at the left sternal edge with no radiation and no thrill. Heart sounds are normal with a single second sound. Femoral pulses are equal in volume to the brachial pulses. Pre-ductal and post-ductal oxygen saturations are both 99 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99 per cent pre-ductal and post-ductal, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Cardiovascular examination: Grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, no thrill, no radiation, normal single second heart sound
data_table.Pulses: Femoral pulses equal in volume to brachial pulses
data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3200 g, current weight 4100 g, tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the murmur at the twelve month health check
Arrange a chest radiograph and an electrocardiogram before deciding on referral
Measure four limb blood pressures and reassure the parents if the readings are equal
Review her in the practice in three months and refer only if the murmur persists
Refer for paediatric cardiology review with echocardiography within the next few weeks

subtopic_detail: Adolescent knee pain with obligate external rotation on hip flexion and the weight bearing decision
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy who has had a dull ache in his left knee for about seven weeks. His mother says he has been walking 'with his foot turned out' and no longer plays soccer at lunchtime.

He recalls no injury. The pain is worse after activity and settles with rest. He has not been febrile and has not been unwell in any other way. His weight is above the 97th centile and his height is on the 25th centile.

On examination the left knee is not warm, has no effusion and moves through a full painless range. The tibial tuberosity is not tender. When you flex the left hip the thigh rolls into external rotation and you cannot flex it in the neutral plane, and internal rotation of the left hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right.

data_table.Knee examination: No effusion, no warmth, full painless range of movement, tibial tuberosity not tender
data_table.Hip examination: Obligate external rotation of the left thigh on hip flexion; left internal rotation 10 degrees, right 40 degrees
data_table.Growth: Weight above the 97th centile, height on the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange knee radiographs and refer to physiotherapy for quadriceps strengthening
Advise activity modification with simple analgesia and review him again in six weeks
Keep him non-weight bearing and arrange urgent orthopaedic review with pelvic films
Arrange an urgent knee ultrasound and aspirate any joint effusion that is identified
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and review him once the report arrives

subtopic_detail: Frequency of slit lamp screening in antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular juvenile arthritis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a rheumatology clinic. A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen, warm left knee for four months and a swollen right ankle for six weeks. Her mother says she is stiff and clingy in the mornings and loosens up by mid-morning, and that she has not been febrile at any point.

There is no rash and no lymphadenopathy. Both eyes look white and quiet and she has never complained that they hurt or that light bothers her, and she does not rub them.

Investigations show an antinuclear antibody titre of 1:320 with a negative rheumatoid factor. Inflammatory markers are mildly raised. A diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is made and intra-articular corticosteroid injection is planned.

data_table.Joints: Left knee and right ankle swollen and warm; morning stiffness easing by mid-morning
data_table.Eyes: White and quiet on external inspection; no pain, photophobia or eye rubbing reported
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody 1:320, rheumatoid factor negative, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 15)
data_table.Systemic features: No fever, no rash, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ophthalmic surveillance plan?

options.text: Arrange ophthalmology review only if she develops a red or a painful eye
Arrange annual visual acuity testing by an optometrist from the time of school entry
Arrange slit lamp examination now and then repeat it every twelve months
Arrange fundoscopy at each rheumatology visit and refer her if it looks abnormal
Arrange slit lamp examination now and then repeat it every three months

subtopic_detail: Urgency of referral for a unilateral white pupillary reflex noticed on family photographs
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 14-month-old girl whose father shows you four photographs taken over the past two months. In each one her right pupil looks white while the left shows the usual red glow of a camera flash.

Her mother adds that over the last three weeks the right eye 'drifts in towards her nose' when she is tired, and that she seems to bump into things on that side. The girl was born at term, has no relevant family history and her development is on track.

On examination visual behaviour is asymmetric: she objects when you occlude the left eye but not when you occlude the right. The right red reflex is dull and pale compared with a bright red reflex on the left. The cornea is clear and the eye is white and not watering, and there is no proptosis. Cover testing reveals an inward shift of the right eye.

data_table.Ocular examination: Right red reflex dull and pale, left bright red; cornea clear, conjunctiva white, no watering, no proptosis
data_table.Visual behaviour: Objects to occlusion of the left eye but not the right
data_table.Cover test: Inward shift of the right eye on cover testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ophthalmology for examination under anaesthesia within this week
Refer to orthoptics for a squint assessment at the next available clinic appointment
Arrange an outpatient orbital ultrasound and review her with the result in a month
Reassure the parents that the appearance is a camera flash artefact and review as needed
Prescribe patching of the left eye and refer to ophthalmology within the next three months

subtopic_detail: Score threshold for starting pharmacological treatment of neonatal abstinence and the feeding decision
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward caring for a 4-day-old boy born at 38 weeks to a mother who has been on supervised methadone 60 mg daily for two years through an opioid treatment program. Urine drug screening at booking and at delivery detected methadone only.

He was born by normal vaginal delivery weighing 2900 g. He is rooming in with his mother in a quiet, dimly lit single room, is being swaddled and held skin to skin, and is breastfeeding every two to three hours.

Over the last twelve hours the midwife has recorded modified Finnegan scores of 9, 10 and 9 on three consecutive four hourly assessments. He is tremulous when disturbed, has a high pitched cry that settles with holding, sleeps less than an hour after feeds and has had three loose stools. Glucose, electrolytes and temperature are all within normal limits and there are no seizures.

data_table.Scores: Modified Finnegan scores 9, 10 and 9 on three consecutive four hourly assessments
data_table.Clinical features: Tremor on handling, high pitched cry settling with holding, sleep less than one hour after feeds, three loose stools
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose, electrolytes and temperature within normal limits; no seizure activity
data_table.Care to date: Rooming in, quiet dim environment, swaddling, skin to skin, breastfeeding two to three hourly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral phenobarbital, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
Commence oral morphine, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
Continue non-pharmacological care alone and rescore him on four hourly cycles
Commence oral clonidine, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
Advise formula feeding, transfer him to the nursery and commence oral morphine

subtopic_detail: Imaging and drainage decision in parapneumonic collection failing 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl who was admitted 48 hours ago with right sided pneumonia and started on intravenous benzylpenicillin. Her mother says she is 'no better at all' and is still hot and breathing fast.

She remains febrile to 39.2°C with ongoing tachypnoea and now lies curled towards her right side and cries when moved. Her oxygen requirement has risen from room air to 2 L/min by nasal prongs to keep saturations at 94 per cent.

On examination there is stony dullness to percussion over the right lower zone with absent breath sounds and reduced chest wall movement on that side. A repeat chest radiograph shows opacification of the right hemithorax to the level of the hilum with a meniscus. Blood cultures taken on admission remain negative and inflammatory markers have risen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 94 per cent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 39.2°C
data_table.Examination: Stony dullness and absent breath sounds over the right lower zone with reduced chest wall movement
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows right hemithorax opacification to hilar level with a meniscus
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 218 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 24.6 x10^9/L (4.0-12.0), blood cultures negative at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the intravenous antibiotics for a further 48 hours and repeat the chest film
Arrange contrast computed tomography of the chest and refer her to cardiothoracic surgery
Perform a diagnostic pleural tap and discharge her home on oral antibiotics afterwards
Arrange chest ultrasound then insert a chest drain with an intrapleural fibrinolytic agent
Change to intravenous vancomycin and meropenem and repeat the blood cultures every day

subtopic_detail: Isolated breast development in a toddler with normal growth velocity and unadvanced bone age
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 2-year-old girl referred because of breast development. Her mother noticed 'small lumps under both nipples' at around 18 months and says they have waxed and waned since, being more obvious some weeks than others.

There has been no change in body odour, no acne, no pubic or axillary hair and no vaginal bleeding. She takes no medications and there are no creams, gels or supplements in the house.

On examination she has Tanner stage 2 breast tissue bilaterally with no areolar enlargement or pigmentation, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair and no clitoromegaly. Her height has tracked steadily along the 60th centile across four measurements since 12 months of age, giving a growth velocity of 8 cm per year. A bone age radiograph reports a skeletal age of 2 years 1 month against a chronological age of 2 years 2 months.

data_table.Pubertal staging: Tanner stage 2 breast bilaterally without areolar enlargement, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, no clitoromegaly
data_table.Growth: Height tracking along the 60th centile across four measurements; growth velocity 8 cm per year
data_table.Imaging: Bone age 2 years 1 month against chronological age 2 years 2 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test and repeat the bone age film
Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary within the next month
Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist and refer her to endocrinology
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and measure serum oestradiol and the adrenal androgens
Reassure the parents and review her growth and pubertal staging again in six months

subtopic_detail: Setting for influenza vaccination in a child with previous anaphylaxis to egg
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy in early autumn whose parents want him vaccinated against influenza before a family trip.

At 11 months of age he developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting and audible wheeze within ten minutes of his first taste of scrambled egg, and was treated with intramuscular adrenaline in an emergency department. Skin prick testing was subsequently positive to egg white and he carries an adrenaline autoinjector.

He has received his measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at 12 months without any reaction. He is well today, has no asthma and has had no recent febrile illness. Your practice has an adrenaline autoinjector, oxygen and a resuscitation trolley, and a second staff member is on site.

data_table.Allergy history: Anaphylaxis to egg at 11 months treated with intramuscular adrenaline; skin prick test positive to egg white
data_table.Vaccine history: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at 12 months tolerated without reaction
data_table.Practice resources: Adrenaline autoinjector, oxygen, resuscitation trolley and a second staff member available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer the influenza vaccine in the practice with 15 minutes of observation
Refer him to a specialist immunisation clinic for the influenza vaccine in hospital
Give the influenza vaccine in two divided doses 30 minutes apart in the practice
Withhold the influenza vaccine and rely on vaccination of his household contacts
Perform skin prick testing to the influenza vaccine before administering the dose

subtopic_detail: Cyanosis with pulmonary venous congestion and a normal sized heart where prostaglandin does not help
stem: A 2-day-old boy born at 39 weeks began grunting overnight. He has deteriorated on nasal continuous positive airway pressure and now needs 80 per cent oxygen.

data_table.Hyperoxia test: Arterial oxygen tension 32 mmHg in air, 41 mmHg after 10 minutes of 100 per cent oxygen
data_table.Examination: Quiet precordium with no murmur, liver 4 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph: normal cardiac silhouette with diffuse granular opacification and prominent interstitial markings

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prostaglandin E1 infusion and cardiac retrieval
Inhaled nitric oxide and neonatal retrieval
Surfactant, continue airway pressure and observe
Intubate and ventilate, arrange surgical retrieval
Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, arrange retrieval

subtopic_detail: Feeding decision in a jaundiced septic neonate with positive urinary reducing substances and negative urine glucose
stem: An 8-day-old exclusively breastfed girl has vomited every feed for four days and is now floppy, sleepy and anuric. Birth weight 3400 g, now 3020 g.

data_table.Examination: Deep jaundice, hypotonia, capillary refill 4 seconds, liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 268 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 96, INR 2.4, glucose 1.9 mmol/L
data_table.Urine: Reducing substances positive, glucose oxidase dipstick negative
data_table.Microbiology: Blood culture positive at 9 hours, Gram negative bacilli

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her feeds?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding with intravenous antibiotics alone
Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula
Stop lactose containing feeds and start soy formula
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and continue breastfeeding
Start phenobarbital and continue breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: deciding against radiographs before reducing a radial head subluxation in a toddler
stem:
You are the doctor on the afternoon shift in a regional emergency department. A 2-year-old girl is brought in by her father, who lifted her by one hand onto a kerb about an hour ago to stop her stepping onto the road. She cried immediately and has not used her left arm since.

She is fully immunised, has had no previous fractures and is otherwise well. She sits happily on her father's lap eating a biscuit with her right hand. The left arm hangs at her side with the elbow slightly flexed and the palm facing backwards. She lets you palpate the clavicle, humerus, forearm and wrist without protest, and there is no swelling, bruising or deformity anywhere along the limb. She cries only when you attempt to turn the left palm upwards.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held adducted, elbow flexed about 20 degrees, forearm pronated; no swelling, bruising, deformity or focal bone tenderness; distal pulses and capillary refill normal; skin intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a supination and flexion manoeuvre at the elbow and reassess her use of the arm after fifteen minutes
Apply a broad arm sling for comfort and arrange review in the paediatric fracture clinic within one week
Immobilise the limb in an above elbow backslab and repeat clinical assessment with radiographs in ten days
Refer for an urgent ultrasound of the elbow to look for a joint effusion before deciding on treatment
Arrange radiographs of the elbow and forearm before attempting any manipulation of the limb

subtopic_detail: dietary management of chronic non-specific loose stools in a thriving preschooler
stem: A 2-year-old boy has passed three to five loose stools a day for four months, worse later in the day and often containing recognisable carrot and corn. He drinks 900 mL of juice and cordial daily on a low fat diet.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 60th centile without crossing
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology, ferritin and faecal calprotectin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: A strict four week cow milk protein elimination diet
Three faecal specimens for microscopy and parasites
An oral probiotic with a bulking agent for three months
Referral for endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies
Reduce juice and cordial, increase dietary fat, review in six weeks

subtopic_detail: separating benign nocturnal limb pains from a pain pattern that requires investigation
stem:
You are the doctor seeing a 6-year-old girl brought by her mother because she wakes crying with leg pain two or three nights a week. The pain is in both calves and behind both knees, lasts about half an hour, and settles with a cuddle and rubbing. By morning she is running around normally and she has never limped or refused to walk. She has not lost weight, has had no fevers and plays a full season of netball.

Her mother is frightened because a family friend's child was recently diagnosed with leukaemia. On examination she is well grown and afebrile. There is no joint swelling, warmth or restriction, no bony tenderness over the tibiae or femora, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising and no hepatosplenomegaly. Her gait, spine and hips are normal.

data_table.Examination: No joint swelling, warmth or restricted range; no bone tenderness on direct palpation of long bones; no lymphadenopathy, bruising, pallor or hepatosplenomegaly; normal gait and hip range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe regular evening ibuprofen for six weeks and review her response to the trial at the end of that period
Explain the benign pain pattern, advise simple measures at night, and arrange review if any daytime pain or limp appears
Order a full blood count, blood film, inflammatory markers and a lactate dehydrogenase before offering any reassurance
Arrange plain radiographs of both femora and tibiae to exclude an osteoid osteoma or an occult bone lesion
Refer her to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of possible juvenile idiopathic arthritis and enthesitis related disease

subtopic_detail: making a positive diagnosis of a functional abdominal pain disorder in a school aged child
stem: An 8-year-old girl has six months of central abdominal pain on most school mornings and never overnight. She has missed fourteen school days this term. Her mother calls her a worrier who recently changed schools.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, periumbilical tenderness that disappears with distraction
data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking the 45th centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A dietitian led low fermentable carbohydrate diet
Repeat the blood tests and calprotectin in eight weeks
Upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies for review
A positive functional diagnosis and school return plan
An eight week proton pump inhibitor trial instead

subtopic_detail: investigation priorities for a capillary malformation involving the ophthalmic trigeminal territory
stem:
You are the doctor in a paediatric clinic seeing a 7-week-old girl whose parents want advice about a birthmark. A flat, sharply demarcated dark pink patch has been present since birth over the right forehead, upper eyelid and the bridge of the nose. It has not grown thicker or raised, has not ulcerated, and has not changed in size relative to her face. There are no other skin lesions.

She was born at term, feeds well and is gaining weight normally. Her parents have read about birthmarks that shrink on their own and want to know whether she needs any treatment. Neurological examination is normal with symmetrical tone and movements, and she fixes and follows. The lesion blanches incompletely with pressure and the underlying tissues feel soft and non-pulsatile.

data_table.Examination: Flat, sharply demarcated, incompletely blanching dark pink patch over the right forehead, upper eyelid and nasal bridge; no thickening, warmth, bruit or ulceration; head circumference on the 50th centile; normal tone, symmetrical movements, fixes and follows

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast and refer her for a formal ophthalmological assessment of intraocular pressure
Reassure the parents that this mark will fade substantially over the first year and arrange review at her eighteen month immunisation visit
Refer her directly for pulsed dye laser therapy as the first intervention and defer any further investigation until after treatment
Organise an electroencephalogram now and commence prophylactic levetiracetam because of the high lifetime risk of epilepsy
Commence oral propranolol with an escalating dose schedule and cardiovascular monitoring during the first week of therapy

subtopic_detail: choosing first line treatment for impairing motor and vocal tics in a school aged child
stem:
You are the doctor in a community paediatric clinic reviewing a 9-year-old boy. For two years he has had repeated eye blinking and head jerking, and over the past eight months he has added throat clearing and a repeated grunting noise. The movements wax and wane, worsen when he is tired or anxious, and briefly disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He can suppress them for a short period at a cost of mounting inner tension.

His teacher has moved him to the back of the class and other children have started imitating the grunting, and he now asks to stay home. He has no compulsions, no ritualised checking and no intrusive thoughts. There is no exposure to stimulant medication. Neurological examination including gait, tone, power, coordination and eye movements is normal, and he is growing along the 55th centile.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking, head jerking, throat clearing and grunting observed during consultation; suppressible with subsequent rebound; neurological examination including gait, tone, power, coordination and eye movements normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Reassure the family that childhood tics remit spontaneously and advise that no active treatment is required at this stage
Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and titrate over four weeks with review of tic frequency thereafter
Refer him for a structured behavioural therapy program teaching competing responses and tic awareness training
Commence low dose risperidone with baseline weight, fasting glucose and lipid measurement and regular metabolic review
Commence clonidine titrated slowly with blood pressure and heart rate monitoring at each dose increase over eight weeks

subtopic_detail: selecting focal tone treatment for dynamic equinus in an ambulant child with spastic cerebral palsy
stem: A 5-year-old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy walks independently but tires quickly and has begun toe walking on both sides. He has had twice weekly physiotherapy with ankle foot orthoses worn consistently for eight months.

data_table.Examination: Increased calf tone with catch on fast dorsiflexion; ankle dorsiflexes to neutral with the knee extended and 15 degrees past neutral with the knee flexed; no fixed deformity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral baclofen titrated over four weeks
Refer for selective dorsal rhizotomy assessment
Apply weekly serial below-knee casts for six weeks
Refer for bilateral gastrocnemius lengthening surgery
Inject botulinum toxin A into both gastrocnemius muscles

subtopic_detail: recognising an inflammatory myopathy from a photodistributed rash with proximal weakness in a child
stem: A 6-year-old girl has three months of tiredness and a rash. She asks to be carried upstairs and cannot brush her own hair, but runs on the flat.

data_table.Examination: Dusky violet upper eyelids, scaly pink plaques over the knuckles, dilated nailfold capillaries, shoulder abduction 4/5 with full distal power
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 1850 U/L (less than 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Dystrophin deletion and duplication analysis with neuromuscular referral
Urgent rheumatology referral for corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy
A potent topical corticosteroid for the rash, review in six weeks
Antinuclear antibody and extractable nuclear antigen testing first
Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis before immunosuppression

subtopic_detail: illness planning after newborn screening detects a medium chain fatty acid oxidation defect
stem:
You are the doctor in a metabolic clinic seeing the parents of a 3-week-old boy. Newborn screening flagged a raised octanoylcarnitine, and confirmatory acylcarnitine profiling and ACADM gene testing have established medium chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency. He is thriving on demand breastfeeding, is neurologically normal, and has never been unwell.

His parents have been told the condition is serious and want to know what they should actually do. They ask specifically what to do when he next gets a viral illness, since their older child vomits with every winter virus. Examination is normal with no hepatomegaly and no dysmorphism. His most recent blood glucose taken at the confirmatory visit was 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5) and liver function tests were within normal limits.

data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Investigations: Acylcarnitine profile shows raised octanoylcarnitine; ACADM gene testing confirms two pathogenic variants; blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5); liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What advice about intercurrent illness is most appropriate?

options.text: Withhold all protein containing feeds during illness and provide intravenous dextrose with lipid until the illness resolves
Commence daily oral carnitine supplementation and reserve hospital attendance for episodes of documented hypoglycaemia
Reassure them that the condition rarely causes problems after infancy and that standard childhood illness advice is sufficient
Give a prescribed glucose polymer drink at set intervals during illness and present to hospital if feeds are not tolerated
Restrict dietary long chain fat substantially and supplement with medium chain triglyceride oil added to each daily feed

subtopic_detail: choosing a rehydration rate when a breastfed neonate presents with a markedly raised serum sodium
stem: A 9-day-old exclusively breastfed boy is sleepy and feeding poorly for two days, with two wet nappies in 24 hours. Birth weight 3400 g, now 2890 g.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken fontanelle, doughy skin, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 168 mmol/L (135 to 145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid management?

options.text: 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9%, then correct over 48 hours at 0.5 mmol/L/hour
20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% repeated to 60 mL/kg, then maintenance fluid
Replace the whole deficit over 12 hours with 0.225% sodium chloride
No intravenous fluid; nasogastric expressed breast milk and top ups
3 mL/kg sodium chloride 3%, then standard maintenance fluid

subtopic_detail: abdominal pain during a nephrotic relapse where the diagnosis is peritoneal infection rather than oedema
stem: A 4-year-old girl admitted with her third relapse of steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome, started on prednisolone, has six hours of abdominal pain unrelieved by paracetamol. She is reluctant to move.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 146 /min, BP 88/50 mmHg, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, shifting dullness, diffuse guarding, periorbital oedema
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 12 g/L, neutrophils 15.1 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase prednisolone and add an acid suppressant for gastric irritation
Request urgent surgical review for appendicitis and imaging
Perform a diagnostic ascitic tap and start intravenous ceftriaxone
Give intravenous albumin 20% then furosemide for the tense ascites
Arrange Doppler ultrasound for renal vein thrombosis before antibiotics

subtopic_detail: insulin route and disposition when new diabetes presents with marked hyperglycaemia but no acidosis
stem: A 10-year-old girl 240 km from the nearest paediatric unit has four weeks of thirst, polyuria and 4 kg of weight loss. She is alert, hungry and has not vomited.

data_table.Examination: Moist mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds, no Kussmaul breathing
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 24.6 mmol/L, ketones 1.1 mmol/L (less than 0.6), venous pH 7.36

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test and HbA1c before starting insulin
Oral metformin with dietary advice and endocrinology review in two weeks
Intravenous insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour with two bag fluid therapy
A 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus and repeat gas in two hours
Subcutaneous insulin and oral fluids, with same day transfer discussion

subtopic_detail: watering eye present since the neonatal period with a white conjunctiva and a normal cornea
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic. A 4-month-old girl is brought in because her left eye waters all day and is crusted shut most mornings. Her mother says it has been like this since about three weeks of age and that wiping it with cotton wool clears it easily.

The baby feeds well, is thriving, and does not seem bothered by light. On examination the left eye has a pool of tears at the lid margin, the white of the eye is not red, and the cornea is clear and of normal diameter. Gentle pressure over the lacrimal sac expresses a small amount of mucoid material. The red reflex is present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Left tear lake, white conjunctiva, clear cornea of normal diameter, symmetrical red reflex, mucoid reflux on lacrimal sac pressure
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer now for probing of the tear duct under general anaesthesia
Prescribe chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops four times daily for a week
Teach lacrimal sac massage and review again at twelve months of age
Refer for urgent measurement of intraocular pressure under anaesthesia
Swab the discharge for chlamydia and start oral azithromycin therapy

subtopic_detail: early tachypnoea after elective caesarean at term with fluid in the horizontal fissure and no sepsis risk factors
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward. A boy was born at 38 weeks and 4 days by elective caesarean for maternal request, with Apgar scores of 9 and 9. From 30 minutes of age he has been breathing fast with intermittent grunting that has settled over the last hour.

He is now 3 hours old, pink, alert, and rooting. Membranes were ruptured at delivery, the mother was afebrile throughout, and her group B streptococcus screen at 36 weeks was negative. A chest radiograph shows prominent perihilar vascular markings and fluid in the horizontal fissure, with normal lung volumes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 74/min, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild intercostal recession, no grunting at rest, air entry equal, no murmur, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph: perihilar streaking with fluid in the horizontal fissure, normal lung volumes; blood glucose 3.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Observe in the nursery with regular monitoring and support oral feeding
Start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after blood cultures
Commence nasal continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cm of water
Give intratracheal surfactant and transfer to the neonatal unit urgently
Start intravenous fluid and withhold feeds for the next twenty four hours

subtopic_detail: occipital flattening with a parallelogram head shape, open sutures and full neck rotation at five months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-month-old boy whose parents are worried about the shape of his head. They noticed flattening at the back on the right from about 8 weeks of age and say he always sleeps with his head turned to the right.

On examination the right occiput is flat, and viewed from above the right ear and right forehead sit forward of the left. The sutures are palpable and open, with no ridging. He turns his head fully to both sides when following a toy, and passive neck rotation is equal and unrestricted. Head circumference is on the 50th centile and has tracked there since birth. He rolls both ways and reaches for objects with either hand.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with anterior displacement of the right ear and right forehead, open non-ridged sutures, full passive neck rotation both directions
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile, following the same line since birth
data_table.Development: Rolls both directions, reaches with either hand, social smile present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for sternocleidomastoid stretching exercises now
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with reconstruction
Refer for a moulding helmet orthosis to be fitted within this month
Advise repositioning and supervised tummy time, and review in eight weeks
Refer to neurosurgery for assessment of premature fusion of a suture

subtopic_detail: deep soil-contaminated puncture wound in a child whose vaccination history cannot be verified
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 7-year-old boy who stood on a garden fork six hours ago while helping in the vegetable patch. One tine went through his shoe into the sole of his right foot.

The wound is a deep puncture with soil visible at its base; you irrigate and debride it. The family arrived in Australia last year and no vaccination records travelled with them. His mother recalls needles being given when he was a baby but cannot say how many or when, and the Australian Immunisation Register has no entries for him. He is otherwise well, with no immunosuppressive illness or treatment. Distal sensation, capillary refill and toe movement are normal.

data_table.Examination: Deep plantar puncture wound with visible soil contamination, no foreign body on inspection after debridement, neurovascularly intact
data_table.Immunisation: No entries on the Australian Immunisation Register; parental recall of infant doses only, number and dates unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tetanus specific management?

options.text: Give a single dose of a tetanus containing vaccine and no immunoglobulin
Give tetanus immunoglobulin now and begin a tetanus containing vaccine course
Give tetanus immunoglobulin alone and check tetanus antibody titres in a month
Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and arrange wound review in two days
Give no tetanus specific treatment and arrange catch up vaccines next week

subtopic_detail: irritability, tachycardia and poor weight gain in the second week of life in the infant of a mother treated with radioiodine years earlier
stem:
You are the doctor in a general practice seeing a 10-day-old girl whose mother says she will not settle, feeds frantically then pulls off, and is sweaty during feeds. She has lost weight since discharge rather than regaining it.

Her mother had Graves disease treated with radioiodine six years ago and now takes thyroxine, and her own thyroid function during pregnancy was normal on that dose. The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth. On examination she is alert with a wide eyed stare, warm peripheries and a smooth firm swelling palpable in the front of the neck. She is afebrile with no rash, her fontanelle is soft, and her respiratory and abdominal examinations are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 194/min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert with wide eyed stare, warm and sweaty, smooth firm anterior neck swelling, no murmur, liver edge 1 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3.4 kg, weight today 3.05 kg, having been 3.15 kg on day 5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents that a mother on thyroxine cannot affect her baby
Arrange routine review with the child health nurse in two weeks' time
Start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after blood cultures
Start propranolol and arrange outpatient review in three to four weeks
Measure the infant's thyroid function today and admit for monitoring

subtopic_detail: fourth stereotyped episode of prolonged vomiting with complete wellness between episodes and ketosis on arrival
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department. A 6-year-old girl has been vomiting since 4 am, about eight times an hour at the start and now every 20 minutes. Her mother says this is the fourth time in a year, that each episode begins in the early hours, lasts most of a day, and that between episodes she is completely well and eats normally.

She has vomited only stomach contents with no green colour and has not opened her bowels today. She is quiet and pale but rouses easily and answers you. Her abdomen is soft with no guarding, and bowel sounds are present. An abdominal ultrasound during a previous episode last year was normal, and her development and growth have been normal throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds, soft non-tender abdomen, no guarding, normal neurological examination with no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), blood ketones 2.1 mmol/L (<0.6), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), weight 700 g below her clinic weight last month

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Give oral rehydration solution in small volumes and review in four hours
Start intravenous fluid containing dextrose and give intravenous ondansetron
Arrange an urgent computed tomography scan of the brain before treatment
Start regular propranolol as prophylaxis and discharge with a plan today
Arrange an abdominal radiograph to exclude a mechanical cause of vomiting

subtopic_detail: postprandial dystonic arching in an infant with preserved awareness, a normal EEG and falling weight centiles
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old girl referred after two emergency presentations with suspected seizures. Her mother describes episodes where the baby suddenly stiffens, arches her back and twists her head to one side for a minute or two before relaxing.

The episodes always happen within about 20 minutes of a feed, never during sleep. Her mother says that during them the baby keeps looking at her and follows her around the room with her eyes, there is no blueness, and she is back to her normal self as soon as it passes. She brings up milk after most feeds. An electroencephalogram recorded between episodes last week was normal. Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile over two months. Neurological examination and development are normal today.

data_table.Examination: Normal tone, symmetrical movements, no focal neurological signs, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Interictal electroencephalogram normal; full blood count, electrolytes and calcium within normal limits
data_table.Growth: Weight down from the 50th to the 25th centile over 8 weeks, length and head circumference tracking the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start levetiracetam and arrange an outpatient sleep deprived recording
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain under sedation
Start oral omeprazole and review the pattern of episodes in four weeks
Trial thickened feeds with upright positioning and review growth in two weeks
Refer for metabolic screening including ammonia and urine organic acids

subtopic_detail: descending weakness with ptosis and sluggish pupils after several days of constipation in a previously well infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional hospital. A previously well 5-month-old boy is brought in because he has gone floppy. His parents say he had not opened his bowels for four days before this started, and over the last two days his cry has become weak and he has been slow to feed, dribbling milk from the corners of his mouth.

He is afebrile and alert, and his eyes follow you, but both eyelids droop and his pupils react sluggishly. Tone is reduced throughout with poor head control and diminished reflexes. His breathing is shallow with a weak cough. The family live on a rural property and his mother mentions that they have been dipping his dummy in honey for teething.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, sluggish pupillary responses, weak cry, generalised hypotonia with reduced reflexes, shallow respiration with weak cough, alert and tracking
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), electrolytes and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for airway monitoring and arrange botulism immune globulin urgently
Start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after taking blood cultures
Give a trial of intravenous immunoglobulin for a suspected acute neuropathy
Arrange nerve conduction studies as an outpatient and review within one week
Start oral metronidazole and arrange abdominal imaging for the constipation

subtopic_detail: a positive newborn bloodspot result for a motor neuron disorder in an infant who is still feeding and moving normally
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar telephoned by the newborn screening laboratory about a 17-day-old boy. The bloodspot taken on day two shows an absence of exon 7 of the survival motor neuron 1 gene, with two copies of the closely related survival motor neuron 2 gene.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and is the first child of unrelated parents. When you review him that afternoon he is breastfeeding well, has regained his birth weight, cries strongly and moves all four limbs, although you note mild head lag on pull to sit. His tongue is not fasciculating, his reflexes are present, and his respiratory effort is normal with no paradoxical chest movement.

data_table.Examination: Strong cry, breastfeeding well, antigravity movement in all four limbs, mild head lag on pull to sit, reflexes present, no tongue fasciculation, no paradoxical breathing
data_table.Investigations: Newborn bloodspot screen showing homozygous absence of survival motor neuron 1 exon 7 with two copies of survival motor neuron 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the newborn screening sample and review the result in four weeks
Reassure the parents and review the baby at the six week check instead
Refer urgently to a neuromuscular service for confirmation and treatment
Arrange nerve conduction studies and a muscle biopsy before any referral
Start physiotherapy and arrange review once weakness becomes apparent

subtopic_detail: alkali ingestion with drooling and refusal to drink but no visible oral burns
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 2-year-old girl is brought in 90 minutes after her father found her in the laundry with an open bottle of drain cleaner and a wet chin. The label lists sodium hydroxide. She coughed and vomited once at home.

She is now sitting on her father's lap, drooling saliva onto her shirt and turning her head away from the cup of water offered by the nurse. Her voice sounds normal when she cries and there is no stridor. Her lips and the visible parts of her mouth and tongue look normal, with no blistering or white patches. Her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drooling with refusal of oral fluid, normal voice, no stridor, no visible oral or perioral burns, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give milk to drink in order to dilute and neutralise the ingested substance
Give activated charcoal now and observe in the department for four hours
Discharge home with oral analgesia as the mouth shows no visible burns today
Arrange an urgent barium swallow to assess the oesophagus before any feeding
Keep fasted, admit, and arrange upper endoscopy within twenty four hours

subtopic_detail: long standing dysphagia with a food bolus episode and no response to a full dose acid suppression trial
stem:
You are the paediatrician seeing a 9-year-old boy with eight months of food sticking in his chest. He drinks water with every mouthful, cuts meat into very small pieces, and is always the last to finish a meal.

Three months ago he came to the emergency department after a piece of steak stuck for 40 minutes before passing on its own. He has asthma and eczema, both well controlled. His general practitioner prescribed a full dose proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks, which he took reliably and which made no difference at all. His weight and height are on the 50th centile and have not changed lines. He has no night cough, no weight loss and no abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Well grown, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and iron studies within normal limits
data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking the 50th centile with no change in trajectory

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the proton pump inhibitor dose and review after another eight weeks
Refer for gastroscopy with biopsies from the proximal and distal oesophagus
Arrange a barium swallow to look for a structural cause of these symptoms
Refer to an allergist for skin prick testing to a panel of common food allergens
Start an empirical dairy free diet and review his symptoms in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: focal seizure and fever at nine days with unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid, thrombocytopenia and a markedly raised transaminase
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on the neonatal unit. A 9-day-old boy born at term by normal vaginal birth is brought in after 12 hours of poor feeding and a three minute episode of rhythmic jerking of the right arm that stopped spontaneously.

He is now lethargic and mottled with a temperature of 38.4 °C. There are no skin vesicles anywhere, including the scalp and the conjunctivae. His mother is 22 and has never had genital lesions, she was afebrile in labour, membranes ruptured two hours before birth, and her group B streptococcus screen was negative. You have taken cultures and given intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin. The lumbar puncture and blood results are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 58/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, mottled, no vesicular rash on skin, scalp or conjunctivae, anterior fontanelle soft, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid white cells 9 x10^6/L (0-20 in the neonate), protein 0.9 g/L (0.4-1.2), glucose 3.1 mmol/L with paired blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L, Gram stain negative; C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (<5); white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (5.0-21.0); platelets 98 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (<45)

lead_in: In addition to the antibiotics already given, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add intravenous aciclovir 20 mg/kg eight hourly and send herpes simplex PCR
Add intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg six hourly for suspected meningitis
Await the culture and PCR results before adding further antimicrobial treatment
Add oral valaciclovir 20 mg/kg eight hourly once oral feeding is tolerated
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging before any change to treatment now

subtopic_detail: toddler refusing to use one arm after axial traction with no bony tenderness or swelling
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 2-year-old girl is brought in by her father, who says she stopped using her right arm about an hour ago after he swung her up by both hands to lift her over a puddle. She cried for a minute at the time and has been settled since, but she will not reach for her drink bottle with that hand.

She sits comfortably on her father's lap with the right arm held slightly bent at the elbow and the palm turned in towards her body, and she reaches across herself for a toy with her left hand. There is no swelling, bruising or deformity anywhere on the limb, and she keeps playing while you palpate her collarbone, upper arm, forearm and wrist in turn. She pulls the arm away and cries when you try to turn the forearm palm-up. She is otherwise well and there have been no previous injuries or presentations.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling, bruising or deformity
data_table.Palpation: No tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna or wrist
data_table.Provocation: Distress on attempted passive supination of the right forearm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform bedside supination of the forearm followed by flexion of the elbow
Immobilise the limb in an above elbow backslab and review in fracture clinic
Arrange an urgent elbow ultrasound to look for a posterior joint effusion
Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm before any manipulation
Apply a broad arm sling and arrange orthopaedic review within a week

subtopic_detail: persistent head tilt with limited passive neck rotation and occipital flattening in a well three month old
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 3-month-old boy at his immunisation visit. His mother says his head always leans towards his right shoulder and that he only ever looks off to the left, even when she calls him from the other side. He was born at term by ventouse after a long second stage.

On examination the head is tilted to the right with the chin rotated to the left. You can passively rotate the chin towards the right only about 45 degrees before he resists, and there is a firm painless olive-shaped thickening in the lower third of the right sternocleidomastoid. The back of the head is flattened on the left with the left ear displaced forward. He fixes and follows with both eyes through a full range, the red reflex is symmetrical, and tone, power and the primitive reflexes are normal in all four limbs. He smiles responsively and is gaining weight along the 50th centile.

data_table.Neck examination: Head tilted right, chin rotated left, passive rotation to the right limited to 45 degrees
data_table.Palpation: Firm painless olive-shaped thickening in the lower right sternocleidomastoid
data_table.Head shape: Left occipital flattening with the left ear displaced anteriorly
data_table.Neurological and eye findings: Fixes and follows fully with both eyes, symmetrical red reflex, normal tone and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ophthalmology to assess for a compensatory ocular tilt
Refer to paediatric physiotherapy for stretching and positioning advice
Arrange an urgent neck ultrasound to exclude a malignant soft tissue mass
Refer for a moulding helmet to correct the skull asymmetry at this stage
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and the cervical spine

subtopic_detail: offensive discharge from one nostril only for three weeks in an afebrile toddler
stem: A 3-year-old boy has had offensive green discharge from the right nostril for three weeks, unchanged by saline spray and a course of oral antibiotic. The left nostril is dry. He is afebrile and well.

data_table.Examination: Thick offensive discharge at the right naris with an excoriated vestibule, clear left nasal cavity, normal tympanic membranes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Saline irrigation twice daily with review in one month
Intranasal corticosteroid spray with review in four weeks
Examine the nasal cavity with a speculum and remove any foreign body
Two week course of oral amoxicillin with clavulanate
Computed tomography of the sinuses before any intervention

subtopic_detail: greasy adherent yellow scale on the scalp and behind the ears of a thriving unbothered six week old
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-week-old boy whose parents are worried about thick yellowish flaking on the top of his head that has built up over the past fortnight. They say it looks greasy rather than dry and that some of it is now behind both ears, and they have been afraid to wash it off in case they hurt him.

On examination there are adherent greasy yellow scales over the vertex and in both retroauricular folds, with mild underlying erythema and no excoriation, weeping or crusting. The nappy area shows a faint salmon-coloured erythema in the inguinal folds without satellite lesions. He does not scratch or rub at his head while you examine him, sleeps through the night between feeds, and has gained 900 grams since birth. His mother has psoriasis affecting her elbows.

data_table.Skin examination: Adherent greasy yellow scale over the vertex and both retroauricular folds with mild erythema
data_table.Nappy area: Faint salmon erythema in the inguinal folds without satellite lesions
data_table.Growth: Weight gain of 900 grams since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start oral cefalexin for seven days and swab the scalp lesions for bacteria
Exclude cow's milk protein from the diet of the breastfeeding mother now
Apply a topical antifungal cream to the scalp and the nappy area every day
Apply a bland emollient to soften the scale then brush it out after bathing
Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice each day

subtopic_detail: bilateral evening leg pains in a well six year old who runs normally the following morning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose mother says he cries with sore legs in the evening two or three nights a week, usually after he has gone to bed. She points to the front of both thighs and the backs of both calves when asked where he holds them. Rubbing his legs and a warm pack settle him within about twenty minutes and he goes back to sleep.

He plays soccer at lunchtime and runs to the car without difficulty the next morning, and his teacher has raised no concerns. He has not limped at any point, has had no fevers or sweats, and his weight and height are tracking along the 75th centile as they have since he was two. On examination he is well, with no joint swelling, warmth or restriction anywhere, no bony tenderness on firm palpation of both legs, no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly. His gait, including heel and toe walking, is normal.

data_table.Examination: No joint swelling, warmth or restriction, no bony tenderness on palpation of both legs
data_table.Systemic findings: No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, normal gait including heel and toe walking
data_table.Growth: Height and weight tracking the 75th centile since age two

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request radiographs of both femora and tibiae to exclude a bone lesion
Refer to paediatric rheumatology for assessment of juvenile arthritis
Start a six week trial of ibuprofen each evening and repeat the examination
Arrange a full blood count, film and inflammatory markers before reassuring
Explain the benign pattern, advise massage and simple analgesia, and review

subtopic_detail: symmetrical bow legs in an eighteen month old of normal stature walking without pain
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18-month-old girl whose grandmother has told the family her legs are bending outwards and that she needs braces. She started walking at 13 months, runs after her brother, and has never complained of leg pain or refused to weight bear.

On examination she stands with the medial malleoli together and there is a gap of about 5 cm between the medial femoral condyles, which is symmetrical on the two sides. The bowing is centred at the knees, the tibiae are not sharply angulated, and there is no lateral thrust of either knee as she walks. There is no tenderness, no swelling and no restriction of hip or knee movement. Her height and weight are both on the 50th centile and have tracked there since birth. She has a varied diet including dairy, plays outdoors daily, and takes no medications. Her wrists and costochondral junctions feel normal.

data_table.Lower limb examination: Symmetrical intercondylar distance of 5 cm with the malleoli together, bowing centred at the knees
data_table.Gait: Walks and runs without a limp and with no lateral thrust at either knee
data_table.Growth: Height and weight both on the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Other findings: No wrist or costochondral widening, full hip and knee range of movement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, record the intercondylar distance and review the gait in six months
Request standing long leg alignment radiographs of both lower limbs today
Check serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D level
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for consideration of bracing this year
Arrange a skeletal survey to look for an underlying skeletal dysplasia

subtopic_detail: boggy scalp swelling crossing the suture lines with tachycardia and pallor hours after a ventouse delivery
stem: A 4-hour-old term boy delivered by ventouse is pale and sleepy; the midwife says his head feels soft and squelchy all over.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse fluctuant scalp swelling crossing the sagittal suture to the nape; central capillary refill four seconds
data_table.Serial measurement: Head circumference up 2.5 cm since birth
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (145-225)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Measure head circumference hourly and observe on the ward
Transfer to the neonatal unit for volume replacement and transfusion
Arrange urgent computed tomography of the head before transfer
Give intramuscular phytomenadione and repeat coagulation
Apply a compression bandage and recheck the haemoglobin

subtopic_detail: firm bright red umbilical lesion unchanged after two courses of topical treatment in a five week old
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 5-week-old girl whose umbilical stump separated at day nine. Her parents were shown how to apply table salt to a small red lump at the navel three weeks ago, and when that made no difference your colleague cauterised it with silver nitrate a fortnight later. The lump is unchanged and the parents describe a clear sticky discharge that keeps staining her singlets.

On examination there is an 8 mm bright red firm lesion protruding from the umbilicus with a smooth glistening surface that looks like the inside of a lip. It does not blanch on pressure, it feels solid rather than soft, and it did not shrink or whiten with either treatment. The surrounding skin is normal in colour with no induration, no warmth and no tenderness. She is afebrile and thriving with a weight gain of 240 grams in the past week. There is no cough on handling and no leakage of urine or intestinal content from the lesion.

data_table.Umbilical examination: 8 mm firm bright red protruding lesion with a smooth glistening non-blanching surface
data_table.Surrounding skin: Normal colour without induration, warmth or tenderness
data_table.Treatment response: No change after three weeks of topical salt and one silver nitrate cauterisation
data_table.Growth: Weight gain of 240 grams over the past week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a further course of topical salt therapy for seven more days
Cauterise the lesion with silver nitrate again at this consultation
Refer to paediatric surgery for excision and histological examination
Swab the umbilicus and start oral cefalexin for suspected omphalitis
Request an abdominal ultrasound to look for a patent urachal remnant

subtopic_detail: anterior chest wall depression in a tall adolescent with arachnodactyly and a high arched palate
stem: A 14-year-old boy asks about surgery for the dip in his chest, which deepened over two years of rapid growth. A maternal uncle died suddenly at 41.

data_table.Anthropometry: Height 97th centile, parents of average height, arm span exceeding height by 6 cm, positive thumb and wrist signs
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical lower sternal depression, high narrow palate, early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Reassure and review after the pubertal growth spurt
Chest radiograph to calculate the Haller index before referral
Referral to paediatric surgery for minimally invasive repair
Transthoracic echocardiography with aortic root measurement
Spirometry with a formal cardiopulmonary exercise test

subtopic_detail: irreducible tender groin lump in a vomiting four month old with a previously intermittent swelling
stem: A 4-month-old boy born at 32 weeks has screamed for five hours and vomited bile three times. A right groin lump that came and went has stayed up.

data_table.Examination: Firm tender 3 cm right groin swelling to the scrotum, no upper border; testes normal; abdomen distended, bowel sounds high-pitched

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Book an elective herniotomy on the next operating list
Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed strangulated bowel
Apply ice and review the swelling in the morning if he settles
Arrange an urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler first
Give analgesia, attempt gentle reduction, involve surgeons urgently

subtopic_detail: unilateral in-toeing with a painless limp and reduced hip abduction in a three year old
stem: A 3-year-old girl who started walking at 15 months has always dipped to the right as she walks, painlessly, and her right foot turns in when she runs.

data_table.Hip examination: Abduction in flexion 70 degrees left and 40 degrees right, increased right internal rotation
data_table.Leg length: Right knee lower than left with hips and knees flexed
data_table.Distal examination: Normal thigh-foot axis and foot border bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis and both hips
Night time derotation brace with review in twelve months
Gait analysis and in-shoe orthotics through podiatry
Ultrasound of both hips to assess the acetabular angle
Reassurance that rotational profiles correct with growth

subtopic_detail: postauricular swelling pushing the ear outwards five days into oral treatment for an ear infection
stem: A 4-year-old girl started oral amoxicillin five days ago for right ear pain. The pain settled, then returned worse, with swelling behind the ear since yesterday.

data_table.Examination: Tender fluctuant postauricular swelling, loss of the crease, pinna displaced down and out, bulging tympanic membrane
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 128 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to oral cefalexin and review her again in two days
Admit for intravenous antibiotics with urgent otolaryngology review
Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin drops and continue the oral course
Arrange an outpatient computed tomography of the temporal bones
Aspirate the swelling in clinic and send fluid for culture

subtopic_detail: limping toddler with a normal initial tibial radiograph after a low height twisting fall
stem:
You are the registrar in a suburban emergency department. An 18-month-old boy is brought in because he has refused to walk since yesterday afternoon, when he slid off the bottom step of a play fort and his foot caught under him. His mother says he screamed briefly, settled with a cuddle, and has been his usual cheerful self since, but he now crawls everywhere and cries if she stands him up.

He is afebrile and has been eating and drinking normally, with no rash and no recent illness. On examination he lies happily on the trolley and moves both hips and knees through full range without complaint. There is no swelling, warmth or bruising of either leg. He cries reproducibly when you gently rotate the right foot relative to the shin, and settles as soon as you stop. Radiographs of the right tibia and fibula in two planes are reported as showing no fracture.

data_table.Examination: Full painless range at both hips and knees, no joint swelling, warmth or effusion
data_table.Palpation: Distress on gentle torsion of the right tibia, no focal bony tenderness elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Right tibia and fibula radiographs, two views: no fracture identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Request an urgent magnetic resonance scan of the right leg under sedation today
Arrange an urgent hip ultrasound to look for a joint effusion before discharge
Discharge with simple analgesia and advice to mobilise as tolerated at home
Apply an above ankle walking boot and review clinically in seven to ten days
Send blood cultures with inflammatory markers and admit for intravenous antibiotics

subtopic_detail: infant with a persistently watering eye and crusted lashes since the first weeks of life
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-month-old boy whose mother says his left eye has watered constantly since he was about two weeks old. Tears spill down the cheek even when he is content, and most mornings the lashes are stuck together with a yellowish crust that wipes away easily with a warm washer. She has been given two courses of antibiotic drops by a colleague, each of which cleared the crusting for a few days before it returned.

He was born at term and is growing along the 50th centile. On examination he fixes and follows your face with each eye covered in turn, and the left conjunctiva is white and quiet with no injection. Pressing over the area between the inner corner of the eye and the nose produces a bead of mucoid material at the lid margin. The corneas are clear and of equal size, and the red reflex is present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Left epiphora with quiet white conjunctiva, no lid or periorbital swelling, no photophobia
data_table.Eye assessment: Red reflex present and symmetrical, corneal diameters equal and corneas clear, fixes and follows with either eye
data_table.Provocation: Mucoid reflux at the punctum on pressure over the lacrimal sac

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management at this visit?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin and arrange paediatric review within forty eight hours
Arrange urgent ophthalmology review the same day for measurement of intraocular pressure
Teach lacrimal sac massage with lid hygiene and review him at twelve months of age
Refer for probing of the nasolacrimal duct under general anaesthesia within the month
Prescribe a further week of chloramphenicol eye drops four times daily and reassess

subtopic_detail: day one newborn not moving one arm fully after a delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia
stem:
