You are the paediatric resident asked to review a term baby boy on the postnatal ward at 18 hours of age. His birth weight was 4320 g and the delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia relieved with the McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure. The midwife has noticed he is not moving his right arm as freely as his left during cares and cries when she dresses him.

On examination he is pink, alert and feeding well at the breast. He grips your finger firmly with both hands and flexes and extends both elbows and wrists spontaneously when he is unwrapped. The right Moro reflex is reduced in amplitude compared with the left. You feel a step and crepitus over the middle of the right collarbone and he grimaces as you do so. The overlying skin is intact with no bruising, and there is no swelling of the arm or forearm.

data_table.Examination: Palpable step and crepitus over the mid right clavicle, intact overlying skin, no arm swelling
data_table.Neurological: Symmetrical palmar grasp, spontaneous elbow and wrist movement bilaterally, asymmetrical Moro
data_table.Feeding: Breastfeeding established, alert and pink between feeds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Pin the sleeve to the body for three weeks and arrange orthopaedic review in clinic
Reassure the parents, give regular paracetamol and handle the arm gently for two weeks
Request a skeletal survey and notify the child protection team before discharge home
Arrange an ultrasound of the shoulder joint to exclude a proximal humeral separation
Refer urgently to the brachial plexus clinic for nerve conduction studies within the week

subtopic_detail: school aged child with nasal symptoms that worsened again after an initial improvement at day seven
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old girl brought back by her father. She started with a blocked nose and a cough twelve days ago, was clearly getting better by about day six, and then over the last three days has become worse again with thick discoloured nasal discharge, a daytime cough and a temperature her father measured at home at 38.6 degrees.

She has missed two days of school and complains that her face aches when she leans forward to put on her shoes. She has had no previous sinus problems and takes no regular medications. On examination she is alert and well perfused with moist mucous membranes. There is mucopurulent discharge in both nasal passages and tenderness over both cheeks. The tympanic membranes are pearly and mobile, the pharynx is mildly injected without exudate, and the chest is clear on auscultation. There is no periorbital swelling, no proptosis and eye movements are full and painless.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Examination: Bilateral mucopurulent nasal discharge with maxillary tenderness, clear chest, pearly mobile tympanic membranes
data_table.Eye assessment: No periorbital swelling or proptosis, full painless eye movements, normal visual acuity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide intranasal saline with analgesia and advise review if not settling in a week
Start intranasal mometasone with an oral decongestant for a seven day course
Commence oral amoxicillin and arrange clinical review in forty eight to seventy two hours
Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone with urgent ophthalmology and otolaryngology review
Refer for a computed tomography scan of the sinuses before deciding on treatment

subtopic_detail: toddler whose thumb has become fixed in a bent position at the end joint over several months
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 2-year-old girl whose mother has noticed over the past four months that the end of her right thumb stays bent. It was intermittent at first and would click straight when her mother pulled on it, but for the last six weeks it has stayed bent all the time.

There was no injury that anyone recalls. She uses the hand normally for feeding herself and building towers, and does not appear to be in pain. On examination the right thumb is held flexed at the joint nearest the nail and you cannot passively straighten it fully. There is a firm mobile nodule on the palmar surface at the base of the thumb that moves with the tendon. The thumb is warm, pink and not tender, and the skin creases are normal. The left thumb extends fully and there is no nodule. All other digits move normally and she has no joint swelling elsewhere.

data_table.Examination: Fixed flexion at the right interphalangeal joint of the thumb, full passive range at all other digits
data_table.Palpation: Firm mobile nodule over the palmar aspect of the first metacarpophalangeal joint, non-tender
data_table.Systemic: No joint swelling, warmth or effusion elsewhere, normal skin creases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inject the flexor sheath with corticosteroid and review the thumb again in four weeks
Refer to a paediatric hand surgeon for consideration of release of the tendon sheath
Reassure the parents that this resolves spontaneously and review her in twelve months
Arrange hand therapy for a night extension splint and passive stretching for six months
Request inflammatory markers with an antinuclear antibody and refer to rheumatology

subtopic_detail: toddler with brief stiffening and jerking after a minor knock, going pale before losing consciousness
stem: A 20-month-old girl knocked her forehead lightly on a table, opened her mouth to cry but made no sound, went white around the lips and limp within seconds. Her limbs then stiffened and jerked for 15 seconds before she came round. Two similar episodes have followed minor bumps.

data_table.Examination: Afebrile, small forehead bruise, symmetrical tone and reflexes, dual heart sounds with no murmur

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain
Sleep deprived electroencephalogram within four weeks
Twelve lead electrocardiogram with corrected QT
Full blood count with ferritin and iron studies
Venous blood gas with glucose and electrolytes

subtopic_detail: toddler refusing all fluids with painful mouth ulcers and swollen bleeding gums on day two
stem: A 22-month-old boy has refused all drinks since yesterday and is drooling constantly. Fever and irritability began two days ago.

data_table.Mouth: Shallow ulcers on tongue, buccal mucosa and hard palate; gingivae swollen and bleeding on contact
data_table.Skin: No vesicles on hands, feet or buttocks
data_table.Hydration: Dry lips, moist tongue, capillary refill under two seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluids with intravenous aciclovir
Give intranasal fentanyl, offer oral fluids, start oral aciclovir
Give oral dexamethasone and arrange paediatric review tomorrow
Prescribe oral amoxicillin with metronidazole and dental review
Give oral paracetamol and discharge with topical lidocaine gel

subtopic_detail: early adolescent boy with breast tissue development and asymmetrical testicular size on examination
stem: A 13-year-old boy has had breast development for eight months. He takes no medications, supplements or creams and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: 3 cm of firm concentric glandular tissue beneath both areolae, mildly tender
data_table.Genital examination: Pubic hair Tanner stage 3; right testicular volume 12 mL, left 20 mL with a firm irregular upper pole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ultrasound of the testes with beta human chorionic gonadotrophin
Referral for tamoxifen with review of response at three months
Thyroid and liver function tests with a serum prolactin
Reassurance that this is pubertal, reassessing in six months
Karyotype with morning testosterone and gonadotrophins

subtopic_detail: school aged boy with ballooning on voiding and a pale scarred ring at the tip of the foreskin
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9-year-old boy brought in by his father because the tip of his foreskin puffs up when he passes urine and the stream comes out as a thin spray that goes everywhere. Over the past year the opening has become progressively tighter and he has had two episodes of a red sore tip treated with oral antibiotics.

His father says the foreskin used to pull back a little further when he was younger than it does now. He is toilet trained, dry day and night, and has never had a urinary tract infection. On examination he is well grown and systemically well. The foreskin cannot be retracted at all, and the distal end has a firm pale ring of tissue that does not stretch when gentle traction is applied. The glans cannot be visualised. There is no surrounding erythema, discharge or tenderness today, and the testes are descended with no inguinal swelling.

data_table.Examination: Non retractile foreskin with a firm pale sclerotic ring at the preputial orifice, glans not visualised
data_table.Voiding: Ballooning of the prepuce with a thin spraying stream, no dysuria today
data_table.History: Two prior episodes of balanoposthitis, progressive loss of previously achieved retraction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the father that the foreskin separates naturally and review again in twelve months
Refer to a paediatric surgeon for circumcision and histological examination of the foreskin
Perform preputial adhesiolysis in the treatment room with topical anaesthetic gel applied
Prescribe topical betamethasone with gentle daily retraction for six weeks then review
Arrange a renal tract ultrasound with a urine culture before making a referral decision

subtopic_detail: preschooler with a painless neck lump enlarging over six weeks and overlying violaceous thinning skin
stem: A 3-year-old girl has a painless lump under the right jaw that has grown slowly over six weeks. Courses of cefalexin and amoxicillin with clavulanate have not changed it.

data_table.Examination: Firm 3 cm non-tender right submandibular mass fixed to thinned violaceous skin; no other lymphadenopathy
data_table.History: No fever, night sweats or weight loss; no tuberculosis contact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Incision and drainage in theatre with pus sent for culture
Oral clarithromycin with rifampicin and reassess in one month
Chest radiograph with an interferon gamma release assay
Full blood examination with lactate dehydrogenase and oncology review
Complete surgical excision of the node with mycobacterial culture

subtopic_detail: immunised school aged child with a third episode of one sided swelling in front of the ear
stem: A 6-year-old boy has a tender 4 cm swelling over the left parotid that lifts the earlobe, developing over a day. The same happened twice in eighteen months, each settling in a week. He is fully immunised and afebrile.

data_table.Duct: Clear saliva expressed from the left Stensen duct, no pus
data_table.Investigations: Serum amylase 186 U/L (30 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Mumps polymerase chain reaction swab and public health notification
Oral flucloxacillin for ten days with review in one week
Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies with paediatric rheumatology referral
Ultrasound of both parotid glands, with massage and sialogogues
Serum lipase and abdominal ultrasound for the raised amylase

subtopic_detail: imaging a midline neck swelling before excision to confirm functioning thyroid tissue is present elsewhere
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 6-year-old boy. His mother first noticed a soft painless lump in the middle of the front of his neck about three months ago and thought it would go away.

Two weeks ago it became red, tender and larger during a head cold, and a week of oral antibiotics from his general practitioner settled the redness and the tenderness. The lump itself remains. He has had no weight loss and no night sweats. When you ask him to swallow and then to poke his tongue out, the lump rides upwards with both.

data_table.Examination: Smooth 2 cm midline swelling just below the hyoid bone, moves superiorly on swallowing and on tongue protrusion, overlying skin now normal, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Referral for excision of the cyst and the central hyoid body now
Neck ultrasound to confirm normally positioned thyroid tissue is present
Incision and drainage of the lump under local anaesthetic today
Fine needle aspiration cytology of the lump at the next clinic visit
A further two weeks of oral antibiotics with review in the clinic after

subtopic_detail: first line management of a persistent head tilt with a palpable neck mass in early infancy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7-week-old girl brought by her parents because her head is always tilted. She was delivered by forceps after a prolonged second stage.

Her parents noticed a firm pea sized lump in the right side of her neck at about three weeks of age, which has not changed since. Her head tilts to the right and her chin points to the left, and they find it hard to turn her face to the right when settling her. She is feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile, and moves all four limbs equally. Her eye movements are full in all directions.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted to the right with chin rotated to the left, firm non-tender 1 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid, passive rotation of the head to the right limited to about 50 degrees, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed, red reflex present and symmetrical, hips clinically stable on Ortolani and Barlow testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for surgical release of the sternocleidomastoid within a month
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine
Refer to physiotherapy for a stretching and positioning program
Arrange botulinum toxin injection of the shortened neck muscle
Reassure the parents that no intervention is needed at this age

subtopic_detail: timing of repair for a reducible groin swelling in a young ex preterm infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 6-week-old boy born at 32 weeks gestation. His parents noticed a bulge in his right groin about ten days ago, which appears when he cries or strains and settles when he is asleep.

It is present when you examine him. He is feeding well, has had no vomiting, opens his bowels normally and his nappies are unremarkable. The swelling extends downwards from the groin toward the scrotum, and you are unable to feel a normal cord above it. It flattens with steady gentle pressure and the right testis is palpable separately below the swelling. The left side is normal.

data_table.Examination: Right groin swelling extending toward the scrotum, upper border not palpable, reducible with gentle sustained pressure, overlying skin normal in colour with no tenderness, right testis palpable separately in the scrotum, abdomen soft and not distended
data_table.Investigations: Weight tracking along the 25th centile, no investigations performed, no vomiting and no abdominal distension reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this resolves on its own by twelve months
Arrange a groin ultrasound and review in the clinic in three months
Arrange emergency theatre tonight for exploration of the right groin
Refer to paediatric surgery for repair on the next available list
Advise observation with review only if the swelling becomes painful

subtopic_detail: proceeding to division of a restrictive lingual frenulum after optimised attachment has failed
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-day-old breastfed boy in the assessment unit. His mother describes severe pain throughout every feed and her nipples are cracked and bleeding.

He feeds for about fifty minutes and wants to feed again within ninety minutes. A lactation consultant has seen the pair twice over the past four days and has worked on positioning and attachment at both visits, with no improvement in pain or in the pattern of feeding. His birth weight was 3480 g. On examination his tongue cannot be lifted above the level of the lower gum and the tip is notched when he cries.

data_table.Examination: Frenulum attached close to the tip of the tongue restricting elevation and lateral movement, tongue tip notched on crying, palate intact, no ankyloglossia of the upper lip, mother's nipples cracked with a compressed shape after the feed
data_table.Investigations: Weight 3090 g, representing 11 per cent below birth weight, serum bilirubin below the treatment threshold for age, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise cessation of breastfeeding and establish full formula feeding
Supply nipple shields for the mother and review the weight in one week
Commence formula top up feeds after each breastfeed and review weekly
Treat both mother and baby for candida and review in one week
Refer for division of the tongue tie after the review of attachment

subtopic_detail: sequencing refractive correction before occlusion therapy in unilateral reduced vision found at screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy referred after a preschool vision screening visit. His parents had noticed nothing wrong and say he plays and draws normally.

He was born at term with no perinatal problems and there is no family history of childhood eye disease. On testing, the vision in his right eye is 6/6 and in his left eye is 6/24. The cover test reveals an inward shift of the left eye when the right eye is covered. The red reflex is present, symmetrical and normal in both eyes, and the fundus appears normal on both sides. Cycloplegic refraction has been performed in the clinic.

data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/6 right and 6/24 left, cover test shows an inward shift of the left eye on covering the right, red reflex symmetrical and normal bilaterally, fundi normal, ocular movements full
data_table.Investigations: Cycloplegic refraction plus 5.00 dioptres in the left eye and plus 0.75 dioptres in the right eye

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe spectacles for the refractive error and review in four months
Commence occlusion of the right eye for six hours daily from today
Refer for surgical correction of the eye alignment within three months
Commence daily atropine drops to the right eye as penalisation therapy
Repeat the vision screening in twelve months at the school entry check

subtopic_detail: identifying the treatable association behind stereotyped cyanotic episodes provoked by crying in a toddler
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 18-month-old girl whose parents describe three frightening episodes over the past two months. The most recent happened yesterday when she was told she could not have a biscuit before dinner.

She cried hard, then went silent with her mouth open, her lips turned dusky blue and she went floppy and slid to the floor. She was unresponsive for about twenty seconds with a few jerks of her arms at the end, then cried, wanted a cuddle and was back to her usual self within a minute. Each of the three episodes has begun in exactly this way after she was upset or hurt. She is otherwise well, walks and runs normally and has around six bottles of cow's milk a day in addition to her meals.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, no murmur, normal heart sounds, femoral pulses palpable and symmetrical, neurological examination normal, development age appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105 to 135), mean cell volume 68 fL (70 to 86), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (15 to 150), electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography and refer to a paediatric neurologist
Commence oral iron with dietary advice and parental reassurance
Commence regular sodium valproate and review in the clinic in a month
Refer to paediatric cardiology for a 24 hour Holter monitor recording
Advise the parents to avoid confrontation that triggers the episodes

subtopic_detail: recognising that raised transaminases with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase are of muscle origin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy referred by a gastroenterology colleague for a second opinion. He was referred to that clinic three months ago after routine bloods taken during an episode of gastroenteritis showed raised liver enzymes, and repeat testing has shown the same pattern.

His parents mention that he is slower than the other children at kindergarten, falls frequently, and climbs the stairs at home one step at a time putting the same foot first. He walked at 19 months and his speech is also behind his peers. When you ask him to get up from sitting on the floor he turns onto his front and pushes on his own thighs with his hands to stand. His calves look bulky for his build.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral calf hypertrophy, proximal lower limb weakness, positive Gowers manoeuvre, waddling gait, reflexes present at the knees, no hepatomegaly and no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 35), gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits, bilirubin within normal limits, albumin within normal limits, creatine kinase 12400 U/L (less than 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps with immunohistochemical staining
Liver ultrasound with viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen
Dystrophin gene testing for deletions and duplications on a blood sample
Electromyography with nerve conduction studies under sedation
Repeat liver function tests and creatine kinase in three months

subtopic_detail: discordance between pubic hair development and testicular volume in a tall adolescent boy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 15-year-old boy referred by his school because of longstanding difficulty with reading and written work and because he finds it hard to make friends. His parents also wonder whether he is developing normally.

He is taller than both parents were at his age, and his height sits on the 97th centile against a mid parental centile of 40. His arm span exceeds his height by 7 cm. He has adult type pubic hair and has been shaving occasionally for a year. On examination his testes measure 4 mL on each side by orchidometer and he has firm breast tissue palpable behind both nipples. He takes no medication and uses no supplements.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 97th centile, arm span exceeding height by 7 cm, pubic hair Tanner stage 4, testicular volume 4 mL bilaterally and firm to palpation, bilateral glandular breast tissue, no abdominal or scrotal mass
data_table.Investigations: Luteinising hormone raised, follicle stimulating hormone raised, testosterone at the lower end of the reference range for age, prolactin within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat early morning testosterone with sex hormone binding globulin
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
Scrotal ultrasound to assess testicular volume and architecture
Peripheral blood karyotype requested through the clinical genetics service
Radiograph of the left hand and wrist to determine the bone age

subtopic_detail: ear position distinguishing a fused suture from positional moulding in occipital flattening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6-month-old girl whose parents are worried about the shape of the back of her head. They first noticed flattening on the right at about three months of age. She sleeps on her back as they were advised, and they have tried turning her head to the other side at night without any change.

She is meeting her developmental milestones, feeds well and has no vomiting or irritability. Looking down on the top of her head from above, you see that the right ear sits further back and lower than the left, and that the left side of her forehead is more prominent than the right. There is a firm ridge palpable running across the back right of her skull and a bulge behind the right ear.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening, right ear displaced posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the left, contralateral left frontal bossing, palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture, ipsilateral mastoid bulge, anterior fontanelle soft, head circumference tracking the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Neurological examination normal, red reflex present and symmetrical, no papilloedema visualised, developmental milestones age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretches and tummy time coaching
Give repositioning advice and review the head shape in two months
Refer for a moulding helmet to be fitted in the next four weeks
Arrange plain skull radiographs and review the result in the clinic
Refer to the craniofacial surgical service for specialist assessment

subtopic_detail: biphasic noisy breathing unchanged by position in an ex preterm infant with previous intubation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-month-old girl in the emergency department with noisy breathing. She was born at 27 weeks gestation and was ventilated through an endotracheal tube for three weeks in the neonatal unit.

Her parents say the noise started at about three weeks after she came home and has slowly become louder. It is present when she breathes in and also when she breathes out, and they have not been able to find any position that makes it better or worse. This is her third presentation in two months with what has each time been treated as croup, and on each occasion she improved for a day and then returned to her usual noisy breathing. She is feeding adequately and growing along the 25th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 52, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor audible at rest and unchanged by prone or supine positioning, mild intercostal and subcostal recession, no drooling, chest otherwise clear, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, no fever documented at any of the three presentations, growth tracking the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat for microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy
Commence a proton pump inhibitor trial and review in six weeks
Reassure the parents that the noise resolves by eighteen months
Arrange a chest radiograph and review the film in the clinic
Give nebulised adrenaline with oral dexamethasone and review after

subtopic_detail: extrahepatic features redirecting a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia away from the default diagnosis
stem: A 7-week-old girl has been jaundiced since day four with pale stools and dark urine. Her weight has fallen from the 50th to the 3rd centile.

data_table.Examination: Deep set eyes, broad forehead, pointed chin; ejection systolic murmur radiating to the back; posterior embryotoxon
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 168 micromol/L, conjugated 110 micromol/L; gamma glutamyl transferase 620 U/L (less than 100); alpha 1 antitrypsin normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Extrahepatic biliary atresia of the perinatal type
Syndromic paucity of the intrahepatic bile ducts
Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency of the PiZZ phenotype
Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2
Congenital cytomegalovirus infection of the liver

subtopic_detail: exertional collapse with a borderline corrected QT interval and a family history of unexplained sudden death
stem: A 14-year-old girl collapsed during a 400 m race, unresponsive for 40 seconds with a few limb jerks, then spoke normally, with no tongue biting or postictal confusion. Two years ago she collapsed diving into a pool. Her father died at 33 in an unexplained single-vehicle crash.

data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm 62 /min, corrected QT 468 ms, no delta wave

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that the corrected QT is not diagnostic
Arrange electroencephalography and neurology review
Refer to a cardiac genetic service for evaluation
Arrange a 24-hour Holter monitor and clinic review
Commence propranolol with review in six months

subtopic_detail: the narrow window in which a sample can still distinguish congenital from postnatally acquired infection in a newborn who failed hearing screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 19-day-old boy referred after he did not pass the newborn hearing screen in either ear on day two and again on a repeat test on day fourteen.

He was born at term with a birth weight on the tenth centile. His mother had a mild flu like illness with sore throat and fatigue at around sixteen weeks of pregnancy and did not seek medical attention. He is feeding and growing, and his mother reports no fevers. On examination he has scattered petechiae over his trunk that his mother says have been present since birth, and his liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. His anterior fontanelle is soft and his neurological examination is otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Weight tenth centile, head circumference third centile, scattered petechiae, liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows platelets 88 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haemoglobin 148 g/L (140 to 220), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 45)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M serology taken from the infant now
Polymerase chain reaction on the stored newborn screening dried blood spot
Urine collected for viral polymerase chain reaction within the next two days
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any laboratory testing is done
Repeat automated auditory brainstem response testing at three months of age

subtopic_detail: which hip imaging modality is reliable once the femoral head has begun to ossify in a seven month old with limited abduction
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 7-month-old girl brought by her mother, who has noticed that one leg does not seem to move out to the side as easily as the other when she changes her nappy.

She was the first baby and was breech from thirty two weeks until delivery by caesarean section at term. There is no family history of hip problems. She was examined in the newborn period and again at six weeks and no abnormality was documented on either occasion. She is not yet pulling to stand. On examination the right hip abducts to eighty degrees and the left to fifty degrees, there is an extra skin crease on the left thigh, and the left knee sits lower than the right when both hips and knees are flexed with the feet together on the couch.

data_table.Examination: Limited left hip abduction to 50 degrees, asymmetrical thigh creases, Galeazzi sign positive on the left, no leg length discrepancy on standing assessment
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips with dynamic stress views performed by a sonographer
Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips performed under general anaesthesia
Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis with the hips in neutral position
Computed tomography of the pelvis reconstructed in three planes for planning
No imaging at this stage with a repeat clinical examination at twelve months

subtopic_detail: a teenager with a meat bolus obstruction who has quietly adapted his eating for years, and what is needed to establish the cause
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy who came in three hours ago unable to swallow after a mouthful of steak. While he was waiting the obstruction resolved spontaneously and he is now drinking comfortably.

His mother mentions that he is always the last to finish a meal, cuts everything very small, drinks a full glass of water with every few mouthfuls and will not eat bread crusts. He has had eczema since infancy and uses a preventer inhaler for asthma. He has not lost weight and his growth is tracking on the fiftieth centile. He has no heartburn, no regurgitation and no nocturnal cough. There is no history of caustic ingestion and no previous oesophageal surgery.

data_table.Examination: Comfortable, no drooling, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, weight and height on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Barium swallow to assess the calibre and motility of the oesophagus
Gastroscopy with multiple biopsies from the proximal and distal oesophagus
Trial of a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks with review of his symptoms
Empirical elimination of dairy and wheat with a dietitian and review in twelve weeks
High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise the pattern of contraction

subtopic_detail: unexplained bruising with a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio and normal platelets in a six week old whose parents declined the birth injection
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department seeing a 6-week-old boy brought in by his parents because of bruising over his back and thighs that appeared over the past two days.

He is exclusively breastfed, feeding well and gaining weight along the fiftieth centile. His parents declined all injections at birth and he has had no immunisations. He bled from the heel prick site for about twenty minutes at his newborn screening. He is alert, afebrile and interactive, with a soft anterior fontanelle and a normal neurological examination. His mother took no medication during pregnancy and there is no family history of bleeding. His stools are yellow and his urine is pale.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, blood pressure 76/44, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bruises over the back and both thighs, no petechiae, fontanelle soft and flat, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 6.4 (0.9 to 1.3), activated partial thromboplastin time 78 seconds (25 to 38), platelets 312 x10^9/L (150 to 400), fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (1.5 to 4.0), haemoglobin 108 g/L (100 to 140), bilirubin and alanine aminotransferase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Transfuse platelets and repeat the coagulation profile after the transfusion
Give fresh frozen plasma as the sole treatment and observe him overnight
Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics after taking blood cultures
Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection before treating him
Give intravenous vitamin K slowly and recheck the clotting profile afterwards

subtopic_detail: daily soiling in a five year old with a palpable faecal mass, and the consequence of starting maintenance laxative without clearing the load first
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-year-old boy whose prep teacher has sent a note home about a smell in the classroom. His mother is exasperated and says he is soiling his underwear most days and has started hiding the dirty pairs behind the couch.

She says he passes an enormous hard stool in the toilet about once every seven to ten days, and that he sometimes goes up on his toes, crosses his legs and holds onto furniture when he looks like he needs to go. He has a good appetite and drinks water and milk. He was toilet trained at three without difficulty and the soiling began about nine months ago after a painful episode with an anal fissure. His growth is tracking along the fiftieth centile, he has never had delayed passage of meconium, and his neurological and spinal examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with a firm non-tender mass palpable in the left lower quadrant and suprapubically, normal anal position, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, no sacral dimple or hair tuft
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology and thyroid stimulating hormone both within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in treatment?

options.text: Increase dietary fibre and fluid intake and review his progress in four weeks
Arrange an abdominal radiograph to assess the extent of the faecal loading
Refer to a child psychologist for behavioural management of the soiling
Give an escalating macrogol regimen for disimpaction before daily maintenance
Administer a phosphate enema in the clinic and start maintenance macrogol after

subtopic_detail: choosing between a hydrolysed and an amino acid based formula for an infant with blood streaked stools, eczema and centile loss
stem: A 4-month-old girl changed from breast to cow's milk formula at six weeks has since vomited after most feeds and passes six or seven loose stools daily with blood-streaked mucus. Her eczema has not improved on moisturiser and hydrocortisone. Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 15th centile.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C-reactive protein normal; stool culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her feeding?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula
Change to a soy protein based formula
Change to an amino acid based formula
Change to a lactose free cow's milk formula
Change to a thickened anti-reflux formula

subtopic_detail: the silent sight threatening complication that must be screened for in a young girl with a persistently swollen knee and a positive antinuclear antibody
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl who has limped for four months. Her mother says she is at her worst first thing in the morning and hobbles for about an hour before loosening up, and that she is back to running by the afternoon.

There was no injury. She has had no fevers, no rash, no weight loss and no night pain that wakes her. Her right knee has been visibly swollen throughout and she has begun to keep it slightly bent when standing. She has no eye pain, no redness and no photophobia, and her mother has noticed nothing wrong with her vision. The rheumatology team has confirmed a diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and is starting an intra-articular corticosteroid injection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm with an effusion and a 10 degree fixed flexion deformity, no other joint involved, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, white eyes with no injection
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count within normal limits, antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What additional step is most important in her ongoing care?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the right knee to assess for synovial thickening
Aspiration of the knee effusion for cell count, Gram stain and bacterial culture
Testing for human leucocyte antigen B27 to define the arthritis subtype further
Slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist arranged within the next few weeks
Visual acuity assessment at each clinic visit performed by the practice nurse

subtopic_detail: whether a sleep study is required before surgical referral in an otherwise well preschooler with classic obstructive symptoms and large tonsils
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-year-old boy whose parents are worried about his breathing at night. He has snored every night for two years and they now hear him stop for several seconds and then gasp, several times an hour.

He sleeps with his neck extended and his mouth open, thrashes about, and sweats through his pyjamas. He was dry at night for eight months and has been wetting the bed again for the past four. His kindergarten teacher has raised concerns that he is inattentive and cannot sit still at mat time. His weight and height are both on the fiftieth centile. He has no craniofacial abnormality, no neuromuscular disorder and no chromosomal condition, and his tonsils touch in the midline on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tonsils meeting in the midline, mouth breathing, no adenoid facies, chest clear, heart sounds dual with no murmur, body mass index on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry at home and refer only if desaturations are recorded
Arrange laboratory polysomnography and refer once the study confirms the diagnosis
Commence an intranasal corticosteroid with montelukast and review in three months
Refer to an otolaryngologist for consideration of adenotonsillectomy without delay
Refer to a sleep physician for assessment for nocturnal continuous positive pressure

subtopic_detail: separating nutritional from inherited phosphate wasting rickets in a toddler with worsening bow legs using the parathyroid hormone level
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 20-month-old boy in Melbourne whose mother is worried that his legs are becoming more bowed rather than less. He began walking at seventeen months and tires quickly.

He was breastfed exclusively until fourteen months and has never received a vitamin supplement. He now eats family foods but refuses dairy. His mother has deeply pigmented skin and wears clothing that covers her arms and legs when outdoors, and he spends most days indoors at home. There is no family history of short stature, bone disease or bowed legs in either parent. On examination his wrists are widened, there are palpable beading swellings along his costochondral junctions, and his forehead is prominent. His length is on the third centile having previously tracked along the twenty fifth.

data_table.Examination: Widened wrists, costochondral beading, frontal bossing, symmetrical genu varum with an intercondylar distance of 7 cm, no limb asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.13 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20 to 2.20), alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (100 to 350), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 16 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone 16.4 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of both legs with review of the angle in six months
Commence high dose colecalciferol with adequate dietary or supplemental calcium
Commence oral phosphate supplements with calcitriol and monitor renal ultrasound
Commence an oral calcium supplement alone and repeat his biochemistry in three months
Reassure that this is physiological bowing and arrange review at three years of age

subtopic_detail: persistent delayed sleep onset in an autistic school aged child after a documented adequate trial of behavioural sleep measures
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old autistic boy whose parents say bedtime has become the hardest part of the day. Lights go out at half past seven and he is still awake at half past nine or later, almost every night.

Over the past three months the family has worked with a psychologist on a written plan: the same routine every night, screens off an hour before bed, a dark and quiet bedroom, no daytime naps, morning outdoor light and a consistent wake time. His parents have kept a diary showing they followed it and that sleep onset latency has not changed. Once asleep he stays asleep and wakes at half past five. He does not snore, has no witnessed pauses in breathing and has no urge to move his legs at night. He takes no regular medication, his ferritin is normal and he has never had a stimulant prescribed.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils small, body mass index on the fiftieth centile, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 48 micrograms/L (20 to 200), full blood count and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before considering any medication for sleep
Prescribe promethazine at bedtime and review his sleep diary again in four weeks
Reinforce the existing behavioural plan and review his sleep diary in three months
Trial melatonin given before bedtime while continuing the behavioural measures
Prescribe clonidine at night and monitor his blood pressure and pulse at review

subtopic_detail: separating recurrent wheeze occurring only with colds from asthma needing a daily preventer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 2-year-old boy brought by his father after a fourth episode of wheeze in twelve months. Each episode has begun with a runny nose and a cough, lasted about five days, and settled completely.

His father says that between episodes he runs around the park without stopping, sleeps through the night, and has never coughed at night or after running when he is well. He has no eczema and no food allergies, and neither parent nor either sibling has asthma, hay fever or eczema. He attends childcare three days a week. He was born at term and has never been admitted to hospital. Today he is at the end of an episode, is not distressed, and his chest is clear on auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Speaking in phrases and playing, no accessory muscle use or tracheal tug, chest clear with no wheeze audible today, no eczema, growth tracking along the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start a daily inhaled corticosteroid preventer and review him in eight weeks
Start a daily oral leukotriene receptor antagonist taken through the winter months
Arrange skin prick testing to aeroallergens before deciding on any preventer
Provide an inhaled bronchodilator with a spacer and a written action plan
Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone for the family to begin at each illness

subtopic_detail: recognising heavy proteinuria in a preschooler whose facial swelling has been treated as an allergy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old girl referred by her general practitioner. Her mother first noticed puffiness around both eyes three weeks ago, worst on waking and easing through the day, and a locum prescribed an antihistamine for presumed allergy.

The swelling has not improved and over the past week her abdomen has become distended and her ankles swollen, so that her shoes no longer fit. She has had no rash, no urticaria and no wheeze, and there has been no new pet, detergent or food. She has passed normal coloured urine throughout and has had no dysuria and no fever. She had a sore throat about six weeks ago that settled without treatment. Her blood pressure is normal for her age and her growth is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked periorbital oedema, pitting oedema to both mid shins, abdominal distension with shifting dullness, no rash or purpura, no joint swelling, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 4 plus with no blood, urine protein creatinine ratio markedly raised, serum albumin 16 g/L (35-50), total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L (less than 5.5), creatinine 32 micromol/L (20-50), complement C3 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue the antihistamine and add a short course of topical corticosteroid
Arrange urgent percutaneous renal biopsy before commencing any drug treatment
Give intravenous albumin with furosemide and observe the diuretic response
Start oral penicillin and await antistreptolysin O titres before further treatment
Commence oral prednisolone daily with a planned taper after four weeks

subtopic_detail: choosing between oral and intravenous glucose for a large newborn of a diabetic mother whose repeat sugar stays low
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward at two hours of age. The baby is a term boy born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery weighing 4 420 g to a mother whose pregnancy was complicated by insulin treated gestational diabetes.

He was put to the breast at thirty minutes and fed briefly. A routine pre feed blood glucose at one hour was 1.9 mmol/L, so the midwife gave 0.5 mL/kg of 40 percent oral glucose gel and a breastfeed, and the repeat pre feed level one hour later is 1.6 mmol/L. He is pink and well perfused, has a normal cry, has not had a seizure and is not jittery at present. His temperature has been stable since birth and there are no respiratory signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142/min, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well perfused with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, normal tone and normal cry, anterior fontanelle soft, no respiratory distress, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Pre feed blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L at one hour, repeat pre feed blood glucose 1.6 mmol/L at two hours, formal laboratory glucose sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: A second dose of 40 percent oral glucose gel with a further breastfeed
Top up with expressed breast milk hourly and recheck in three hours
Give an intramuscular glucagon dose and continue to feed on the ward
Start empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after cultures
Admit for intravenous 10 percent glucose with hourly glucose monitoring

subtopic_detail: investigating an adolescent girl with heavy periods since menarche and lifelong easy bruising
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 14-year-old girl referred with heavy periods. She reached menarche at twelve and says every period since then has been heavy, requiring a change of pad every hour on the first two days and causing her to miss school.

She has also had nosebleeds since early childhood, two of which needed nasal packing, and she bruises on her thighs without recalling any injury. She bled for several hours after a dental extraction at age ten. Her mother describes her own periods as heavy and had a postpartum haemorrhage after her second child. She takes no aspirin, no anti-inflammatory medication and no herbal preparations. On examination she has scattered bruises of differing ages over both thighs, no petechiae, no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, bruises of varying age on both thighs, no petechiae or purpura, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no joint swelling or deformity
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (120-160), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (30-300), prothrombin time 12 seconds (11-14), activated partial thromboplastin time 41 seconds (25-38)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess megakaryocyte number and morphology
Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity with a factor VIII level
Factor IX assay with genetic testing for a haemophilia B carrier state
Pelvic ultrasound to identify a structural cause for her menstrual bleeding
Antinuclear antibody with antiphospholipid antibodies and a lupus anticoagulant

subtopic_detail: advising a family about the single highest yield change when several sudden infant death risk factors are present together
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-week-old boy for his immunisations. He was born at 35 weeks and is feeding well and gaining weight.

His mother mentions that she is exhausted. She tells you she smokes ten cigarettes a day outside the house, that the baby sleeps in a bassinet beside her bed on his back, and that when he wakes at three in the morning she feeds him lying down on the sofa in the lounge room and they both usually fall asleep there until the morning. She uses a light muslin wrap and the bassinet has a firm mattress and no bumpers or soft toys. She asks whether a home apnoea monitor would let her relax, because a friend has offered to lend one.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure not recorded, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and well grown, weight tracking along the 25th centile, chest clear, heart sounds normal with no murmur, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: Which single change would you advise first to reduce this baby's risk of sudden unexpected death?

options.text: Borrow the home apnoea monitor and use it whenever the baby sleeps
Swaddle the baby more firmly with arms contained during every sleep
Feed the baby on a bed and return him to his own cot before sleeping
Move the bassinet out of the bedroom into a separate quiet nursery
Position the baby on his side with a rolled towel to stop him rolling

subtopic_detail: responding to a request for contraception from a young adolescent who does not want her parents informed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl who has come to the clinic alone and asks for the contraceptive pill. She tells you she does not want her parents to know and asks whether you have to tell them.

She explains that she has been in a relationship for eight months with a boy in her year at school who is sixteen, that they have not yet had sex, and that she wants to be prepared before they do. She describes the relationship as happy and says there has been no pressure, no violence and no exchange of money or gifts. She can explain how the pill works, what happens if she misses one, and that it does not protect against sexually transmitted infection. She is attending school regularly, is not using alcohol or other drugs, and her mood and weight are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well grown with body mass index on the 50th centile, no bruising or injury, engaged and articulate throughout the consultation, no features of low mood
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, no other investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Decline to prescribe until at least one parent attends with her in person
Notify child protection services because of her age before prescribing anything
Prescribe the pill without exploring the relationship or discussing confidentiality
Provide condoms only and review her request again when she turns sixteen
Assess her competence and capacity to consent, then provide confidential care

subtopic_detail: choosing an anticonvulsant when brief staring episodes coexist with early morning jerks in an adolescent
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric neurology clinic seeing a 13-year-old girl referred after a convulsion at school. Her mother reports that for the past two years she has had brief episodes at home where she stops mid sentence and stares for a few seconds, then carries on as though nothing happened.

Her mother adds that for the past six months she has been dropping her cereal spoon at breakfast and has smashed two bowls, always within an hour of waking, and that she is fully aware when this happens. The convulsion at school followed a sleepover at which she had about four hours of sleep. She takes no regular medication and is not sexually active. Her electroencephalogram shows generalised polyspike and wave discharges that increase markedly on photic stimulation.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal with no focal deficit, no neurocutaneous stigmata, normal fundi, normal gait and coordination
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram shows generalised polyspike and wave at 4 to 6 Hz with a photoparoxysmal response, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Levetiracetam titrated to effect with monitoring of mood and behaviour
Sodium valproate at a standard weight based dose with liver function testing
Carbamazepine as a modified release preparation with slow upward titration
Ethosuximide with a review of seizure frequency after four weeks of therapy
Sleep hygiene advice with a plan to review before starting any medication

subtopic_detail: planning the follow up that matters after a palpable purpuric rash with arthralgia in a school aged child
stem: A 6-year-old boy developed a rash on his buttocks and legs four days ago, a week after a sore throat. He has colicky abdominal pain and swollen tender ankles.

data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura over buttocks and extensor legs, none above the waist; no scrotal swelling
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 386 x10^9/L, normal coagulation profile, urinalysis 1 plus blood, no protein

lead_in: Alongside analgesia, what most matters in his ongoing management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin to shorten the rash
Oral corticosteroid to prevent later kidney disease
Referral for renal biopsy now to grade involvement
Scheduled blood pressure and urinalysis for six months
Empirical antibiotics for the preceding throat infection

subtopic_detail: recognising anterior horn cell disease in a floppy infant whose face and eyes remain fully active
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-month-old boy referred because he cannot hold his head up. His mother says he moved vigorously in the womb but has become less active over the last two months and no longer kicks the play mat.

She describes his cry as quieter than it was and says he takes longer to finish a bottle and sweats while feeding. He smiles readily at her, follows her across the room with his eyes and babbles. He has had no fever and no seizures, and his weight is tracking along the 10th centile having been on the 50th at birth. On examination he lies with his hips abducted and externally rotated, has no head lag correction on pull to sit, and the deep tendon reflexes cannot be elicited at the knees, ankles or biceps. His tongue shows fine rippling movements at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked hypotonia with a bell shaped chest and paradoxical breathing, absent deep tendon reflexes throughout, fine tongue fasciculations, full facial expression and full extraocular movements, alert and socially responsive
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 142 U/L (60-305), full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Methylation testing of the chromosome 15 imprinted region on a blood sample
Survival motor neuron gene deletion testing with urgent neurology referral
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine under anaesthesia
Serum lactate with urine organic acids and plasma amino acid quantification
Repetitive nerve stimulation with an edrophonium test performed at the bedside

subtopic_detail: blue episodes provoked by frustration in a toddler whose milk intake has displaced solid food
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18-month-old girl whose mother describes six episodes in three months. Each begins when she is hurt or told no, she cries hard, stops breathing out, turns blue around the lips and goes limp for about twenty seconds, then wakes irritable.

Her mother says two of the episodes ended with a few seconds of stiffening of the arms. There has never been an episode during sleep, during exercise or without an obvious trigger, and she has never been incontinent or drowsy for long afterwards. She walks, runs and says twenty words. She drinks about 1.4 litres of cow milk each day and eats very little meat or cereal. There is no family history of sudden death or of fainting, and her electrocardiogram taken last week was reported as normal with a corrected QT interval of 410 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no murmur, femoral pulses equal, neurological examination normal, weight on the 25th centile and length on the 50th
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with corrected QT interval 410 ms (below 440), no bloods taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Supply buccal midazolam for the parents to give during the longer episodes
Reassure the parents that the episodes are harmless and need no further assessment
Arrange a sleep deprived electroencephalogram to characterise the stiffening movements
Refer for 24 hour ambulatory cardiac monitoring before any other investigation
Take a full blood count with iron studies and replace iron if the stores are low

subtopic_detail: deciding whether repeated nosebleeds in a well child need a bleeding disorder workup
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old boy who has had about eight nosebleeds in the past two months. His mother says each one comes from the right nostril, starts while he is watching television or soon after he has been picking his nose, and stops within ten minutes when she pinches the bridge of his nose for him.

He has never bled from the gums or into a joint, has never bruised without an injury, and had a tonsillectomy at five without excessive bleeding. No relative has a bleeding problem or has needed transfusion after surgery. The family has recently started using ducted heating through the winter. On examination the anterior part of the right septum is crusted and reddened, and the rest of the examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Crusted excoriated area on the anterior right nasal septum, no petechiae, no bruises beyond both shins, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Correct the pressure technique and prescribe an antiseptic nasal ointment for two weeks
Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for chemical cautery of the septal vessels
Advise a saline spray alone and review him again only if the bleeding worsens
Request a full blood count, coagulation profile and von Willebrand factor studies
Arrange nasal endoscopy to exclude a mass in the posterior nasal space

subtopic_detail: anterior knee pain in a growing athlete where the site of tenderness decides the management
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13-year-old boy who plays basketball four times a week and has had three months of pain at the front of his right knee. He says it is worst going up stairs and during jumping drills, settles within a day of rest, and has never woken him at night.

He has grown 9 cm in the past year. He has not had fevers, weight loss or night sweats, and the knee has never given way, locked or swollen. On examination he is tender over a prominent bony lump below the kneecap, the joint line is not tender, and there is no effusion. Extending the knee against resistance reproduces his pain, and hip rotation is full and painless on both sides.

data_table.Examination: Prominent tender tibial tubercle on the right, no joint effusion, no joint line tenderness, full painless internal rotation of both hips, no warmth or erythema
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for consideration of excision of the bony prominence
Request plain radiographs of the knee in two planes before starting any treatment
Inject corticosteroid around the tender prominence and allow return to sport
Request pelvic radiographs including frog lateral views of both hips today
Advise relative rest with a quadriceps stretching program and simple analgesia

subtopic_detail: responding to parental refusal of the newborn intramuscular prophylaxis without losing the protection entirely
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward asked to see the parents of a healthy boy born two hours ago at 39 weeks by normal vaginal birth, weighing 3480 g. They have declined the intramuscular vitamin K injection after reading that the dose is far larger than a newborn would receive naturally, and they say they will not consent to an injection under any circumstances.

They are articulate, have asked good questions, and say they will accept anything given by mouth. The mother took no medications in pregnancy, has no liver disease, and plans to breastfeed exclusively. The baby has fed once, has normal tone and colour, and his examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 140/min, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 98% in air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, blood pressure not indicated
data_table.Examination: Term male infant, normal tone and cry, no bruising or cephalohaematoma, red reflex present bilaterally, femoral pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What should you do next?

options.text: Notify child protection services because refusal places the infant at risk of harm
Advise the mother to take a daily supplement so that her breastmilk supplies enough
Offer the three dose oral regimen and document the discussion of the residual bleeding risk
Give the injection once the parents have left the room and record it in the notes
Accept the refusal and arrange close follow up with the child health nurse instead

subtopic_detail: deciding on removal versus observation for a swallowed metallic object using its position and appearance
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl brought in ninety minutes after her brother saw her put a coin from his money box into her mouth and swallow it. She coughed twice at the time and has been entirely well since, running around the waiting room and asking for food.

She is drooling no more than usual, is swallowing her own saliva, and has no stridor, wheeze or chest pain. Her chest and abdomen are unremarkable on examination. A single plain radiograph of the neck, chest and abdomen shows a uniform round metallic disc, about 20 mm across, lying below the left hemidiaphragm with no surrounding halo or step on either view.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Handling secretions normally, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, no subcutaneous emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Plain film shows a uniform round metallic disc 20 mm diameter in the left upper abdomen, no double ring or step off, no free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent endoscopic removal from the stomach within the next two hours
Refer for oesophagoscopy because a coin of this size lodges above the diaphragm
Give a stimulant laxative and keep her fasted until the object has been passed
Discharge her with advice to watch the stools and to return if pain or vomiting develops
Admit for observation with repeat radiography in four hours to confirm it is moving

subtopic_detail: timing of first exposure to a high risk food in an infant whose eczema places her in the highest risk group
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-month-old girl for her immunisations. Her mother mentions that she has had moderate eczema since eight weeks of age, currently controlled on a daily moisturiser and intermittent hydrocortisone 1 per cent ointment, and asks when it would be safe to give her peanut butter.

The infant has never eaten peanut or tree nuts and has never had a reaction to any food. She has had smooth cereal, pureed vegetables and yoghurt over the past three weeks without any problem. The mother has a sister with a peanut allergy and has been avoiding peanut herself while breastfeeding because she read that it would help. The infant is thriving, growth is tracking along the 50th centile, and her skin today shows mild dryness with no active flare.

data_table.Examination: Dry skin at the antecubital fossae with no excoriation or weeping, growth on the 50th centile for weight and length, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What advice should you give about introducing peanut?

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to peanut and introduce it only if the result is negative
Have the mother resume eating peanut so the infant is exposed through the breastmilk
Defer peanut until the eczema has been clear for three months and then introduce it
Give smooth peanut paste at home in the next week and continue it regularly thereafter
Refer to an immunologist for the first dose to be given under supervised observation

subtopic_detail: scaly scalp and flexural rash in a young infant where the absence of itch redirects the diagnosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10-week-old boy whose parents are distressed by thick yellowish scale that has built up over his scalp during the past month and has spread to his eyebrows and the creases of his neck. They have been told by relatives that it is eczema and that he needs a special formula.

He is exclusively breastfed, feeds well and has gained weight along the 60th centile since birth. He does not scratch, rub his head or cry when the areas are touched, and he sleeps through his night feeds. There is no family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever, and no blood or mucus in his stools. On examination the scale is greasy and adherent with mild underlying redness, there are salmon coloured patches in both axillae and the nappy flexures, and the skin elsewhere is soft with no excoriation, weeping or crusting.

data_table.Examination: Greasy adherent scale over the vertex, eyebrows and neck creases, salmon coloured patches in the axillae and nappy flexures with no satellite lesions, no excoriation, no petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly, weight on the 60th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and stop breastfeeding for a two week trial
Soften the scale with an emollient before washing, using a mild shampoo regularly
Refer urgently to dermatology for skin biopsy to exclude an infiltrative condition
Prescribe oral cefalexin because the thick adherent crust indicates bacterial infection
Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid to the scalp and the flexures twice daily

subtopic_detail: why a scaly scalp patch with broken hairs will not respond to the treatment used for body ringworm
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose mother has been applying a topical antifungal cream to a patch on his scalp for the past four weeks with no improvement. The patch has grown and a second smaller one has appeared behind his ear.

He is otherwise well, has no fever and no pain, and attends a school where two other children have had something similar. He has no eczema and no history of hair pulling. On examination there is a 4 cm scaly patch on the vertex with hairs broken off a few millimetres above the scalp surface, a further 1 cm patch behind the right ear, and two small mobile tender nodes at the back of his neck. There is no boggy swelling and no pustulation.

data_table.Examination: Two scaly scalp patches with hairs broken close to the surface, mild occipital lymphadenopathy, no boggy mass, no pustules, no scarring, nails normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid because the appearance suggests scalp psoriasis
Change to a stronger topical antifungal cream applied twice daily for eight weeks
Take hair and scale samples for fungal studies and begin oral griseofulvin
Prescribe oral cefalexin because the tender neck nodes indicate bacterial infection
Use an antifungal shampoo twice weekly and keep him home from school until it clears

subtopic_detail: treating an itchy infestation across a household where only one child has symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 2-year-old girl whose parents report three weeks of an itchy rash that is much worse at night and wakes her repeatedly. Her mother has begun to notice an itch on her own wrists over the past week.

The child attends family day care. She has had no fevers and is eating and playing normally. On examination there are excoriated papules on the trunk and thin wavy tracks in the web spaces of both hands and along the inner wrists, with a few papules on the soles. Her father and her 5-year-old brother have no symptoms at all. There is no weeping, crusting or surrounding cellulitis.

data_table.Examination: Linear tracks in finger web spaces and on the flexor wrists, excoriated papules on the trunk, papules on both soles, no honey coloured crusting, no fever
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the child alone and treat other family members only if they develop an itch
Prescribe oral ivermectin for the child as a single weight based dose
Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid to the itchy areas for two weeks
Treat every member of the household on the same day and repeat the application in one week
Prescribe oral cefalexin because the excoriated lesions are likely to be infected

subtopic_detail: bone deformity in a toddler where the dietary and sun exposure history points away from a physiological cause
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20-month-old boy whose mother is worried that his legs have become more bowed rather than less over the past six months, and that he is slow to walk any distance.

He was born at term and is still breastfed four times a day with small amounts of family food. The family covers up outdoors for cultural reasons and rarely spends time in direct sunlight. He has had no fractures and no bone pain that the family has noticed, and his bowels are regular with no diarrhoea or greasy stools. On examination he has symmetrical bowing of both tibiae, palpable widening at both wrists, and a row of small bony prominences along the costochondral junctions. His height has fallen from the 50th to the 10th centile over the past year while his weight has stayed on the 25th.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical tibial bowing, widened wrists, costochondral prominences, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, waddling gait, height dropping across centiles
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone
Send coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A as the first line test
Arrange a bone density scan to quantify the degree of bone loss
Start high dose oral vitamin D now and reassess the legs in three months
Request standing long leg radiographs to measure the tibiofemoral angle

subtopic_detail: resisting acid suppression in a thriving infant whose vomiting distresses the parents more than the child
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-month-old boy whose parents describe vomiting after almost every feed since about three weeks of age. They have been given a proton pump inhibitor prescription by an after hours service and want your view before starting it.

The vomiting is effortless, happens within twenty minutes of a feed, and is milk that looks unchanged. He does not arch, scream or refuse feeds, and he settles quickly afterwards. There is no blood or green colour in the vomit, no constipation and no fevers. He is formula fed, taking 180 mL every three hours, which the parents have been increasing because they assume he is bringing most of it back up. His weight has tracked steadily along the 75th centile since birth, and examination including the abdomen is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, blood pressure not indicated
data_table.Examination: Alert and settled, abdomen soft with no mass, anterior fontanelle normal, weight on the 75th centile tracking since birth, no dehydration
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula for a two week trial of dairy exclusion
Explain the natural history, reduce the feed volume per feed and do not start the medicine
Advise raising the head of the cot and putting him down to sleep on his left side
Request an abdominal ultrasound to assess the pylorus before changing anything
Start the proton pump inhibitor for a four week trial and review the response

subtopic_detail: night waking maintained by the conditions under which a toddler falls asleep
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the exhausted mother of a 2-year-old girl who wakes three or four times every night and will not resettle unless a parent lies on the floor beside her cot until she is asleep again. This has been the pattern for eight months and the mother is now falling asleep at work.

The child falls asleep at bedtime only with a parent lying next to her. She snores only with colds, has never been seen to stop breathing, and has no mouth breathing or daytime sleepiness. She naps once for an hour in the early afternoon, is dry overnight, has no pain, and her tonsils are not enlarged. Growth and development are normal and her behaviour during the day is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils small, no adenoidal facies, nasal airway clear, ears normal, growth and development appropriate for age
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the mother that this resolves with age and review again in six months
