Teach a graduated settling approach so she learns to fall asleep without a parent present
Prescribe melatonin at bedtime for four weeks to consolidate the overnight sleep
Refer for overnight sleep study to assess for obstructive sleep apnoea
Advise dropping the daytime nap so that she builds more sleep pressure by bedtime

subtopic_detail: how background rheumatic fever risk changes the threshold for treating a sore throat before the swab returns
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote clinic in the Northern Territory seeing a 9-year-old Aboriginal boy with two days of sore throat and fever. His community has a high rate of acute rheumatic fever and two children from his school were diagnosed with it last year.

He has no cough and no runny nose. He is drinking, has no drooling, no trismus and no neck swelling, and his voice is normal. On examination his tonsils are enlarged and red with exudate on the left, and there are two tender anterior cervical nodes. He has no rash and no joint pain or swelling, and there is no history of a previous episode of rheumatic fever. A throat swab has been taken and the laboratory is four days away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Enlarged erythematous tonsils with left sided exudate, two tender anterior cervical nodes, no rash, no murmur, joints normal, hydration adequate
data_table.Investigations: Throat swab taken and sent, no result available for four days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and treat the fever, starting treatment only if the swab is positive
Give a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin as secondary prophylaxis
Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for seven days to cover resistant organisms
Prescribe oral azithromycin for three days to improve the chance of completing treatment
Start oral phenoxymethylpenicillin now for ten days without waiting for the swab result

subtopic_detail: Sticky eyes with lid swelling first appearing on day ten of life in a baby born vaginally at term
stem:
A 10-day-old baby girl is brought to your general practice because both her eyes have been gluey since yesterday and her lids look puffy. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and her mother had no antenatal screening swabs taken.

She is feeding well and gaining weight. Her mother mentions that she has been a little snuffly but has no cough. On examination the conjunctivae are injected with a copious sticky discharge and moderate lid oedema, and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining. You take a swab for nucleic acid testing before starting treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure 72/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctival injection with copious sticky discharge, moderate lid oedema, clear corneas on fluorescein staining, red reflex present bilaterally
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.6 kg, tracking along the birth centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin for the baby and referral of both parents for testing and treatment
Topical chloramphenicol eye drops for the baby with review arranged in forty eight hours
Saline eye toilet and reassurance, with review only if the discharge has not settled
Admit for intravenous cefotaxime and hourly saline irrigation of both eyes
Oral aciclovir for the baby with urgent ophthalmology review the same day

subtopic_detail: Oral iron dose and duration for a toddler drinking large volumes of cow milk with microcytic anaemia
stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to your clinic because he is pale and his parents feel he tires easily at playgroup. He drinks about a litre and a half of cow milk each day and eats very little solid food. He was born at term and his development is age appropriate.

His parents are both well and there is no family history of anaemia or blood disorders. His examination is unremarkable apart from pallor, with no organomegaly and no dysmorphic features. His blood film is reported as showing hypochromic microcytic red cells without target cells or basophilic stippling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 64 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (20-200), C-reactive protein within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Pallor of conjunctivae and palmar creases, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily ceased as soon as the haemoglobin has returned to normal
Dietary modification alone with reduced milk intake and review of the blood count in three months
Intravenous iron infusion arranged as a day case with dietary advice given at the same visit
Packed red cell transfusion followed by oral iron and outpatient haematology review
Elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises

subtopic_detail: Alarm versus desmopressin choice for a nine year old with bedwetting only and a normal daytime pattern
stem:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to your practice because he still wets the bed most nights, which is now stopping him accepting invitations to sleep at friends' houses. He has never had a sustained period of dry nights.

He passes urine four to five times during the day with no urgency, no daytime wetting and no pain. He opens his bowels daily without straining. His examination including abdominal, genital, spinal and lower limb neurological assessment is normal, and his urine dipstick and blood glucose are normal. His parents are motivated and ask what will give him the best chance of lasting dryness, mentioning that a school camp is scheduled in eight months.

data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal, genital and spinal examination, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose protein blood and leucocytes, random blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: Enuresis alarm used consistently every night, with review of progress at four weeks
Oral desmopressin taken each night, with review of progress at four weeks
Fluid restriction after the evening meal with a scheduled lift to the toilet overnight
Oral oxybutynin at night with a bladder diary kept over the following four weeks
Referral for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic studies before any treatment is started

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice and timing for a newborn girl with a family history of hip problems and a stable clinical examination
stem:
You review a 3-day-old girl on the postnatal ward before discharge. She was born at term in a cephalic presentation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth, and she is feeding and behaving normally.

Her mother mentions that her own sister was in a harness as a baby for a hip problem. On your examination the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative, hip abduction is full and symmetrical, and leg lengths and skin creases are equal. The rest of the newborn examination including the spine is normal. Her mother asks whether anything further needs to be arranged.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres negative bilaterally, full symmetrical hip abduction, equal leg lengths and symmetrical skin creases, normal spine
data_table.Birth history: Term cephalic vaginal birth, birth weight 3.4 kg, uncomplicated pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound before discharge from the postnatal ward this week
Arrange a hip ultrasound at six weeks of age and review her with the result
Arrange a pelvic radiograph at six weeks of age and review her with the result
Provide double nappy padding and arrange clinical review at six weeks of age
Give routine discharge advice with no imaging and rely on child health checks

subtopic_detail: Spiral tibial fracture in a newly walking toddler with a witnessed low fall and no other injuries
stem:
A 16-month-old boy is brought to your emergency department after his father saw him trip on the edge of a rug while running and twist as he fell onto carpet. He has refused to bear weight on the right leg since.

He began walking independently at 12 months. He is consoled easily and his father's account has been consistent each time it has been taken. On examination there is mild swelling over the lower right shin with tenderness, no bruising anywhere on his body, and full painless movement at the knee, hip and ankle. His skin, frenulum, ears and scalp are normal, and his growth and development are age appropriate. The radiograph shows an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft with an intact fibula.

data_table.Examination: Mild swelling and tenderness over the distal right tibia, no bruising or other skin injury, normal frenulum ears and scalp, full painless movement of knee hip and ankle
data_table.Imaging: Undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal right tibial shaft with an intact fibula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Above knee cast with a child protection notification made before the child leaves
Admit for a skeletal survey and ophthalmology review before any definitive fracture treatment
Above knee cast with routine fracture clinic review, without a child protection notification
Below knee backslab with fracture clinic review and blood tests for bone fragility
Simple analgesia with weight bearing as tolerated and general practitioner review in one week

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and poor feeding in a two week old with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia after a normal newborn check
stem:
A 14-day-old baby is brought to your emergency department with three days of vomiting after feeds and increasing sleepiness. The parents describe the vomit as milky and not green, and say the baby has been taking progressively less at each feed.

The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and the newborn examination was documented as normal. Weight today is 8 per cent below birth weight. On examination the baby is lethargic with dry mucous membranes and a capillary refill of three seconds, the abdomen is soft with no palpable mass, and the external genitalia appear unremarkable. Venous gas and electrolytes are taken while intravenous access is obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 54/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill three seconds, soft abdomen with no palpable mass, unremarkable external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 7.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0), venous pH 7.24 (7.32-7.42), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with correction of the alkalosis and surgical referral
Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with broad spectrum antibiotics after blood and urine cultures
Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with hydrocortisone after a sample is taken for hormone assay
Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with hypertonic saline to raise the sodium concentration rapidly
Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with a trial of a hydrolysed formula and dietitian review

subtopic_detail: Child with stridor that returns forty minutes after nebulised adrenaline with a rising fever and toxic appearance
stem:
A 3-year-old girl was brought to your emergency department with a barking cough and stridor at rest that began two days after a runny nose. She received oral dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline, and her stridor settled well over the following twenty minutes.

Forty minutes later you are called back because the stridor has returned and is now present at rest with moderate chest wall recession. She looks unwell and is not interested in her parents or the toys, and her temperature has climbed since arrival. She is sitting upright but is drooling only minimally and her voice is hoarse rather than muffled. She is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168/min, blood pressure 92/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest with moderate intercostal and subcostal recession, hoarse voice, toxic appearance with reduced interaction, minimal drooling
data_table.Treatment so far: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 given on arrival

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline and continue observation for a further two hours
Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone and admit to the general paediatric ward
Arrange a lateral neck radiograph to assess the airway before involving other teams
Give intravenous dexamethasone and commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy
Urgent anaesthetic and ENT review for airway inspection, with intravenous flucloxacillin

subtopic_detail: Persistent night waking thigh pain in an adolescent with a lamellated periosteal reaction on plain film
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to your clinic with four months of pain above his right knee that has been attributed to growing pains and then to a football injury. The pain now wakes him at night several times a week and is no longer relieved by paracetamol.

He has lost 3 kg over that period without dieting. His mother has noticed a firm fullness over the lower thigh in the past three weeks. On examination there is a firm, deep, tender swelling over the distal femur with overlying warmth, and the knee joint itself has a full painless range of movement. He is afebrile and his inflammatory markers are only mildly raised. The radiograph shows a poorly defined lesion of the distal femoral metaphysis with a lamellated periosteal reaction and cortical destruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Firm deep tender swelling over the distal right femur with overlying warmth, full painless knee range of movement, no regional lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (<5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (60-450)
data_table.Imaging: Poorly defined distal femoral metaphyseal lesion with lamellated periosteal reaction and cortical destruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an open biopsy locally and refer once the histological diagnosis is available
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange bone scintigraphy to assess the lesion
Arrange outpatient magnetic resonance imaging and review him with the result in six weeks
Prescribe a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and review him in four weeks for reassessment
Refer to a specialist bone tumour unit for staging before any biopsy is undertaken

subtopic_detail: Jaundice still present at three weeks of age in a breastfed baby whose stools have become pale
stem:
A 23-day-old breastfed baby girl is brought to your practice because she still looks yellow. Her mother was told at the maternity hospital that breastfed babies often stay a little jaundiced and not to worry.

She is feeding well and has regained her birth weight, and she is alert and active. Her mother mentions in passing that her nappies have been staining a dark colour and that her stools have turned a pale putty colour over the last week. Examination confirms jaundice to the abdomen with a soft abdomen and a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Her newborn screening test was normal.

data_table.Examination: Jaundice visible to the abdomen, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable, alert and well perfused
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.9 kg, regained birth weight by day 12 and tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother that breast milk jaundice is common and review the baby in one month
Measure the conjugated bilirubin fraction urgently on a sample taken today
Measure the total serum bilirubin alone and plot the value on the phototherapy chart
Advise interrupting breastfeeding for 48 hours and reassess the degree of jaundice afterwards
Arrange a direct antiglobulin test and blood group to investigate ongoing haemolysis

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first retinopathy of prematurity examination in a preterm infant weaned to room air by day three
stem:
You are the registrar on the neonatal unit preparing a preterm girl for her discharge planning meeting. She is feeding fully from the breast in an open cot and has gained weight steadily over the past fortnight, with no apnoeic or desaturation episodes recorded in that time.

Her cranial ultrasound and newborn hearing screen were both normal, and she has not needed any supplemental oxygen since her first two days of life. Her mother asks which tests still need to be arranged before they go home.

data_table.Current age: 28 days, corrected age 33 weeks and 4 days
data_table.Respiratory support: Continuous positive airway pressure for 48 hours, in room air since day three

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to retinal examination?

options.text: Defer the first examination until she reaches 36 weeks corrected gestational age
Examine only if she needs supplemental oxygen again before she is discharged
Arrange the first retinal examination now, at four weeks after her birth
Arrange one retinal examination on the day her discharge is planned
Omit retinal examination because her birthweight was above one kilogram

subtopic_detail: Febrile encephalopathy with transaminitis in the second week of life without any vesicular rash
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 9-day-old boy who has been feeding poorly since yesterday and is now difficult to rouse. During your assessment he has a two minute focal seizure affecting the right arm.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and his mother has never had any genital lesions or blistering rash. His skin is examined carefully under good light and shows no vesicles, and his anterior fontanelle is soft. Blood cultures and a lumbar puncture are taken, and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and cefotaxime are commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 58/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes, no rash or vesicles, soft fontanelle, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Blood results: Alanine aminotransferase 640 U/L (less than 45), platelets 74 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count within normal limits
data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 68 x10^6/L with lymphocyte predominance, protein 1.4 g/L (0.2-0.8), glucose within normal limits, Gram stain negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his management?

options.text: Continue the intravenous antibiotics alone and review when the cultures return
Add intravenous ganciclovir and arrange a urine sample for viral culture
Add intravenous dexamethasone before the next dose of antibiotic is given
Add high dose intravenous aciclovir now and send samples for viral testing
Withhold antiviral therapy until the cerebrospinal fluid result is available

subtopic_detail: Operative referral timing once a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale stools is established at seven weeks
stem:
A 7-week-old girl is reviewed in your general practice because she is still yellow. She was born at term, is exclusively breastfed and is gaining weight along her birth centile.

Her mother has photographed several nappies over the past fortnight, and the stools in them are a pale putty colour while the wet nappies look dark. The split bilirubin you requested last week has returned, and her newborn screening test and thyroid function were both normal. She is alert and feeding well, and there is no bruising.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, soft abdomen with a liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no bruising
data_table.Bilirubin: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 92 micromol/L
data_table.Other results: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 45), international normalised ratio within normal limits, newborn screening and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the split bilirubin in two weeks and refer only if it remains elevated
Refer today to a paediatric liver unit for cholangiogram and possible Kasai
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and arrange outpatient review in three weeks
Arrange a sweat test and metabolic screen before making any surgical referral
Reassure that breast milk jaundice resolves and review again at three months

subtopic_detail: Sequencing confirmatory testing after strongly positive coeliac serology in a child still eating gluten
stem:
A 6-year-old girl is reviewed in your general practice after her serology returned. She was tested because her weight has drifted from the 50th to the 10th centile over eighteen months and she complains of a sore tummy and feeling puffy after meals.

Her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease and has already bought gluten free products, asking whether she should start them today. The girl has continued her usual diet up to this appointment. Her abdomen is soft with no organomegaly and her iron studies show mild deficiency.

data_table.Growth: Weight tracking down from the 50th to the 10th centile over eighteen months, height on the 25th centile
data_table.Serology: Tissue transglutaminase IgA strongly positive at more than ten times the upper limit of normal, total IgA within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Keep gluten in her diet and refer for endoscopic small bowel biopsy
Start a gluten free diet now and review her symptoms in six weeks
Repeat the antibody level after four weeks of a gluten free diet
Arrange HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing to confirm the diagnosis before referral
Reassure the family and repeat her growth measurements in six months

subtopic_detail: Preoperative biochemical correction before pyloromyotomy in an infant with hypochloraemic alkalosis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 5-week-old boy whose ultrasound has just been reported. His mother says he brings the whole feed back forcefully, sometimes clearing the edge of the change table, and then wants to feed again straight away.

He has lost 200 g since his two week check and his nappies have been drier than usual for three days. He is alert with a sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. The surgical registrar telephones to say a theatre slot is free this evening and asks whether to take him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 172/min, blood pressure 74/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Ultrasound: Pyloric muscle thickness 4.6 mm, channel length 19 mm
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer to theatre now because the obstruction needs urgent surgical relief
Give a bolus of five per cent dextrose and book theatre for this evening
Rehydrate with sodium chloride and added potassium until the biochemistry corrects
Pass a nasogastric tube and start intravenous antibiotics before theatre
Start oral rehydration solution and recheck the electrolytes in twelve hours

subtopic_detail: Choosing urate lowering prophylaxis for tumour lysis risk when glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is known
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 6-year-old boy with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. He is alert and well perfused, and induction chemotherapy is planned to start tomorrow morning.

His presenting blood film and counts show a heavy circulating blast burden, and his biochemistry already shows a raised urate before any treatment. He was investigated for prolonged jaundice as a newborn and was found then to have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, confirmed on enzyme assay after the jaundice settled. The haematology consultant asks you to write up his tumour lysis prophylaxis.

data_table.Full blood count: White cell count 184 x10^9/L with 88 per cent blasts, haemoglobin 76 g/L (115-135), platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Biochemistry: Urate 0.58 mmol/L (0.12-0.32), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), phosphate 1.9 mmol/L (1.0-1.8), creatinine 74 micromol/L (30-60)
data_table.Past history: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency confirmed on enzyme assay in infancy

lead_in: Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Give rasburicase now because the urate and white cell count are both high
Give rasburicase at half the usual dose with close monitoring of haemoglobin
Withhold urate lowering therapy and rely on intravenous hydration alone
Start urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and give rasburicase
Start allopurinol with generous intravenous hydration and monitor the urate

subtopic_detail: Deciding on prophylactic fixation of the unaffected hip when a slip occurs with an underlying endocrinopathy
stem:
You are the registrar in the orthopaedic clinic seeing an 11-year-old boy referred with three weeks of left knee ache and a limp that his mother says has slowly worsened. There was no injury.

He was diagnosed with hypothyroidism two years ago and takes thyroxine, though his mother admits doses are often missed. On examination the left leg lies in slight external rotation and the hip rolls outwards as you flex it. Plain films of both hips are reviewed with the consultant, who confirms a mild stable slip on the left and asks you to consent the family for surgery.

data_table.Examination: Left leg externally rotated, obligate external rotation on hip flexion, able to weight bear with a limp
data_table.Growth: Weight above the 97th centile, height on the 25th centile
data_table.Imaging: Mild stable slip of the left capital femoral epiphysis, right epiphysis not displaced with an open physis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative plan?

options.text: Pin the affected hip alone and review the other hip clinically each year
Pin the affected hip and pin the opposite hip during the same anaesthetic
Pin the affected hip and arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the other hip
Attempt closed reduction of the slip before any internal fixation is done
Treat in traction without weight bearing and delay any operative fixation

subtopic_detail: Antiviral decision for a symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection confirmed within the first three weeks
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing a 12-day-old girl on the postnatal ward whose newborn hearing screen failed on both sides and was not passed on repeat.

She was born at term but was small, and the midwives noted a scattered rash of pinpoint red spots on her trunk that does not blanch. Her head circumference sits well below her weight centile. A urine sample collected on day 10 has returned positive for cytomegalovirus on nucleic acid testing, and her cranial ultrasound shows scattered calcification. Her mother recalls a flu like illness in the second trimester.

data_table.Growth: Birthweight below the 3rd centile, head circumference below the 3rd centile
data_table.Examination: Non blanching petechial rash over the trunk, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Urine cytomegalovirus nucleic acid test positive on day 10, alanine aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 45), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400), cranial ultrasound shows periventricular calcification
data_table.Hearing: Automated auditory brainstem response failed bilaterally on initial and repeat screening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with audiology follow up alone because antiviral therapy has no benefit
Give intravenous ganciclovir for six weeks and then stop all antiviral therapy
Start oral valganciclovir only if the hearing loss progresses over the first year
Start oral valganciclovir now and continue it for six months with monitoring
Give cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin as a single dose and monitor her hearing

subtopic_detail: First line agent for epileptic spasms when hypopigmented macules point to an underlying neurocutaneous disorder
stem:
A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents, who have filmed what they describe as him suddenly bending forward and throwing his arms out, over and over, in runs of twenty or so just after he wakes. He cries afterwards.

His mother says he used to reach for toys and babble but has stopped doing both over the past month. Under the Wood lamp you find four pale oval patches on his trunk and thigh. His neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable and his head circumference is on the 50th centile. An urgent electroencephalogram is reported as showing a chaotic high amplitude pattern with multifocal spikes.

data_table.Examination: Four hypopigmented oval macules on the trunk and thigh, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Development: Loss of previously acquired reaching and babbling over the past month
data_table.Electroencephalogram: Chaotic high amplitude background with multifocal spikes

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start vigabatrin as the initial agent and arrange specialist follow up
Start high dose oral prednisolone as the initial agent and review shortly
Start sodium valproate and arrange outpatient neurology review in two weeks
Start levetiracetam and repeat the electroencephalogram in four weeks
Observe without treatment because these episodes often settle spontaneously

subtopic_detail: Avoiding percutaneous sampling of a large intrarenal mass in a preschool child before definitive surgery
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3-year-old girl whose mother felt a firm lump in her left tummy while bathing her two days ago. The girl has been well in herself, eating normally and playing as usual, with no fevers, bone pain or weight loss.

On examination there is a smooth firm mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline and moves little with respiration. Her blood pressure is above the 95th centile for age and height, and urinalysis shows blood without protein. Cross sectional imaging has been reported and the surgical team has been contacted. Her catecholamine metabolites are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Smooth firm left flank mass not crossing the midline, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows blood without protein, urinary catecholamine metabolites within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Large mass arising within the left kidney with a claw of surrounding renal parenchyma, no tumour thrombus in the renal vein or inferior vena cava, no pulmonary lesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Percutaneous core biopsy of the mass to establish the histological diagnosis
Percutaneous biopsy followed by chemotherapy before any surgical resection
Refer for primary nephrectomy without a preoperative percutaneous biopsy
Start chemotherapy based on imaging alone and defer any surgical referral
Observe with repeat imaging in six weeks before deciding on any intervention

subtopic_detail: Timing of corticosteroid initiation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy while motor function has plateaued
stem:
You are the registrar in the neuromuscular clinic reviewing a 5-year-old boy whose genetic testing last year confirmed a deletion in the dystrophin gene. His parents have read about steroids and ask whether he should be on them.

His mother says he still runs and manages the playground but he pushes on his thighs to stand up from the floor and asks to be carried on longer walks. Serial timed testing in the clinic shows his rise from the floor and ten metre walk times have been unchanged over the last three visits, having improved steadily before that. His cardiac and respiratory assessments are within normal limits and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Examination: Calf hypertrophy, positive Gowers manoeuvre, proximal weakness of the hip girdle
data_table.Functional testing: Time to rise from the floor and ten metre walk time unchanged across three consecutive visits
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram and spirometry within normal limits, dystrophin gene deletion confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about corticosteroid therapy?

options.text: Defer corticosteroids until he loses the ability to walk independently
Start corticosteroids only once his forced vital capacity begins to fall
Avoid corticosteroids because the adverse effects outweigh any benefit
Start corticosteroids at the time of genetic diagnosis regardless of function
Start daily corticosteroids now while his motor function has plateaued

subtopic_detail: Post exposure prophylaxis choice for an unimmunised infant four days after a measles contact
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by the parents of a 7-month-old boy. Four days ago they sat in a waiting room with a child who has since been confirmed as having measles, and the public health unit has contacted them as part of contact tracing.

Their son has had his scheduled immunisations for his age but has not yet had a measles containing vaccine. He is entirely well today with no fever, rash, cough or red eyes, and he is feeding and behaving normally. His mother was born overseas and does not know whether she had measles or was ever vaccinated. He has no immune deficiency and takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no conjunctivitis, no coryza, no buccal lesions, chest clear
data_table.Exposure: Shared indoor waiting room with a confirmed case four days ago
data_table.Immunisation status: Age-appropriate schedule complete, no measles containing vaccine given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post exposure management?

options.text: Give normal human immunoglobulin and notify the public health unit
Give measles mumps rubella vaccine now as post exposure prophylaxis
Reassure the family that maternal antibody will protect him at this age
Start oral vitamin A and review only if a rash or fever develops
Arrange serology now and decide on prophylaxis once it has returned
